cards.mean: to stay up late into the night to work or study
cards.lit: to drive the night train: keep going through the hours when everyone else is asleep

use.how: A verb-object phrase that can be split: 开夜车, 开了几个夜车, 又开夜车. Said of working or studying late to meet a deadline, never of partying.

near.diff: 熬夜 is any staying up late, for any reason; 开夜车 is staying up specifically to get work or study done.
夜猫子 is a noun for a person who habitually stays up late; 开夜车 is a verb phrase for one late night of work.

cards.cue: Your report is due at nine tomorrow morning and you have not started it, so you will be at your desk until three a.m. What are you doing tonight?

ctx.s: 明天就考试了，我今天晚上得{开夜车}了。
ctx.en: The exam is tomorrow, so I'll have to stay up late studying tonight.

ctx.s: 你眼睛这么红，昨天又{开夜车}了吧？
ctx.en: Your eyes are so red, you were up working late again last night, weren't you?

ctx.s: 为了赶这个项目，他连着三天{开夜车}。
ctx.en: To get this project done in time, he worked late into the night three days running.

ctx.s: 论文截止前一周，宿舍里几乎人人都在{开夜车}。
ctx.en: In the week before the thesis deadline, almost everyone in the dorm was studying late into the night.

ctx.s: 妈妈劝他：“别老{开夜车}，身体要紧。”
ctx.en: His mum urged him: "Don't keep working late into the night, your health comes first."

ctx.s: 上周我{开了好几个夜车}，总算把报告写完了。
ctx.en: Last week I stayed up late working several nights and finally finished the report.

bad.s: 他是个{开夜车}，每天都很晚才睡。
bad.en: (meant: he's a night owl who always goes to bed late)
bad.why: It is a verb phrase for working late on a task, not a noun for a person; a habitual late sleeper is a ye mao zi (night owl).

bad.s: 昨晚我们去酒吧{开夜车}，一直玩到半夜。
bad.en: (meant: last night we went to a bar and partied until midnight)
bad.why: It means staying up to work or study; staying out late to have fun is not this.

cards.mean: to fire someone from their job
cards.lit: to stir-fry squid: the squid pieces curl up into rolls in the hot pan

story.text: The expression comes from Cantonese. In the past a worker who was dismissed rolled up his bedding and left, so being sacked was called rolling up one's bedding. Squid pieces curl into tight rolls when stir-fried, so a fried squid came to stand for the rolled-up bedding of a dismissed worker. The phrase spread from Guangdong and Hong Kong to the rest of China.

use.how: A verb-object phrase, mostly passive (被炒鱿鱼) or split around the person: 炒了他的鱿鱼. Informal; official texts use 开除 or 解聘.

near.diff: 开除 is the formal word and also covers expelling a student or a member; 炒鱿鱼 is casual and only about losing a job.
跳槽 is leaving by choice for another employer; 炒鱿鱼 is being sent away by the employer.

cards.cue: Your friend kept coming in late, and yesterday the manager told him to clear his desk and not come back. What happened to him?

ctx.s: 他上班老迟到，结果被老板{炒鱿鱼}了。
ctx.en: He was always late for work, and in the end the boss fired him.

ctx.s: 你再这样偷懒，小心被{炒鱿鱼}！
ctx.en: If you keep slacking off like this, watch out or you'll get the sack!

ctx.s: 经理一气之下，当场{炒了他的鱿鱼}。
ctx.en: In a fit of anger, the manager fired him on the spot.

ctx.s: 听说公司要裁员，大家都怕自己被{炒鱿鱼}。
ctx.en: Word is the company is cutting staff, and everyone is afraid of being let go.

ctx.s: 与其等着被{炒鱿鱼}，不如自己先辞职。
ctx.en: Rather than wait to be fired, you'd better resign first.

ctx.s: 这个老板脾气很怪，一个月就{炒了三个员工的鱿鱼}。
ctx.en: This boss has a strange temper; he fired three employees in a single month.

bad.s: 学校把那个考试作弊的学生{炒鱿鱼}了。
bad.en: (meant: the school expelled the student who cheated in the exam)
bad.why: It is only about losing a job. Expelling a student is kai chu.

bad.s: 公司公告：经研究决定，对张某予以{炒鱿鱼}处理。
bad.en: (meant: company notice: after review, it has been decided to dismiss Zhang)
bad.why: It is slang and cannot appear in an official notice; a formal text uses kai chu or jie pin (dismiss).

cards.mean: to flatter someone in power to win their favour
cards.lit: to pat a horse on the rump

use.how: A verb-object phrase; the person flattered goes in the middle: 拍领导的马屁, 别拍我马屁. Said disapprovingly of insincere praise aimed upward.

near.diff: 讨好 is trying to please anyone, a child or a friend included, by any means; 拍马屁 is crude flattery of someone above you.
吹牛 is boasting about yourself; 拍马屁 is praising someone else to get something from them.

cards.cue: A new employee laughs loudly at every joke the boss makes and praises his tie every morning, hoping for a promotion. What is he doing?

ctx.s: 他就会{拍马屁}，真本事一点儿也没有。
ctx.en: All he's good at is sucking up; he has no real ability at all.

ctx.s: 你别{拍我马屁}了，有什么事直说吧。
ctx.en: Stop buttering me up. If you want something, just say it.

ctx.s: 我说的是真心话，不是{拍马屁}。
ctx.en: I really mean it, I'm not just flattering you.

ctx.s: 他天天{拍经理的马屁}，就是想早点升职。
ctx.en: He sucks up to the manager every day just so he can get promoted sooner.

ctx.s: 整天夸领导、{拍马屁}，在我们公司是升不了职的。
ctx.en: Praising the boss all day and sucking up won't get you promoted at our company.

ctx.s: 会上几个人轮流{拍领导的马屁}，谁也不提问题。
ctx.en: At the meeting several people took turns flattering the boss, and nobody raised any problems.

bad.s: 老师今天{拍了我的马屁}，说我的作文写得很好。
bad.en: (meant: today the teacher praised me, saying my essay was very good)
bad.why: It is self-serving flattery of someone more powerful, said with contempt; a teacher's honest praise is biao yang.

bad.s: 他很会{拍马屁}领导，所以升得很快。
bad.en: (meant: he is good at flattering the boss, so he rose quickly)
bad.why: It takes no object after it; the person goes inside the phrase: pai lingdao de mapi.

cards.mean: to brag or talk big about oneself
cards.lit: to blow up an ox: puff air into an oxhide until it swells (short for chui niu pi)

use.how: A verb-object phrase with no object of its own; it can be split: 吹什么牛, 吹了一晚上的牛. Often teasing among friends: 别吹牛了。

near.diff: 拍马屁 is praising someone powerful to win favour; 吹牛 is exaggerating your own abilities or deeds.
打包票 is guaranteeing a result, which may be sincere; 吹牛 is boastful talk that others doubt.

cards.cue: Your friend claims he once beat a national table-tennis champion and can drink ten beers without feeling a thing. What is he doing?

ctx.s: 别{吹牛}了，你哪会说五种语言？
ctx.en: Stop bragging. Since when can you speak five languages?

ctx.s: 我不是{吹牛}，这道菜我做得比饭店还好吃。
ctx.en: I'm not boasting, but I make this dish better than any restaurant.

ctx.s: 他喝了点儿酒就开始{吹牛}，说自己认识很多明星。
ctx.en: After a few drinks he starts talking big, saying he knows lots of celebrities.

ctx.s: 你{吹什么牛}啊，上次比赛你不是输了吗？
ctx.en: What are you bragging about? Didn't you lose the last match?

ctx.s: 几个老同学坐在一起，{吹了一晚上的牛}。
ctx.en: A few old classmates sat together and spent the whole evening talking big.

ctx.s: 他在网上总爱{吹牛}，其实生活很普通。
ctx.en: Online he loves to brag, but in fact his life is very ordinary.

bad.s: 你考了第一名，太{吹牛}了！
bad.en: (meant: you came first, that's awesome!)
bad.why: 'Awesome' is tai niu le. This idiom is a verb meaning to brag and cannot be used as an adjective of praise.

bad.s: 他总是{吹牛}老板，说老板特别英明。
bad.en: (meant: he always flatters the boss, saying how wise he is)
bad.why: It is boasting about oneself and takes no person as object; flattering the boss is pai mapi.

cards.mean: to get something done through connections, not proper channels
cards.lit: to go in by the back door instead of the front entrance

use.how: A verb-object phrase, often after 靠 or 通过, or split: 走了他舅舅的后门, 走个后门. Said of jobs, school places, permits or tickets gained unfairly.

near.diff: 开绿灯 is what the person in charge does in letting something through; 走后门 is what the person seeking the favour does.
拉关系 is building up useful connections; 走后门 is actually using them to get around the rules.

cards.cue: The hospital waiting list is three months long, but your neighbour's cousin knows the director and got an appointment for tomorrow. How did he get it?

ctx.s: 听说他的工作是{走后门}找到的。
ctx.en: I heard he got his job through connections.

ctx.s: 这件事按规定办，谁也别想{走后门}。
ctx.en: This will be handled by the rules; nobody should expect to pull strings.

ctx.s: 他{走了舅舅的后门}，才进了这家银行。
ctx.en: It was only through his uncle's connections that he got into this bank.

ctx.s: 你在医院有熟人吗？能不能帮我{走个后门}？
ctx.en: Do you know anyone at the hospital? Could you pull a few strings for me?

ctx.s: 我们要凭考试成绩进名校，不能靠{走后门}。
ctx.en: We should get into a top school on our exam results, not through connections.

ctx.s: 招聘改成公开考试以后，想{走后门}的人少多了。
ctx.en: Since hiring switched to open exams, far fewer people try to get in through the back door.

bad.s: 他靠自己的努力{走后门}，终于考上了大学。
bad.en: (meant: through his own hard work he finally got into university)
bad.why: It means bypassing the rules through connections; it is never earned by effort and is never praise.

bad.s: 我们公司上个月{走后门}了一个大客户。
bad.en: (meant: last month our company landed a big client through networking)
bad.why: It cannot take an object, and it implies getting around rules or queues, not ordinary business networking.

cards.mean: to stand someone up after making plans with them
cards.lit: to let the pigeons go

use.how: A verb-object phrase; the person let down goes in the middle (放我鸽子, 放了他的鸽子) or it is passive (被放鸽子). Said of failing to turn up as agreed.

near.diff: 爽约 is the neutral, more written word for breaking an appointment; 放鸽子 is casual and carries the speaker's annoyance.

cards.cue: You booked a table for two at seven and waited an hour, but your friend never showed up and never called. What did he do to you?

ctx.s: 说好六点见面，他又{放我鸽子}了。
ctx.en: We agreed to meet at six, and he stood me up again.

ctx.s: 你明天可一定要来，别{放我鸽子}啊！
ctx.en: You really must come tomorrow, don't stand me up!

ctx.s: 我被客户{放了鸽子}，在咖啡馆白等了一个小时。
ctx.en: The client stood me up, and I waited in the café for an hour for nothing.

ctx.s: 他答应来参加聚会，结果{放了大家的鸽子}。
ctx.en: He promised to come to the party, but in the end he let everyone down and didn't show.

ctx.s: 这已经是她第三次{放鸽子}了，我再也不信她了。
ctx.en: That's the third time she's failed to show up; I'll never believe her again.

ctx.s: 那位歌手临时取消演出，{放了几万名观众的鸽子}。
ctx.en: The singer cancelled the concert at the last minute, leaving tens of thousands of fans in the lurch.

bad.s: 她{放了我的鸽子}，跟我分手了。
bad.en: (meant: she dumped me and broke up with me)
bad.why: It means failing to turn up for an arranged meeting, not ending a relationship; being dumped is bei shuai le.

bad.s: 昨天我{放鸽子}了他，现在很后悔。
bad.en: (meant: yesterday I stood him up, and now I regret it)
bad.why: The person cannot follow the phrase; it goes inside it: fang le ta de gezi, or fang ta gezi.

cards.mean: to feel jealous over a romantic partner
cards.lit: to eat vinegar: the sour taste of jealousy

story.text: The story usually told to explain it: Emperor Taizong of Tang wanted to give his chancellor Fang Xuanling some concubines, but Fang's wife would not allow it. The emperor offered her a choice between accepting them and drinking a cup of poison. She drank the cup at once, and it turned out to hold only vinegar. The emperor gave up, and jealousy came to be called eating vinegar.
story.source: a popular tale about the Tang chancellor Fang Xuanling and his wife

use.how: A verb-object phrase: 吃醋, 爱吃醋, 吃谁的醋, 吃什么醋. Said, often teasingly, of jealousy within a couple or a romance.

near.diff: 眼红 is envy of what others have, such as money or success; 吃醋 is jealousy about someone you love paying attention to another.
嫉妒 is the general word for jealousy or envy of any kind; 吃醋 is the light, colloquial word for romantic jealousy.

cards.cue: Your girlfriend frowns every time a female colleague texts you and keeps asking who she is. What is going on with her?

ctx.s: 你是不是在{吃醋}？怎么不说话了？
ctx.en: Are you jealous? Why have you gone quiet?

ctx.s: 我只是跟女同事说了几句话，你{吃什么醋}啊？
ctx.en: I only said a few words to a female colleague. What are you jealous about?

ctx.s: 他女朋友很爱{吃醋}，不让他跟别的女生聊天。
ctx.en: His girlfriend gets jealous easily and won't let him chat with other girls.

ctx.s: 看到男朋友给别的女生点赞，她有点儿{吃醋}了。
ctx.en: Seeing her boyfriend like another girl's posts, she got a little jealous.

ctx.s: 别{吃他的醋}了，他只是我的老同学。
ctx.en: Don't be jealous of him, he's just an old classmate of mine.

ctx.s: 丈夫跟前女友吃了顿饭，她{吃了好几天的醋}。
ctx.en: Her husband had a meal with his ex-girlfriend, and she was jealous for days.

bad.s: 看到邻居买了新车，我很{吃醋}。
bad.en: (meant: seeing the neighbours buy a new car, I was very envious)
bad.why: It is jealousy in love, not envy of someone's possessions; for that say yan hong or xian mu.

bad.s: 我真{吃醋}你，你男朋友那么帅！
bad.en: (meant: I'm so jealous of you, your boyfriend is so handsome!)
bad.why: A calque of English 'jealous of you' meaning envy; it takes no object like this, and envy of someone's luck is xian mu.

cards.mean: to leave one's job to work for another employer
cards.lit: to jump to another trough, like a horse leaving its own manger to feed at another

use.how: An intransitive verb-object phrase: 跳槽, 跳槽到某公司, 跳了两次槽. Said of employees moving to another employer, usually for better pay or prospects.

near.diff: 辞职 is simply resigning, with nothing said about what comes next; 跳槽 means moving on to work somewhere else.
炒鱿鱼 is being fired by the employer; 跳槽 is leaving by one's own choice for a new job.

cards.cue: A rival company offers your best engineer a higher salary, and next month she starts working for them. What has she done?

ctx.s: 他去年{跳槽}到了一家外企。
ctx.en: Last year he moved to a job at a foreign company.

ctx.s: 你为什么想{跳槽}？现在的公司不好吗？
ctx.en: Why do you want to change jobs? Is your current company no good?

ctx.s: 年轻人{跳槽}很常见，大多是为了更高的工资。
ctx.en: It's common for young people to switch employers, mostly for higher pay.

ctx.s: 她三年里{跳了两次槽}，现在已经是部门经理了。
ctx.en: She changed companies twice in three years and is now a department manager.

ctx.s: 公司待遇太低，好几个技术骨干都{跳槽}了。
ctx.en: The company pays too little, and several of its key engineers have left for other firms.

ctx.s: 面试官问：“你频繁{跳槽}的原因是什么？”
ctx.en: The interviewer asked: "Why have you changed employers so often?"

bad.s: 我太累了，所以{跳槽}回家休息一年。
bad.en: (meant: I was exhausted, so I quit my job to rest at home for a year)
bad.why: It means moving to another employer; leaving work to rest is ci zhi (resign).

bad.s: 他成绩特别好，从三年级{跳槽}到了五年级。
bad.en: (meant: his grades were so good that he skipped from third to fifth grade)
bad.why: It is only about changing jobs; skipping a grade at school is tiao ji.

cards.mean: to dampen someone's enthusiasm with discouraging words
cards.lit: to throw cold water over someone

use.how: A verb-object phrase, often 给某人泼冷水 or 泼了一盆冷水. Said of discouraging someone's plans, hopes or excitement.

near.diff: 唱反调 is deliberately taking the opposite position; 泼冷水 is deflating someone's hopes or excitement, even with good intentions.
说风凉话 is sneering from the sidelines at someone's trouble; 泼冷水 is discouraging a plan or hope before it starts.

cards.cue: Your friend excitedly tells you she wants to open a café, and you immediately list every reason it will fail. What are you doing to her?

ctx.s: 孩子想学画画，你就别给他{泼冷水}了。
ctx.en: The child wants to learn to paint, so don't discourage him.

ctx.s: 看你这么兴奋，不是我{泼冷水}，这个计划真的太冒险了。
ctx.en: I can see you're excited, and I don't mean to dampen your spirits, but this plan really is too risky.

ctx.s: 我刚说想参加比赛，他就{泼冷水}，说我肯定不行。
ctx.en: As soon as I said I wanted to enter the contest, he poured cold water on it and said I'd never make it.

ctx.s: 大家正兴高采烈地讨论旅行，经理的一句话给大家{泼了一盆冷水}。
ctx.en: Everyone was happily discussing the trip when one remark from the manager killed the mood.

ctx.s: 第一次创业失败后，家人还不停地{泼冷水}，他心里很难受。
ctx.en: After his first business failed, his family kept discouraging him, and it hurt him deeply.

ctx.s: 对新员工的想法，我们应该多鼓励，少{泼冷水}。
ctx.en: We should encourage new employees' ideas more and discourage them less.

bad.s: 他上课迟到了，老师{泼冷水}批评了他一顿。
bad.en: (meant: he was late for class, and the teacher gave him a scolding)
bad.why: It means dampening hopes or enthusiasm, not scolding someone for a mistake; for that say pi ping (criticise).

bad.s: 朋友的鼓励给我{泼了冷水}，我更有信心了。
bad.en: (meant: my friend's encouragement boosted me and made me more confident)
bad.why: It means the opposite: discouraging someone. Encouragement is gei wo da qi (cheer me on).

cards.mean: to take the blame for someone else's mistake
cards.lit: to carry a soot-blackened cooking pot on one's back

use.how: A verb-object phrase, often 替某人背黑锅, 背了黑锅, 背这个黑锅. Said of an innocent person who is blamed, usually with sympathy or resentment.

near.diff: 甩锅 is what the guilty person does in pushing the blame away; 背黑锅 is what happens to the person who ends up carrying it.
替罪羊 is a noun for the person made to take the blame; 背黑锅 is the verb phrase for taking it.

cards.cue: Your manager lost the contract, but in the meeting he said it was your fault, and you were the one who got the warning. What happened to you?

ctx.s: 明明是他弄坏的，凭什么让我{背黑锅}？
ctx.en: He was obviously the one who broke it, so why should I take the blame?

ctx.s: 我可不想替你{背这个黑锅}。
ctx.en: I'm certainly not going to take the blame for you on this one.

ctx.s: 项目出了问题，最后是新来的实习生{背了黑锅}。
ctx.en: When the project went wrong, the new intern ended up taking the blame.

ctx.s: 为了保护朋友，他主动{背了黑锅}。
ctx.en: To protect his friend, he took the blame himself.

ctx.s: 事故原因终于查清楚了，小李不用再{背黑锅}了。
ctx.en: The cause of the accident has finally been established, so Xiao Li no longer has to carry the blame.

ctx.s: 你放心，这件事我不会让你一个人{背黑锅}。
ctx.en: Don't worry, I won't let you take the blame for this alone.

bad.s: 他把自己的错误{背黑锅}给了同事。
bad.en: (meant: he pushed the blame for his own mistake onto a colleague)
bad.why: Pushing your own blame onto others is shuai guo; this idiom describes the innocent person who ends up blamed.

bad.s: 这次失败完全是我自己的错，我应该{背黑锅}。
bad.en: (meant: this failure was entirely my own fault, so I should take responsibility)
bad.why: It implies the blame is undeserved. For your own fault say cheng dan ze ren (take responsibility).

cards.mean: to shift the blame for one's own mistake onto others
cards.lit: to fling the pot off: to throw the blackened pot of blame onto someone else

use.how: A verb, often 甩锅给某人 or 互相甩锅. Recent internet slang, now common in speech and commentary, said of someone dodging blame that is really theirs.

near.diff: 背黑锅 is what the innocent victim does, carrying the blame; 甩锅 is what the guilty person does, throwing it off.

cards.cue: Your manager forgot to send the client the file, and in the meeting he says it was the intern's job to remind him. What is he doing?

ctx.s: 别{甩锅}了，明明是你忘了订票。
ctx.en: Stop passing the buck; you're the one who forgot to book the tickets.

ctx.s: 一出问题他就{甩锅}，从来不承认自己错了。
ctx.en: Whenever something goes wrong he shifts the blame; he never admits he was wrong.

ctx.s: 项目延期了，经理却{甩锅}给了实习生。
ctx.en: The project was delayed, yet the manager pinned it on the intern.

ctx.s: 两个部门互相{甩锅}，问题一直没人解决。
ctx.en: The two departments keep blaming each other, and nobody ever fixes the problem.

ctx.s: 是你自己没看地图，怎么能{甩锅}给导航呢？
ctx.en: You didn't look at the map yourself; how can you blame the satnav?

ctx.s: 面对顾客的投诉，这家公司没有道歉，反而{甩锅}给快递公司。
ctx.en: Faced with customer complaints, the company didn't apologise but blamed the delivery firm instead.

bad.s: 这次是我的错，我愿意{甩锅}。
bad.en: (meant: this was my fault and I'm willing to take the blame)
bad.why: It means throwing your own blame onto others; to accept the blame yourself you say you will carry the pot (bēi guō) or take responsibility.

bad.s: 你表现很好，经理决定把奖金{甩锅}给你。
bad.en: (meant: the manager decided to give you the bonus)
bad.why: The pot is blame, so the expression is only about pushing blame away, never about handing someone something good.

cards.mean: to meet a flat refusal when asking for something
cards.lit: to bump into a nail: to knock against something hard and get hurt

use.how: Verb-object, often split: 碰了个钉子, 碰了一个软钉子. The subject is the one who asked and was rebuffed: 我在他那儿碰了钉子.

near.diff: 碰壁 is meeting obstacles in general, often repeatedly (找工作到处碰壁); 碰钉子 is a rebuff from a particular person you asked.

cards.cue: You ask your landlord to fix the broken heater, and he says curtly that it's not his problem and shuts the door.

ctx.s: 我去找经理请假，结果{碰了个钉子}。
ctx.en: I went to ask the manager for leave and got turned down flat.

ctx.s: 你直接去找他要赞助，肯定会{碰钉子}的。
ctx.en: If you go straight to him asking for sponsorship, you'll definitely be rebuffed.

ctx.s: 他想借钱，连问了三个朋友，都{碰了钉子}。
ctx.en: He wanted to borrow money; he asked three friends in a row and was refused every time.

ctx.s: 刚开始做销售的时候，我几乎天天{碰钉子}。
ctx.en: When I first started in sales, I got doors slammed in my face almost every day.

ctx.s: 你上次去提加薪，是不是{碰了钉子}？
ctx.en: When you asked for a raise last time, did you get shot down?

ctx.s: 记者想采访那位演员，却在经纪人那里{碰了个软钉子}。
ctx.en: The reporter wanted to interview the actor but was politely turned away by the agent.

bad.s: 我这次考试{碰钉子}了，没及格。
bad.en: (meant: I failed this exam)
bad.why: It means being rebuffed by someone you asked, not failing a test; say kǎo zá le or méi kǎo hǎo.

bad.s: 经理{碰钉子}了我。
bad.en: (meant: the manager turned me down)
bad.why: The person refused is the subject and it takes no object; the refuser goes in a phrase like zài jīnglǐ nàr, at the manager's.

cards.mean: to care too much about how one looks in others' eyes
cards.lit: to love face: face here is one's standing and dignity in front of others

use.how: Predicate after 很, 太, 特别, or attribute (爱面子的人). Said of people who avoid admitting weakness, ignorance or need because others are watching.

near.diff: 死要面子 is harsher, for someone who suffers or loses out just to save face; 爱面子 is a milder description of character.

cards.cue: Your uncle gets lost driving but refuses to ask for directions because the whole family is in the car watching him.

ctx.s: 他太{爱面子}了，明明不懂也不肯问。
ctx.en: He cares too much about face; even when he clearly doesn't understand, he won't ask.

ctx.s: 我爸特别{爱面子}，在外人面前从不认错。
ctx.en: My dad is very proud; he never admits he's wrong in front of other people.

ctx.s: 别那么{爱面子}，说一声不会又不丢人。
ctx.en: Don't worry so much about face; saying you can't do it is nothing to be ashamed of.

ctx.s: 你是不是太{爱面子}了，迷路了都不肯问人？
ctx.en: Aren't you a bit too proud? You're lost and you still won't ask anyone.

ctx.s: 很多人{爱面子}，家里再困难也不愿意跟亲戚开口。
ctx.en: Many people are too proud to ask relatives for help, however hard things are at home.

ctx.s: 她是个{爱面子}的人，请客总要去最贵的饭店。
ctx.en: She's someone who cares a lot about appearances; when she treats people it always has to be the most expensive restaurant.

bad.s: 她很{爱面子}，每天出门都要化妆。
bad.en: (meant: she cares about her looks and puts on make-up every day)
bad.why: Face here is social standing, not one's physical face or looks; for caring about looks say ài měi or ài dǎban.

bad.s: 他来参加我的婚礼，真是{爱面子}我。
bad.en: (meant: he did me an honour by coming to my wedding)
bad.why: Doing someone an honour is gěi miànzi, to give face; this expression describes one's own pride and takes no object.

cards.mean: to be completely baffled and unable to make sense of it
cards.lit: a head full of mist and water: as if one's head were wrapped in fog

use.how: Predicate (我一头雾水) or complement after 得 (听得一头雾水), or with 让/搞得. Said of someone who cannot follow an explanation or situation.

near.diff: 莫名其妙 stresses that something is odd and unexplained (他莫名其妙地生气了); 一头雾水 is the confusion of someone who cannot follow what is said or happening.

cards.cue: A colleague rattles through a new spreadsheet formula full of jargon, and when he finishes you have no idea what he just said.

ctx.s: 老师讲得太快，我听得{一头雾水}。
ctx.en: The teacher spoke too fast; I couldn't make head or tail of it.

ctx.s: 这份说明书写得很乱，看完还是{一头雾水}。
ctx.en: The manual is so badly written that after reading it I'm still completely lost.

ctx.s: 你说了半天，我还是{一头雾水}，能再讲一遍吗？
ctx.en: You've been talking for ages and I'm still baffled; could you explain it again?

ctx.s: 他突然问我要那份文件，我{一头雾水}，根本不知道是哪份。
ctx.en: He suddenly asked me for that document; I was baffled and had no idea which one he meant.

ctx.s: 新出的停车规定条款太多，不少司机看得{一头雾水}。
ctx.en: The new parking rules have so many clauses that plenty of drivers are left scratching their heads.

ctx.s: 电影的结局让观众{一头雾水}，网上讨论了好几天。
ctx.en: The film's ending left audiences baffled, and people argued about it online for days.

bad.s: 今天早上雾很大，外面{一头雾水}。
bad.en: (meant: it was very foggy outside this morning)
bad.why: The fog is figurative: it describes a confused person, never the weather.

bad.s: 他是个{一头雾水}，什么都不懂。
bad.en: (meant: he's an ignorant person who knows nothing)
bad.why: It describes being confused about a particular thing, not a person who is stupid or ignorant in general.

cards.mean: something very easy to do, a piece of cake
cards.lit: just one little dish of side vegetables: nothing that takes any effort

use.how: A noun phrase used after 是 or on its own as a reply, often with 对我来说. Said confidently, sometimes boastfully, of a task one finds easy.

near.diff: 易如反掌 is a bookish 成语 used in writing; 小菜一碟 is the casual spoken way to say a task is no trouble.

cards.cue: Your friend is panicking about assembling a flat-pack wardrobe; your brother, a carpenter, grins and says it will take him ten minutes.

ctx.s: 修电脑？对他来说是{小菜一碟}。
ctx.en: Fix a computer? For him that's a piece of cake.

ctx.s: 你一个人做得完这些菜吗？——{小菜一碟}！
ctx.en: Can you cook all these dishes by yourself? — Easy!

ctx.s: 别担心，这点小事{小菜一碟}，包在我身上。
ctx.en: Don't worry, a little thing like this is no trouble; leave it to me.

ctx.s: 跑五公里对专业运动员来说只是{小菜一碟}。
ctx.en: Running five kilometres is nothing to a professional athlete.

ctx.s: 这次考试的题目对她来说简直是{小菜一碟}。
ctx.en: The questions on this exam were a breeze for her.

ctx.s: 他以为当老师是{小菜一碟}，上了一周课才知道有多累。
ctx.en: He thought teaching would be a walk in the park; after one week of classes he found out how exhausting it is.

bad.s: 这家餐厅的{小菜一碟}很好吃。
bad.en: (meant: this restaurant's side dishes are tasty)
bad.why: It is a fixed expression for 'easy'; for real side dishes just say xiǎocài.

bad.s: 这道数学题很{小菜一碟}。
bad.en: (meant: this maths problem is very easy)
bad.why: It is a noun phrase used after shì, not an adjective, so hěn cannot modify it.

cards.mean: a secure job for life, such as a government post
cards.lit: an iron rice bowl: a bowl that can never break, so there is always food in it

story.text: The phrase belongs to the planned-economy decades of the People's Republic, when jobs in state enterprises and government units were allocated and practically could not be lost. When the economic reforms of the 1980s brought in labour contracts, people talked of smashing the iron rice bowl. Today it mostly means a civil-service or other state job.

use.how: A noun: 端铁饭碗, 捧着铁饭碗, 是铁饭碗. Said of stable state jobs, often by parents urging security; 打破铁饭碗 means ending job security.

near.diff: 金饭碗 is a job that pays very well; 铁饭碗 is a job that can't be lost, whatever it pays.

cards.cue: Your parents beg you to sit the civil-service exam instead of joining a startup, because nobody there ever gets fired.

ctx.s: 我妈总说，考上公务员就是端上了{铁饭碗}。
ctx.en: My mum always says that passing the civil-service exam means a job for life.

ctx.s: 当老师算不算{铁饭碗}？
ctx.en: Does being a teacher count as a secure job for life?

ctx.s: 他放弃了{铁饭碗}，辞职去创业了。
ctx.en: He gave up a secure job for life and quit to start his own business.

ctx.s: 毕业时，她拒绝了大公司的高薪，选了一个{铁饭碗}。
ctx.en: When she graduated she turned down a high salary at a big company and chose a safe, permanent job.

ctx.s: 现在很多年轻人觉得，世界上没有真正的{铁饭碗}。
ctx.en: Many young people now feel there's no such thing as a truly secure job.

ctx.s: 有了真本事，到哪儿都有饭吃，这才是真正的{铁饭碗}。
ctx.en: With real skills you can make a living anywhere; that's the true job security.

bad.s: 他做直播一个月挣十万，真是个{铁饭碗}。
bad.en: (meant: he earns a fortune live-streaming; what a great job)
bad.why: An iron rice bowl is about security, not pay; income from streaming is the opposite of secure. A lucrative job is a golden rice bowl.

bad.s: 我的工作很{铁饭碗}，不用担心。
bad.en: (meant: my job is very secure, no need to worry)
bad.why: It is a noun, not an adjective, so hěn cannot modify it; say the job shì tiě fànwǎn.

cards.mean: advice or action that comes only after it could help
cards.lit: the cannon behind the horse, a pattern in Chinese chess; in everyday speech, a shot that comes too late

use.how: A noun: 是马后炮, 放马后炮, or 有点马后炮. Mocks advice, warnings or measures that come only after the event is over.

near.diff: 事后诸葛亮 mocks a person who claims, afterwards, to have known all along; 马后炮 is the belated remark or measure itself.

cards.cue: The picnic is rained out, and only then does your friend say he knew it would rain and you should have gone yesterday.

ctx.s: 比赛都结束了，你现在说这些就是{马后炮}。
ctx.en: The match is already over; saying this now is just hindsight.

ctx.s: 别放{马后炮}了，当时你怎么不提醒我？
ctx.en: Spare me the wisdom after the event; why didn't you warn me at the time?

ctx.s: 车被偷了才装监控，这不是{马后炮}吗？
ctx.en: Putting in cameras only after the car has been stolen: isn't that too little, too late?

ctx.s: 我知道这话有点{马后炮}，但我早觉得那家公司不靠谱。
ctx.en: I know this is a bit late to say, but I always thought that company was unreliable.

ctx.s: 会开完了他才提出反对意见，大家都觉得是{马后炮}。
ctx.en: He raised his objection only after the meeting was over, and everyone felt it came too late.

ctx.s: 股价跌完以后，各种分析文章才冒出来，全是{马后炮}。
ctx.en: All the analysis pieces only appeared after the share price had fallen; every one of them was hindsight.

bad.s: 他做事很{马后炮}，总是提前一个月准备。
bad.en: (meant: he plans ahead, preparing a month early)
bad.why: It mocks advice or action that comes too late, after the event; it can never describe preparing well ahead of time.

bad.s: 你快点儿，别{马后炮}了，火车要开了！
bad.en: (meant: hurry up, stop dawdling, the train is leaving)
bad.why: It is not about being slow; it is advice or action that comes after the event is already over.

cards.mean: to put on airs and act self-important
cards.lit: to set up a frame: to strike a stiff, imposing pose for others to see

use.how: Verb-object, can be split: 摆什么架子, 摆官架子. Said of people who use their position to look down on others; 不摆架子 praises the humble.

near.diff: 耍大牌 is mainly said of celebrities making diva demands; 摆架子 is anyone with status acting aloof and superior.

cards.cue: An old classmate becomes a director and now keeps you waiting an hour, won't shake your hand, and has his assistant speak for him.

ctx.s: 他当了经理以后，就开始{摆架子}了。
ctx.en: After he became a manager, he started putting on airs.

ctx.s: 你不过是个组长，{摆什么架子}？
ctx.en: You're only a team leader; who do you think you are?

ctx.s: 王教授一点儿也不{摆架子}，经常跟学生一起吃饭。
ctx.en: Professor Wang isn't the least bit stuck-up; he often eats with his students.

ctx.s: 新来的主任会不会{摆架子}啊？
ctx.en: Will the new director be the high-and-mighty type?

ctx.s: 那位医生对病人{摆架子}，问话爱答不理，被投诉了。
ctx.en: That doctor acted superior to his patients, barely bothering to answer their questions, and got complained about.

ctx.s: 越是有本事的人，越不{摆架子}。
ctx.en: The more able someone is, the less they put on airs.

bad.s: 我在家里{摆架子}，把书都放好了。
bad.en: (meant: I set up a bookshelf at home and put the books on it)
bad.why: It is figurative only, about acting superior; for arranging books just say bǎi hǎo shū.

bad.s: 他第一次上台演讲，有点{摆架子}，手一直在发抖。
bad.en: (meant: he was stiff and nervous at his first speech)
bad.why: It means acting arrogant towards others, not being stiff from nerves; say hěn jǐnzhāng.

cards.mean: to dwell obsessively on a trivial or insoluble point
cards.lit: to bore into the tip of an ox horn: the further in you go, the narrower it gets, and it leads nowhere

use.how: Verb-object, often 别钻牛角尖, 爱钻牛角尖, 钻进牛角尖. Said of someone stuck on one small point or one gloomy thought, often to coax them out.

near.diff: 死心眼 is a stubborn, inflexible character in general; 钻牛角尖 is getting stuck on one particular point or thought.

cards.cue: Your friend has spent forty minutes of the exam on one question he can't crack, the rest of the paper is blank, and he still won't move on.

ctx.s: 这道题想不出来就先放着，别{钻牛角尖}。
ctx.en: If you can't work this problem out, leave it for now; don't get stuck on it.

ctx.s: 老师随口说了一句，她就{钻牛角尖}，琢磨了好几天是什么意思。
ctx.en: The teacher made an offhand remark, and she got hung up on it, puzzling for days over what it meant.

ctx.s: 你是不是{钻进牛角尖}了？换个角度想想吧。
ctx.en: Aren't you getting too fixated on this? Try looking at it from another angle.

ctx.s: 他做研究爱{钻牛角尖}，一个小问题能想好几个月。
ctx.en: In his research he tends to fixate; he can spend months on one small question.

ctx.s: 他非要弄明白“先有鸡还是先有蛋”，越想越{钻牛角尖}。
ctx.en: He insisted on settling whether the chicken or the egg came first, and the more he thought, the more stuck he got.

ctx.s: 谈合同的时候，对方在一个标点上{钻牛角尖}，拖了一下午。
ctx.en: During the contract talks the other side fixated on a single punctuation mark and dragged it out all afternoon.

bad.s: 这个问题很{钻牛角尖}，大家都答不出来。
bad.en: (meant: this question is very tricky; nobody could answer it)
bad.why: It describes a person getting stuck, not a hard question; for a tricky question say diāozuān.

bad.s: 我们一起{钻牛角尖}，终于把难题解决了。
bad.en: (meant: we dug deep together and finally solved the hard problem)
bad.why: It is criticism of getting stuck to no purpose; for productive deep study say zuānyán.

cards.mean: to make a frantic last-minute effort, such as cramming
cards.lit: to hug the Buddha's feet only when trouble comes, after never having burned incense before

use.how: A verb phrase, often in 平时不烧香，临时抱佛脚. Said, often self-mockingly, of cramming for exams or rushing to prepare when it is almost too late.

near.diff: 火烧眉毛 describes how urgent a situation is; 临时抱佛脚 describes the rushed effort of someone who failed to prepare.

cards.cue: Your roommate skipped every class all term, and ten minutes before the final she is frantically flipping through a classmate's notes.

ctx.s: 考试前一个小时，他才在走廊里{临时抱佛脚}，翻看笔记。
ctx.en: Only an hour before the exam was he cramming in the corridor, leafing through his notes.

ctx.s: 平时不努力，考前{临时抱佛脚}，怎么可能考好？
ctx.en: If you never work and only cram before the exam, how could you do well?

ctx.s: 你又在{临时抱佛脚}吗？报告不是上个月就布置了吗？
ctx.en: Are you leaving it to the last minute again? Wasn't the report set last month?

ctx.s: 面试前一晚，他才{临时抱佛脚}，上网查这家公司是做什么的。
ctx.en: Only the night before the interview did he scramble to look up online what the company does.

ctx.s: 体检前一周他突然戒酒跑步，医生笑他是{临时抱佛脚}。
ctx.en: A week before his check-up he suddenly quit drinking and took up running; the doctor laughed at his last-minute effort.

ctx.s: 学外语靠的是积累，{临时抱佛脚}是没有用的。
ctx.en: Learning a language depends on steady accumulation; last-minute cramming is no use.

bad.s: 他很虔诚，每个周末都去寺庙{临时抱佛脚}。
bad.en: (meant: he is devout and goes to the temple to pray every weekend)
bad.why: It is not about religion at all; it mocks a rushed last-minute effort. Praying at a temple is bài fó or shāo xiāng.

bad.s: 我提前三个月就开始{临时抱佛脚}了。
bad.en: (meant: I started preparing three months in advance)
bad.why: It means a last-minute scramble; starting three months early is the opposite. Say tíqián zhǔnbèi, prepare in advance.

cards.mean: to deal with or have regular contact with someone
cards.lit: to 'do' contact with someone: to have dealings

use.how: Intransitive: the other party comes before it with 跟/和/与: 跟客户打交道. Aspect and duration go inside: 打过交道, 打了十年交道. Can also take things: 跟数字打交道.

near.diff: 来往 is visiting and keeping in touch socially; 打交道 is having dealings with someone, often for work, and can also be used of things like machines or figures.

cards.cue: A friend in customer service says the hardest part of her job is having to handle demanding clients on the phone all day. What does she have to do with them?

ctx.s: 我不太会跟陌生人{打交道}。
ctx.en: I'm not very good at dealing with strangers.

ctx.s: 做销售每天都要和各种各样的客户{打交道}。
ctx.en: In sales you have to deal with all kinds of customers every day.

ctx.s: 我们和这家公司{打过好几次交道}，他们很守信用。
ctx.en: We've had dealings with this company several times; they keep their word.

ctx.s: 当会计的整天跟数字{打交道}，难免觉得枯燥。
ctx.en: Accountants spend all day working with numbers, so it's bound to feel dull at times.

ctx.s: “你跟老王熟吗？”“熟，我们{打了十几年交道}了。”
ctx.en: "Do you know Lao Wang well?" "Yes, we've been dealing with each other for over ten years."

ctx.s: 听说新来的经理不好{打交道}，你跟他说话小心点。
ctx.en: I hear the new manager is hard to deal with, so be careful how you talk to him.

bad.s: 我昨天{打交道}了我的新同事。
bad.en: (meant: yesterday I got to know my new colleague)
bad.why: It takes no object: the person goes before it with gen ('with'), as in 'I have had dealings with my new colleague'.

bad.s: 两个孩子在操场上{打交道}，老师赶紧把他们拉开了。
bad.en: (meant: two children were fighting in the playground)
bad.why: Da here does not mean hitting: the expression is about having dealings with someone, not a fight. Fighting is da jia.

cards.mean: to beat around the bush instead of saying it directly
cards.lit: to go round the bends instead of taking the straight road

use.how: Used of talk, usually as a complaint or negated: 别绕弯子了, 我就不绕弯子了. Can be split: 绕了半天弯子, 绕着弯子问.

near.diff: 卖关子 holds back the key part on purpose to build suspense; 绕弯子 avoids saying the point directly, often out of awkwardness or tact.

cards.cue: Your flatmate talks for ten minutes about the weather and the rent before finally asking to borrow your car. What do you tell them to stop doing?

ctx.s: 有话直说，别{绕弯子}了。
ctx.en: If you've got something to say, say it. Stop beating around the bush.

ctx.s: 我就不{绕弯子}了，这次来是想跟您借点钱。
ctx.en: I'll get straight to the point: I've come to ask if I could borrow some money from you.

ctx.s: 你{绕了这么大一个弯子}，原来就是想让我帮你搬家啊？
ctx.en: You went all round the houses just to ask me to help you move?

ctx.s: 她说话从来不{绕弯子}，这一点我很欣赏。
ctx.en: She never beats around the bush, and I really appreciate that about her.

ctx.s: 他不好意思直接问工资，就{绕着弯子}向同事打听。
ctx.en: He was too embarrassed to ask about pay outright, so he sounded out his colleagues in a roundabout way.

ctx.s: 领导批评人喜欢{绕弯子}，新员工常常听不出自己挨了批评。
ctx.en: The boss criticises people so indirectly that new staff often don't realise they've been told off.

bad.s: 他{绕弯子}了这个问题。
bad.en: (meant: he dodged this question)
bad.why: It takes no object. Say he beat around the bush on this question, or, for dodging it, use a verb meaning 'avoid'.

bad.s: 魔术师故意{绕弯子}，等到最后才揭晓答案，观众都很期待。
bad.en: (meant: the magician kept the audience in suspense until the end)
bad.why: Deliberately holding back the key moment to build suspense is mai guanzi; this one means failing to say something directly.

cards.mean: to keep people in suspense by holding back the key part
cards.lit: to 'sell' the guanzi, the crucial turn of a story, by stopping just before it

use.how: Said of someone who pauses before the key bit while others wait to hear: 别卖关子了, 卖了个关子. Often a light, teasing complaint.

near.diff: 绕弯子 is talking around a point instead of stating it; 卖关子 is knowingly withholding the key part to keep listeners in suspense.

cards.cue: At dinner a friend announces they have big news, then grins and makes everyone guess for five minutes before telling. What are they doing?

ctx.s: 快说结果吧，别{卖关子}了！
ctx.en: Just tell us the result, stop keeping us in suspense!

ctx.s: 爷爷讲故事最会{卖关子}，每次讲到一半就说明天再讲。
ctx.en: Grandpa is a master at keeping you hanging: he always stops halfway through a story and says he'll finish tomorrow.

ctx.s: 先{卖个关子}，等大家到齐了我再公布好消息。
ctx.en: I'll keep you guessing for now; I'll announce the good news when everyone's here.

ctx.s: 这部电视剧每集都在关键时刻{卖关子}，让人忍不住看下一集。
ctx.en: Every episode of this series leaves you hanging at the crucial moment, so you can't help watching the next one.

ctx.s: 主持人故意{卖起了关子}，迟迟不宣布冠军的名字。
ctx.en: The host deliberately drew out the suspense, taking his time to announce the winner's name.

ctx.s: 记者问新产品有什么功能，他笑着{卖了个关子}：“发布会上就知道了。”
ctx.en: When reporters asked what the new product could do, he smiled and teased them: "You'll find out at the launch."

bad.s: 他把这件事{卖关子}了三年，谁也不知道。
bad.en: (meant: he kept this secret for three years)
bad.why: It means teasing listeners in the moment by pausing before the key part, not keeping a secret for years. For that, say 'hid it'.

bad.s: 他在市场上{卖关子}，一天能赚不少钱。
bad.en: (meant: he sells goods at the market)
bad.why: Nothing is sold: 'selling' here means dangling a held-back point. Selling goods at a market is simply mai dongxi.

cards.mean: to let others down at the crucial moment
cards.lit: the chain comes off, as on a bicycle, which then stops dead

use.how: Predicate for a person, team or device that fails when it matters: 关键时刻掉链子, 千万别掉链子. Can be split: 掉了链子.

near.diff: 拖后腿 is holding others back, often over time; 掉链子 is failing yourself at the decisive moment, so those counting on you are let down.

cards.cue: The team's best penalty-taker, who never misses in training, blasts the deciding kick over the bar in the final. What happened?

ctx.s: 明天就比赛了，你可千万别{掉链子}。
ctx.en: The match is tomorrow, so whatever you do, don't let us down.

ctx.s: 他平时成绩很好，没想到高考的时候{掉了链子}。
ctx.en: He usually gets good marks, but he fell apart in the university entrance exam.

ctx.s: 我的电脑偏偏在演示的时候{掉链子}，突然死机了。
ctx.en: My computer chose the moment of the presentation to fail on me and froze.

ctx.s: “这次项目全靠你了。”“放心，我绝不{掉链子}！”
ctx.en: "This project is all on you." "Don't worry, I won't let you down!"

ctx.s: 球队前八十分钟踢得很好，最后十分钟却{掉了链子}，被对手连进两球。
ctx.en: The team played well for eighty minutes, then fell apart in the last ten and conceded two goals in a row.

ctx.s: 每次关键时刻{掉链子}的都是他，大家已经不敢把重要的事交给他了。
ctx.en: He's always the one who fails when it counts, so nobody dares give him anything important any more.

bad.s: 他们俩上个月分手了，感情{掉链子}了。
bad.en: (meant: their relationship broke down)
bad.why: It is not about a bond breaking: it means failing to perform at a crucial moment. A break-up is a relationship that has broken down.

bad.s: 我妈妈总是{掉链子}，不让我出去玩。
bad.en: (meant: my mum always holds me back)
bad.why: Stopping someone or slowing them down is tuo houtui; this one is your own failure at the moment others rely on you.

cards.mean: (of a plan or hope) to fall through and come to nothing
cards.lit: to be soaked in soup, gone soggy and spoiled

use.how: Intransitive, with a plan, hope or deal as subject: 计划泡汤了, 旅行全泡汤了. Also 让…泡汤 and the split form 泡了汤.

near.diff: 打水漂 is money or effort spent for nothing in return; 泡汤 is a plan, hope or arrangement that falls through.

cards.cue: You had booked a beach weekend months ago, then a typhoon closed the airport the day before you were due to fly. What happened to the trip?

ctx.s: 下雨了，我们的野餐{泡汤}了。
ctx.en: It's raining, so our picnic is off.

ctx.s: 签证没办下来，出国旅行的计划全{泡汤}了。
ctx.en: The visa didn't come through, so our whole trip abroad fell through.

ctx.s: 公司突然要求周末加班，我的约会又{泡汤}了。
ctx.en: The company suddenly told us to work the weekend, so my date has fallen through again.

ctx.s: “听说你们那笔生意谈成了？”“别提了，最后一刻{泡汤}了。”
ctx.en: "I heard you closed that deal?" "Don't ask. It fell through at the last minute."

ctx.s: 他本来指望年底能拿一大笔奖金，结果公司效益不好，奖金{泡了汤}。
ctx.en: He had been counting on a big year-end bonus, but the company did badly and the bonus came to nothing.

ctx.s: 他想趁假期好好睡几天，没想到一个电话就让他的计划{泡汤}了。
ctx.en: He wanted to catch up on sleep over the holiday, but a single phone call wrecked his plans.

bad.s: 他考试没考好，他{泡汤}了。
bad.en: (meant: he failed his exam and is finished)
bad.why: The subject must be a plan or hope, not a person: say that his plan to study abroad fell through.

bad.s: 大雨{泡汤}了我们的野餐。
bad.en: (meant: the heavy rain ruined our picnic)
bad.why: It takes no object; the plan is the subject: 'once it rained, the picnic fell through', or 'the rain made the picnic fall through'.

cards.mean: to be stunned and at a loss when something goes wrong
cards.lit: eyes gone foolish: staring blankly in shock

use.how: Intransitive predicate for the moment a sudden setback leaves someone stunned: 他一下子傻眼了, 当场傻了眼; causative 让人傻眼.

near.diff: 一头雾水 is not understanding something at all; 傻眼 is being stunned when something suddenly goes wrong, usually knowing all too well what happened.

cards.cue: You reach the front of a long queue at the airport check-in desk and only then realise your passport is still on the kitchen table at home. What's your reaction?

ctx.s: 考试一开始，他就{傻眼}了，题目全是没复习过的。
ctx.en: As soon as the exam started he froze: every question was on something he hadn't revised.

ctx.s: 他打开钱包准备付钱，才发现里面一分钱也没有，一下子就{傻眼}了。
ctx.en: He opened his wallet to pay and found there wasn't a penny in it, and he was stunned.

ctx.s: 看到房间被弄得乱七八糟，妈妈当场{傻了眼}。
ctx.en: When Mum saw the room turned upside down, she just stood there stunned.

ctx.s: “你怎么站在那儿不动？”“我{傻眼}了，车钥匙锁在车里了。”
ctx.en: "Why are you just standing there?" "I'm stunned. I've locked the car keys inside the car."

ctx.s: 本来以为稳赢，没想到对手最后一分钟进了球，全场球迷顿时都{傻眼}了。
ctx.en: Everyone thought it was in the bag, then the other side scored in the last minute and the whole crowd was stunned.

ctx.s: 搬进新家第一天就停水停电，这让我们彻底{傻眼}了。
ctx.en: On our first day in the new flat both the water and the power went off, and we were completely at a loss.

bad.s: 他是个很{傻眼}的人，常常做错事。
bad.en: (meant: he is a foolish person who often makes mistakes)
bad.why: It is not an adjective for a foolish person; it describes the moment someone is stunned: 'he was stunned at once'.

bad.s: 这个坏消息{傻眼}了我。
bad.en: (meant: this bad news stunned me)
bad.why: It takes no object. Say 'this bad news left me stunned', using rang ('make'), or 'hearing the news, I was stunned'.

cards.mean: to be envious of what others have
cards.lit: one's eyes turn red at the sight of what someone else has

use.how: Predicate for the envious person, about money, success or luck: 看到别人赚钱就眼红; also transitive (眼红别人的成绩) and causative (真让人眼红).

near.diff: 吃醋 is jealousy over a partner's attention to someone else; 眼红 is envy of someone's money, success or luck.

cards.cue: A coworker grumbles all week after a younger new hire gets a bigger bonus and a corner office. What is the coworker feeling?

ctx.s: 看到邻居买了新车，他有点{眼红}。
ctx.en: When he saw the neighbours had bought a new car, he felt a bit envious.

ctx.s: 他一年就升了两次职，不少同事都{眼红}。
ctx.en: He was promoted twice in one year, and plenty of colleagues were envious.

ctx.s: 你别{眼红}别人的工资了，好好提高自己的能力吧。
ctx.en: Stop envying other people's salaries and work on improving your own skills.

ctx.s: 听说她中了大奖，真让人{眼红}！
ctx.en: I hear she's won the big prize. It makes you green with envy!

ctx.s: 这家小店生意越做越好，附近的同行都{眼红}起来。
ctx.en: As the little shop's business kept growing, the other shops nearby started to grow envious.

ctx.s: 这笔奖金数目不小，难免有人{眼红}，你最好别到处说。
ctx.en: That's a big bonus, and someone is bound to be envious, so you'd better not tell everyone.

bad.s: 看到女朋友跟别的男生说话，他{眼红}了。
bad.en: (meant: he got jealous when his girlfriend talked to other boys)
bad.why: Jealousy over a partner is chi cu; this one is envy of someone's money, success or luck.

bad.s: 你的新车真{眼红}！
bad.en: (meant: your new car is really enviable)
bad.why: It describes the envious person, not the thing envied. Say the car 'makes people envious', with rang ren before it.

cards.mean: extremely urgent, needing action right now
cards.lit: the fire is already burning one's eyebrows

story.text: The phrase appears in the Song-dynasty collection of Chan Buddhist dialogues. A monk asks a master, "What is the most urgent phrase?" and the master answers, "Fire burning the eyebrows." The image is of danger so close that it cannot wait a moment.

use.how: Describes a situation, as predicate or attribute: 都火烧眉毛了，你还…; 火烧眉毛的事. Often a reproach to someone who is not hurrying.

near.diff: 临时抱佛脚 is someone's frantic last-minute effort; 火烧眉毛 describes the situation itself as so urgent it cannot wait.

cards.cue: Your visa interview is across town in an hour and the forms aren't printed, yet your flatmate asks if you'd like to watch a film first. How do you describe the situation?

ctx.s: 都{火烧眉毛}了，你怎么还在玩手机？
ctx.en: It's a real emergency and you're still playing on your phone?

ctx.s: 离登机只剩二十分钟了，简直是{火烧眉毛}！
ctx.en: There are only twenty minutes until boarding. It couldn't be more urgent!

ctx.s: 别等到{火烧眉毛}了才着急。
ctx.en: Don't wait until it's an emergency before you start to worry.

ctx.s: “能不能明天再处理？”“不行，客户下午就要，已经{火烧眉毛}了！”
ctx.en: "Can we deal with it tomorrow?" "No, the client needs it this afternoon. It's urgent!"

ctx.s: 公司账上的钱只够发一个月工资，情况已经是{火烧眉毛}，必须马上想办法。
ctx.en: The company only has enough money for one more month of wages; it's critical, and something has to be done at once.

ctx.s: 先处理那些{火烧眉毛}的事，其他的下周再说。
ctx.en: Deal with the really urgent things first; the rest can wait until next week.

bad.s: 他是个{火烧眉毛}的人，做什么都很急。
bad.en: (meant: he is an impatient person who rushes everything)
bad.why: It describes an urgent situation, not a person's temperament. Someone always in a hurry is a ji xingzi.

bad.s: 老板{火烧眉毛}我们，让我们今天交报告。
bad.en: (meant: the boss was hurrying us to hand in the report today)
bad.why: It is not a verb that takes an object. Say the boss urged us, and that the matter was now extremely urgent.

cards.mean: someone soaked to the skin, e.g. caught in the rain
cards.lit: a chicken that has fallen into the soup pot

use.how: A noun for a drenched person, usually after 成了, 淋成, 像只: 被雨淋成了落汤鸡. Light and teasing, often self-mocking.

cards.cue: Your friend arrives at the café after cycling through a sudden downpour, hair dripping and shoes squelching. How do you tease them?

ctx.s: 我忘了带伞，被淋成了{落汤鸡}。
ctx.en: I forgot my umbrella and got soaked to the skin.

ctx.s: 看你浑身湿透，像只{落汤鸡}，快去洗个热水澡吧。
ctx.en: Look at you, you're like a drowned rat. Go and have a hot shower.

ctx.s: 孩子们打水仗，一个个都成了{落汤鸡}。
ctx.en: The children had a water fight and every one of them ended up drenched.

ctx.s: 他划船时不小心掉进湖里，爬上岸时活像一只{落汤鸡}。
ctx.en: He fell into the lake while rowing, and when he climbed out he looked like a drowned rat.

ctx.s: “怎么没打伞？”“伞被风吹坏了，我只好当了一回{落汤鸡}。”
ctx.en: "Why didn't you use an umbrella?" "The wind broke it, so I just had to get soaked for once."

ctx.s: 暴雨来得太突然，街上的行人一下子全变成了{落汤鸡}。
ctx.en: The storm came so suddenly that everyone on the street was drenched in moments.

bad.s: 今天晚饭我们吃{落汤鸡}，汤很好喝。
bad.en: (meant: we had chicken soup for dinner tonight)
bad.why: It is never a dish; it describes a person who is drenched. Chicken soup is ji tang.

bad.s: 这场雨{落汤鸡}了我。
bad.en: (meant: this rain soaked me)
bad.why: It is a noun, not a verb. Use the ba pattern: zhe chang yu ba wo lin cheng le luo tang ji, 'the rain soaked me into a drowned chicken'.

cards.mean: a night owl, someone who habitually stays up late
cards.lit: a 'night cat': a folk name for the owl

use.how: A noun for a person, usually after 是, 当, 变成: 我是个夜猫子. About a habit, not one late night.

near.diff: 开夜车 is staying up on a particular night to finish work or study; 夜猫子 is a person who habitually stays up late.

cards.cue: Your roommate is never in bed before three a.m., not because of work or exams, but simply because that's when they feel most awake. What kind of person are they?

ctx.s: 我是个{夜猫子}，每天都两点以后才睡。
ctx.en: I'm a night owl; I never go to bed before two.

ctx.s: 他是出了名的{夜猫子}，你半夜给他发消息，他马上就回。
ctx.en: He's a notorious night owl: message him in the middle of the night and he replies straight away.

ctx.s: “你早上起得来吗？”“起不来，我是{夜猫子}，上午脑子都不清醒。”
ctx.en: "Can you get up in the mornings?" "No, I'm a night owl. My brain doesn't work before noon."

ctx.s: 自从上了大学，她就变成了{夜猫子}，作息全乱了。
ctx.en: Since starting university she's turned into a night owl, and her sleep schedule is a mess.

ctx.s: 这家便利店通宵营业，专门做{夜猫子}的生意。
ctx.en: This convenience store is open all night and caters to night owls.

ctx.s: 医生劝他别再当{夜猫子}了，长期熬夜对身体不好。
ctx.en: The doctor told him to stop being a night owl, as staying up late all the time is bad for his health.

bad.s: 明天考试，我今晚要{夜猫子}。
bad.en: (meant: I have an exam tomorrow, so I'll stay up all night tonight)
bad.why: It is a noun for a habitual night person, not a verb. Staying up one night to study is kai yeche or aoye.

bad.s: 我家有一只{夜猫子}，每天晚上出去抓老鼠。
bad.en: (meant: our cat goes out mouse-hunting every night)
bad.why: It does not mean a cat. The word is a folk name for the owl, and as an idiom it describes a person who stays up late.

cards.mean: to let one's attention wander from the task at hand
cards.lit: to slip away from one's post; first said of soldiers quietly deserting, now of a mind drifting off

use.how: An intransitive verb phrase, often with 思想 or 注意力 as subject, or 上课开小差. Said of a mind drifting off in class, at a meeting or at work.

near.diff: 走神 is the plain word for a moment of distraction; 开小差 is more colloquial and suggests drifting away from something one should be doing.

cards.cue: During a long lecture a student stares out of the window thinking about the weekend, and the teacher notices. What is the student doing?

ctx.s: 上课不要{开小差}，认真听讲。
ctx.en: Don't let your mind wander in class; listen carefully.

ctx.s: 开会的时候我{开了一会儿小差}，没听到老板说了什么。
ctx.en: My mind drifted off for a while in the meeting, and I didn't hear what the boss said.

ctx.s: 你又{开小差}了吧？我刚才说的你听见了吗？
ctx.en: You've drifted off again, haven't you? Did you hear what I just said?

ctx.s: 开车的时候千万不能{开小差}，一不留神就会出事。
ctx.en: You must never let your attention wander while driving; one lapse and there's an accident.

ctx.s: 他做题时思想{开小差}，把加号看成了减号。
ctx.en: His mind wandered while he was doing the problems, and he read a plus sign as a minus.

ctx.s: 老师看出小明在{开小差}，就点名让他回答问题。
ctx.en: The teacher saw that Xiao Ming wasn't paying attention and called on him to answer a question.

bad.s: 周末我去海边{开小差}了，玩得很开心。
bad.en: (meant: I took a little trip to the seaside at the weekend and had fun)
bad.why: It is not a short break or outing; it criticises a mind wandering (or slipping away from a duty).

bad.s: 我{开小差}了老师的课。
bad.en: (meant: I wasn't paying attention in the teacher's class)
bad.why: It takes no object; put the setting in front instead: 'in the teacher's class I drifted off' (zai ... shang kai xiao chai).

cards.mean: to hold others back and slow their progress
cards.lit: to drag at someone's hind leg so they cannot move forward

use.how: Verb-object, often split: 拖某人(的)后腿, or 给某人拖后腿. Said of a person or factor that holds back a team, a plan or someone's progress.

near.diff: 掉链子 is failing oneself at the crucial moment; 拖后腿 is holding other people back, often over a period of time.
绊脚石 is a noun for the obstacle itself; 拖后腿 is the action of holding others back.

cards.cue: Everyone in the group has finished their part of the project except one member, whose slowness keeps delaying the whole team. What is he doing to them?

ctx.s: 我数学不好，总是给全班{拖后腿}。
ctx.en: I'm bad at maths and always drag the whole class's results down.

ctx.s: 你放心去国外读书吧，我不会{拖你后腿}的。
ctx.en: Go and study abroad without worrying; I won't hold you back.

ctx.s: 为了不{拖大家的后腿}，她每天晚上都偷偷加练。
ctx.en: So as not to hold everyone back, she secretly put in extra practice every evening.

ctx.s: 就因为你一个人迟到，全组都晚了一个小时，你说你是不是在{拖后腿}？
ctx.en: The whole group was an hour late just because of you. Tell me, aren't you holding us back?

ctx.s: 交通不便一直在{拖着这个小镇经济的后腿}。
ctx.en: Poor transport links have long held back the town's economy.

ctx.s: 他想辞职创业，可是父母一直{拖他后腿}。
ctx.en: He wants to quit his job and start a business, but his parents keep holding him back.

bad.s: 别生气，我只是{拖你后腿}，开个玩笑。
bad.en: (meant: don't be angry, I'm just pulling your leg)
bad.why: It is not 'pulling your leg'; it means holding someone back. For teasing say kai wanxiao (to joke).

bad.s: 这块大石头{拖后腿}了我们的路。
bad.en: (meant: this big rock blocked our road)
bad.why: It is about people or factors slowing progress, not a physical blockage, and it cannot take an object after it.

cards.mean: to guarantee that something will be so
cards.lit: to write out a guarantee slip, like the written warranty a shop once gave with its goods

use.how: Verb-object: 我敢打包票, 我(跟你)打包票, and in the negative 打不了包票 or 不敢打这个包票. The speaker stakes their word on an outcome.

near.diff: 拍胸脯 is a confident gesture of taking responsibility; 打包票 is the promise that a particular result will come true.

cards.cue: A friend worries that the restaurant you picked will be disappointing. You are completely sure it is excellent and stake your word on it. What do you say?

ctx.s: 这家店的菜绝对好吃，我{打包票}。
ctx.en: The food here is definitely good, I guarantee it.

ctx.s: 我敢{打包票}，他明天一定会准时来。
ctx.en: I'll bet you anything he'll be on time tomorrow.

ctx.s: 这件事能不能办成，我可{打不了包票}。
ctx.en: Whether this can be done, I really can't promise.

ctx.s: 卖家一再{打包票}，说这台二手手机没有任何问题。
ctx.en: The seller kept assuring us that this second-hand phone had nothing wrong with it.

ctx.s: 医生说手术成功率很高，但谁也不敢{打这个包票}。
ctx.en: The doctor said the operation's success rate is high, but nobody would dare guarantee it.

ctx.s: 你凭什么{打包票}说他不会骗我们？
ctx.en: What makes you so sure you can guarantee he won't cheat us?

bad.s: 吃不完的菜我们{打包票}带回家吧。
bad.en: (meant: let's box up the leftovers and take them home)
bad.why: Boxing up leftovers is just dabao; adding piao makes it 'to guarantee', which has nothing to do with packing food.

bad.s: 我{打包票}明天可能会下雨。
bad.en: (meant: I reckon it might rain tomorrow)
bad.why: A guarantee expresses full certainty, so it cannot go with 'might' (keneng) or a mere guess.

cards.mean: to go through the motions just for show
cards.lit: to cross the stage: walk on from one side and off the other without stopping to perform

story.text: In Chinese opera a guochang is a brief crossing of the stage: a character comes on from one side and walks straight off the other without stopping to sing or act, simply to show a journey or link two scenes. From this stage practice, 'walking a guochang' came to mean doing something in form only, passing through it without any real substance.

use.how: A verb phrase: 只是走过场, 走走过场, 走个过场, 不能走过场. Said of inspections, meetings, procedures or interviews carried out in form only.

near.diff: 做样子 is putting on a show to impress someone; 走过场 is carrying out a required procedure in form only, without substance.

cards.cue: Inspectors arrive to check a factory's safety, chat with the manager over tea for ten minutes, sign the forms and leave. What was the inspection?

ctx.s: 这次检查要认真一点，别{走过场}。
ctx.en: Be thorough with this inspection; don't just go through the motions.

ctx.s: 所谓的面试只是{走个过场}，人早就定好了。
ctx.en: The so-called interview was just a formality; the person had been chosen long ago.

ctx.s: 每次开会都{走走过场}，什么问题也解决不了。
ctx.en: Every meeting is just for show; nothing ever gets solved.

ctx.s: 群众提出的意见要认真处理，不能{走过场}。
ctx.en: Complaints raised by the public must be dealt with seriously, not handled as a mere formality.

ctx.s: 这个培训到底有没有用？还是又在{走过场}？
ctx.en: Is this training actually any use, or is it just another box-ticking exercise?

ctx.s: 那天领导来视察，工厂{走完过场}，第二天一切又恢复原样。
ctx.en: The day the leaders came to inspect, the factory put on its show, and the next day everything went back to how it was.

bad.s: 我每天下班都{走过场}，经过那家咖啡馆。
bad.en: (meant: every day after work I walk past that café)
bad.why: It is not literal walking past a place; it criticises doing something in form only.

bad.s: 他工作非常认真，每个细节都{走过场}。
bad.en: (meant: he works very carefully and goes over every detail)
bad.why: It means perfunctory and is a criticism; it cannot describe careful, thorough work.

cards.mean: to deliberately say or do the opposite of others
cards.lit: to sing the opposite tune from everyone else

use.how: Verb-object, usually 跟/和某人唱反调, 老唱反调, 唱起反调来. Said of someone who deliberately or habitually opposes others' views or plans.

near.diff: 泼冷水 dampens someone's enthusiasm with discouraging words; 唱反调 takes the opposite position and argues or acts against it.

cards.cue: Whatever the rest of the team proposes, one colleague always argues for the exact opposite, as if on principle. What does he keep doing?

ctx.s: 你怎么老{唱反调}？我说东你就说西。
ctx.en: Why do you always contradict me? I say east, you say west.

ctx.s: 大家都同意去爬山，就他一个人{唱反调}，非要去看电影。
ctx.en: Everyone agreed to go hiking; he alone took the opposite line and insisted on going to the cinema.

ctx.s: 孩子到了青春期，总爱跟父母{唱反调}。
ctx.en: Once children hit adolescence, they love to do the opposite of what their parents say.

ctx.s: 我不是故意跟你{唱反调}，只是觉得这个计划有风险。
ctx.en: I'm not trying to oppose you on purpose; I just think this plan is risky.

ctx.s: 他在会上公开跟老板{唱起了反调}，气氛一下子变得很尴尬。
ctx.en: He openly took the opposite line to the boss in the meeting, and the atmosphere turned awkward at once.

ctx.s: 这本书的作者偏偏{唱反调}，认为早起并没有什么好处。
ctx.en: The author of this book deliberately goes against the grain, arguing that getting up early has no real benefit.

bad.s: 尊敬的评委，我想对您的观点{唱反调}。
bad.en: (meant: respected judges, I would like to respectfully disagree with your view)
bad.why: It is colloquial and critical, implying deliberate contrariness; for polite disagreement say 'I see it differently' (wo you butong de kanfa).

bad.s: 他经常{唱反调}我。
bad.en: (meant: he often contradicts me)
bad.why: It takes no direct object; the person goes before it with gen or he: 'he often sings the opposite tune with me'.

cards.mean: advice that goes in one ear and out the other
cards.lit: wind blowing past the ear: heard for a moment, then gone

use.how: A noun, almost always in 把…当(成)耳边风 or 当耳边风. Said of advice, warnings or instructions that someone ignores. Also said 耳旁风.

cards.cue: A mother has told her son again and again to wear a coat, but he never listens and goes out in a T-shirt once more. How does she complain?

ctx.s: 我跟你说了多少遍了，你全当{耳边风}！
ctx.en: How many times have I told you? It just goes in one ear and out the other!

ctx.s: 医生让他戒烟，他却把医生的话当成了{耳边风}。
ctx.en: The doctor told him to quit smoking, but he just ignored what the doctor said.

ctx.s: 别把老师的提醒当{耳边风}，这些内容考试真的会考。
ctx.en: Don't ignore the teacher's reminders; this material really will be on the exam.

ctx.s: 经理提醒过好几次要备份文件，大家都当{耳边风}，结果电脑一坏全没了。
ctx.en: The manager reminded us several times to back up our files, but nobody listened, and when the computer died everything was lost.

ctx.s: 我的话在你那儿是不是就是{耳边风}？
ctx.en: Does anything I say to you ever actually sink in?

ctx.s: 父亲的忠告他当年当作{耳边风}，现在后悔也来不及了。
ctx.en: Back then he let his father's advice go in one ear and out the other; now it's too late for regrets.

bad.s: 老师的建议对我帮助很大，真是{耳边风}。
bad.en: (meant: the teacher's advice helped me a lot; it was wise words in my ear)
bad.why: It means advice that is ignored, so it cannot describe advice that helped.

bad.s: 他{耳边风}了我的话。
bad.en: (meant: he ignored what I said)
bad.why: It is a noun, not a verb; use the frame 'take my words as wind past the ear' (ba ... dang er bian feng).

cards.mean: a miser who will never part with a penny
cards.lit: an iron rooster: as the saying goes, you cannot pluck a single feather from it

use.how: A noun for a person: 他是个铁公鸡, or used as a nickname. Often teasing among friends, but insulting if said in earnest.

near.diff: 一毛不拔 is a four-character idiom describing stingy behaviour; 铁公鸡 is a noun that labels the stingy person.

cards.cue: A colleague earns a good salary but has never once paid for a round of coffee and always 'forgets' his wallet. What do people call him?

ctx.s: 他是有名的{铁公鸡}，从来不请客。
ctx.en: He's a famous skinflint; he never treats anyone.

ctx.s: 想让那个{铁公鸡}借钱给你？别做梦了。
ctx.en: You want that miser to lend you money? Dream on.

ctx.s: 没想到这位{铁公鸡}今天居然请大家吃饭了！
ctx.en: Who'd have thought our resident skinflint would actually buy everyone dinner today!

ctx.s: 老板连年终奖都不发，真是个{铁公鸡}。
ctx.en: The boss won't even pay a year-end bonus; what a tightwad.

ctx.s: 我不是{铁公鸡}，只是最近手头有点紧。
ctx.en: I'm not a cheapskate; I'm just a bit short of money lately.

ctx.s: 村里人都叫他{铁公鸡}，因为他连一根葱都舍不得送人。
ctx.en: The villagers all called him the iron rooster, because he wouldn't even give away a single spring onion.

bad.s: 我爸爸身体很强壮，像{铁公鸡}一样。
bad.en: (meant: my dad is very strong, as tough as iron)
bad.why: The image is about not giving up a feather, i.e. stinginess, not strength or toughness.

bad.s: 她很会省钱，真是个{铁公鸡}，我很佩服她。
bad.en: (meant: she is so good at saving money, I admire her)
bad.why: It is an insult for a miser; to praise thrift say jiejian (frugal) instead.

cards.mean: spending money freely and wastefully
cards.lit: big hands and big feet: letting money slip through wide-open hands

use.how: A predicate or adverbial: 花钱大手大脚, 大手大脚地花钱. Said of someone's spending habits, sometimes of wasting materials.

near.diff: 挥金如土 is a bookish, stronger idiom for squandering money lavishly; 大手大脚 is the everyday criticism of loose spending habits.

cards.cue: A student gets his monthly allowance and spends it all on takeaways and new trainers in the first week, then has to borrow. How do his parents describe his spending habits?

ctx.s: 他花钱{大手大脚}，每个月都不够用。
ctx.en: He spends money like water and never has enough by the end of the month.

ctx.s: 刚工作的年轻人，千万别{大手大脚}地花钱。
ctx.en: Young people who have just started work really shouldn't spend money carelessly.

ctx.s: 你以前{大手大脚}惯了，现在得学会省着点。
ctx.en: You're used to splashing money around; now you need to learn to economise.

ctx.s: 公司最近效益不好，各部门不能再{大手大脚}了。
ctx.en: The company is doing badly these days; no department can keep spending freely.

ctx.s: 你一个月才挣多少钱啊？怎么这么{大手大脚}？
ctx.en: How much do you even earn a month? Why are you so free with your money?

ctx.s: 中了奖以后，他变得{大手大脚}，不到两年就把钱花光了。
ctx.en: After winning the lottery he started spending lavishly, and the money was gone in under two years.

bad.s: 这个月钱不够用，我只好{大手大脚}地过日子。
bad.en: (meant: money is short this month, so I have to live frugally)
bad.why: It means spending freely and wastefully, the opposite of scrimping; for living frugally say shengchijianyong.

bad.s: 他对朋友很{大手大脚}，经常慷慨地帮助别人。
bad.en: (meant: he is very generous to his friends and often helps them)
bad.why: It criticises wasteful spending; for generosity say dafang or kangkai.

cards.mean: (of money or effort) to be wasted with nothing in return
cards.lit: to skip a stone across water: it bounces a few times, then sinks without a trace

use.how: With money, investment or effort as subject: 钱全打水漂了, 几十万打了水漂. An agent can use 拿: 拿钱打水漂. Said when what was put in brings nothing back.

near.diff: 泡汤 is a plan or hope falling through; 打水漂 is money or effort already spent being lost.

cards.cue: You paid a full year's gym membership in advance, and a month later the gym shut down and the owner disappeared. What happened to your money?

ctx.s: 我买的那只股票跌没了，钱全{打水漂}了。
ctx.en: The stock I bought collapsed; all my money went down the drain.

ctx.s: 他投资朋友的饭店，结果几十万都{打了水漂}。
ctx.en: He invested in a friend's restaurant, and hundreds of thousands were simply lost.

ctx.s: 要是现在退学，前面交的几万块学费不就{打水漂}了吗？
ctx.en: If you drop out now, won't the tens of thousands you've paid in fees have been thrown away?

ctx.s: 装修公司跑路了，我们交的定金全{打了水漂}。
ctx.en: The renovation company did a runner, and our whole deposit was lost.

ctx.s: 这么多钱不能就这么{打水漂}，我们得想办法要回来。
ctx.en: We can't just let all that money vanish; we have to find a way to get it back.

ctx.s: 项目最后被取消了，公司投进去的几百万和团队三个月的心血全{打了水漂}。
ctx.en: The project was cancelled in the end, and the millions the company put in and three months of the team's hard work were all lost.

bad.s: 他很会理财，每笔投资都{打水漂}，赚了不少钱。
bad.en: (meant: he is good with money; every investment paid off and he earned a lot)
bad.why: It means money lost with nothing back, the opposite of a profitable investment.

bad.s: 我{打水漂}了很多钱。
bad.en: (meant: I wasted a lot of money)
bad.why: The money must be the subject ('my money skipped away'), not the object; to name the person who wastes it, use na: na qian da shuipiao (throw money away).

cards.mean: to fake an accident or injury to extort compensation
cards.lit: to bump into porcelain, so that it 'breaks' and the other side must pay

use.how: A verb or noun: 他在碰瓷, 被人碰瓷, 碰瓷的 (the scammer). Said of staged accidents, typically someone throwing themselves at a car or bike and demanding money.

cards.cue: A man suddenly drops to the ground in front of a slowly moving car and demands money from the driver, though the car never touched him. What is he doing?

ctx.s: 那个人根本没被撞到，他是在{碰瓷}！
ctx.en: That man wasn't hit at all; he's faking it to get money!

ctx.s: 幸好车上有行车记录仪，不然就被人{碰瓷}了。
ctx.en: Luckily the car had a dashcam, otherwise we'd have been scammed with a fake accident.

ctx.s: 最近这条路上有人专门{碰瓷}，开车要小心。
ctx.en: Lately someone has been staging accidents on this road; drive carefully.

ctx.s: 他突然倒在你车前，会不会是{碰瓷}的？
ctx.en: He suddenly fell in front of your car; could he be a scammer faking an accident?

ctx.s: 警察调出监控，证明那个男人是故意{碰瓷}。
ctx.en: The police pulled the surveillance footage and proved the man had staged the accident on purpose.

ctx.s: 有人故意往豪车上撞，想借{碰瓷}讹一大笔钱。
ctx.en: Some people deliberately throw themselves at luxury cars, hoping a faked accident will extort a big payout.

bad.s: 我不小心{碰瓷}了妈妈的花瓶，花瓶碎了。
bad.en: (meant: I accidentally knocked over my mum's vase and it broke)
bad.why: It is not literally knocking porcelain; it means a deliberate scam with a faked accident.

bad.s: 他在路上真的被车撞伤了，这是一次{碰瓷}。
bad.en: (meant: he really was hit and injured by a car; it was an accident)
bad.why: A genuine accident is not pengci; the word means the accident or injury was faked to get money.

cards.mean: to take away someone's job or livelihood
cards.lit: to snatch someone's rice bowl

use.how: Verb-object phrase, often split: 抢(某人的)饭碗, 被抢了饭碗. Said of rivals, newcomers or machines taking the work people live on; often voiced as a worry.

near.diff: 炒鱿鱼 is an employer dismissing you; 抢饭碗 is a rival, newcomer or new technology taking the work you live on.
挖墙脚 is luring away a rival's people; 抢饭碗 is taking over the work that someone else earns a living from.

cards.cue: Translators worry that machine translation will soon do their work for free and leave them with nothing. What do they fear it will do?

ctx.s: 别担心，我不是来{抢你的饭碗}的，只是帮几天忙。
ctx.en: Don't worry, I'm not here to take your job; I'm just helping out for a few days.

ctx.s: 新来的实习生干得这么好，老员工都怕他{抢饭碗}。
ctx.en: The new intern is doing so well that the old staff are afraid he'll take their jobs.

ctx.s: 很多翻译担心人工智能会{抢走他们的饭碗}。
ctx.en: Many translators worry that AI will take their livelihood away.

ctx.s: “你这么会做菜，干脆开个餐厅吧！”“我爸就是厨师，那不是{抢我爸的饭碗}吗？”
ctx.en: "You cook so well, why not open a restaurant?" "My dad is a chef; wouldn't that be taking his job?"

ctx.s: 外地的出租车越来越多，本地司机觉得被{抢了饭碗}。
ctx.en: With more and more taxis from out of town, local drivers feel their livelihood has been taken.

ctx.s: 网上书店兴起以后，不少小书店被{抢了饭碗}，只好关门。
ctx.en: When online bookshops took off, many small bookshops lost their trade and had to close.

bad.s: 我总是迟到，所以老板昨天{抢了我的饭碗}。
bad.en: (meant: my boss fired me yesterday because I'm always late)
bad.why: Being dismissed by your own employer is chao youyu; this idiom is a rival or newcomer taking over the work you live on.

bad.s: 他在银行工作，是个{抢饭碗}，很稳定。
bad.en: (meant: he works at a bank, a secure job)
bad.why: A secure job for life is tie fanwan. This is a verb phrase about taking someone's job, not a kind of job.

cards.mean: (of someone with power) to make life hard for a person out of spite
cards.lit: to make someone wear shoes that are too small

use.how: Usually 给某人穿小鞋 or 被穿小鞋. Said of a boss or official quietly punishing someone under them, e.g. one who offended or criticised them.

near.diff: 眼中钉 is the person someone hates; 穿小鞋 is what a superior does to such a person: quietly making their work life hard.

cards.cue: You criticised your department head at a meeting; since then she keeps giving you the worst shifts and turning down your leave requests. What is she doing to you?

ctx.s: 他得罪了经理，以后恐怕要被{穿小鞋}了。
ctx.en: He offended the manager; I'm afraid he'll be made to suffer for it from now on.

ctx.s: 你放心提意见，我保证没人会给你{穿小鞋}。
ctx.en: Feel free to speak your mind; I promise no one will make things hard for you because of it.

ctx.s: 老板是不是因为那件事在给你{穿小鞋}？
ctx.en: Is the boss making life hard for you because of that business?

ctx.s: 自从我在会上反对了主任，她就总给我{穿小鞋}，最累的活儿都派给我。
ctx.en: Ever since I opposed the director at the meeting, she's been getting back at me, giving me all the hardest jobs.

ctx.s: 有的领导心胸狭窄，谁说了实话就给谁{穿小鞋}。
ctx.en: Some narrow-minded bosses make life difficult for anyone who tells the truth.

ctx.s: 他的业绩明明最好，却年年评不上先进，大家都知道是有人给他{穿小鞋}。
ctx.en: His results are clearly the best, yet he's never named a model worker; everyone knows someone is punishing him.

bad.s: 我得罪了经理，所以我给他{穿小鞋}了。
bad.en: (meant: I offended the manager, so he made life hard for me)
bad.why: The one with power does it to the weaker person, so the manager must be the subject (or use bei). As written, you punished the manager.

bad.s: 我妹妹总是给我{穿小鞋}，老抢我的玩具。
bad.en: (meant: my little sister is always mean to me and takes my toys)
bad.why: It needs someone with power over you, such as a boss, abusing it out of spite; a squabbling sibling does not fit.

cards.mean: to lure away another's staff or partner, undermining them
cards.lit: to dig away at the foot of someone's wall

use.how: Verb-object phrase: 挖(某人/某公司的)墙脚, 被挖了墙脚. Said of a rival luring away key staff or clients, or someone pursuing another person's partner.

near.diff: 跳槽 is the employee choosing to leave; 挖墙脚 is the rival who actively lures them away.
抢饭碗 is taking over someone's work and livelihood; 挖墙脚 is pulling away the people a team or company depends on.

cards.cue: A rival firm secretly offers your three best engineers double pay to join them, and they all leave. What has the rival done to your company?

ctx.s: 我们团队刚有起色，你就来{挖墙脚}，太不够意思了吧？
ctx.en: Our team has only just got going and you come poaching our people? That's not on.

ctx.s: 对手公司出高薪{挖我们的墙脚}，一下子走了三个工程师。
ctx.en: A rival company poached our staff with high salaries; three engineers left at once.

ctx.s: 他明知道那个女孩是朋友的女朋友，还天天约她，这不是{挖墙脚}吗？
ctx.en: He knew that girl was his friend's girlfriend and still kept asking her out. Isn't that trying to steal her from him?

ctx.s: 公司给骨干员工涨了工资，就是怕被别人{挖了墙脚}。
ctx.en: The company raised its key staff's pay precisely because it was afraid of having them poached.

ctx.s: 老板问我最近是不是有人来{挖墙脚}，我说没有。
ctx.en: The boss asked me whether anyone had been trying to poach me lately; I said no.

ctx.s: 他说是来谈合作的，其实是来{挖墙脚}的，一个月就带走了我们一半的客户。
ctx.en: He claimed he'd come to discuss working together, but he was really poaching: within a month he'd taken half our clients.

bad.s: 这家公司工资太低了，我想{挖墙脚}，换一份工作。
bad.en: (meant: the pay here is too low, I want to change jobs)
bad.why: Leaving for another employer yourself is tiaocao; this idiom is what the rival does when it lures people away.

bad.s: 那家公司的待遇特别好，很{挖墙脚}。
bad.en: (meant: that company pays so well it attracts people away)
bad.why: It is a verb-object phrase, not an adjective, so it cannot follow hen; say the company often poaches others' staff.

cards.mean: to give the go-ahead or let something through
cards.lit: to switch on the green light

use.how: Usually 给某人/某事开绿灯, or 一路开绿灯. Said of those with authority allowing something or easing its way; can criticise improper favours.

near.diff: 拍板 is the person in charge making the final call; 开绿灯 is letting something go ahead or easing its way past the usual hurdles.
走后门 is what the person seeking a favour does; 开绿灯 is what the person granting passage does.

cards.cue: A hospital lets patients over seventy skip the queue and see a doctor straight away. What is the hospital doing for them?

ctx.s: 经理已经{开了绿灯}，我们下周就可以开始。
ctx.en: The manager has given us the go-ahead; we can start next week.

ctx.s: 妈妈，我周末想去同学家住，你就{开个绿灯}吧！
ctx.en: Mum, I want to stay at my classmate's this weekend. Please just say yes!

ctx.s: 为了方便老人看病，医院给七十岁以上的患者{开绿灯}，不用排队。
ctx.en: To make things easier for the elderly, the hospital fast-tracks patients over seventy so they don't have to queue.

ctx.s: 市里对新能源汽车一路{开绿灯}，审批时间缩短了一半。
ctx.en: The city has cleared the way for new-energy vehicles at every step, cutting approval times by half.

ctx.s: 这种不合规定的项目，谁给它{开的绿灯}？
ctx.en: Who let a project that breaks the rules like this go through?

ctx.s: 有些官员给亲戚的公司{开绿灯}，结果出了大问题。
ctx.en: Some officials waved their relatives' companies through, and it ended in serious trouble.

bad.s: 我{开绿灯}了，所以终于可以出国留学了。
bad.en: (meant: I got permission, so I can finally study abroad)
bad.why: The one who switches on the green light grants the permission; to receive it, make the school the subject: the school gave me the green light.

bad.s: 这个领导很{开绿灯}，什么都同意。
bad.en: (meant: this boss is very permissive and agrees to everything)
bad.why: It is a verb phrase, not an adjective, so hen cannot modify it; say he gives everything the green light.

cards.mean: to make the final decision as the person in charge
cards.lit: to slap the board

use.how: A verb, used alone or split as 拍了板: 这事得老板拍板. Said of the person with authority settling a matter after discussion.

near.diff: 开绿灯 is allowing something or easing its way; 拍板 is the person in charge settling the matter once and for all.

cards.cue: Your team has argued for hours over two plans; nothing is settled until the director finally says which one you will go with. What does the director do?

ctx.s: 年会去北京还是去上海，我说了不算，得老板{拍板}。
ctx.en: Whether the annual party is in Beijing or Shanghai isn't up to me; the boss has to make the call.

ctx.s: 买房子这么大的事，你们家谁{拍板}？
ctx.en: For something as big as buying a flat, who makes the final call in your family?

ctx.s: 两个方案各有优点，最后用哪个，还要董事会来{拍板}。
ctx.en: Both proposals have their merits; which one we finally use is for the board to decide.

ctx.s: 他是部门经理，这点小事可以当场{拍板}。
ctx.en: He's the department manager; he can settle a small matter like this on the spot.

ctx.s: 大家讨论了一个下午，最后还是校长{拍了板}：明年春天搬校区。
ctx.en: Everyone talked all afternoon; in the end the principal made the call: the school moves campus next spring.

ctx.s: 两家公司谈了半年，终于在昨天{拍板}成交。
ctx.en: After six months of talks, the two companies finally sealed the deal yesterday.

bad.s: 他气得{拍板}大骂。
bad.en: (meant: he slapped the table in anger and swore)
bad.why: Slapping the table in anger is pai zhuozi; this idiom only means making the final decision.

bad.s: 这个问题太难了，我还在{拍板}，明天再告诉你。
bad.en: (meant: this is hard, I'm still deciding; I'll tell you tomorrow)
bad.why: It is the moment the decision is settled, not the process of weighing it up; for that say you are still considering it.

cards.mean: to coast on past achievements without new effort
cards.lit: to live by eating into one's original capital

use.how: Verb-object phrase, often with 靠, 光, 不能: 不能吃老本. Criticises a person or business living off old success or old skills. Can also mean living off one's savings.

near.diff: 走下坡路 describes a steady decline; 吃老本 names a cause: living off past success instead of making new effort.

cards.cue: A singer had one hit album twenty years ago and has toured with the same songs ever since without writing anything new. What is he doing?

ctx.s: 学习不能{吃老本}，要不断学新东西。
ctx.en: In learning you can't rest on what you already know; you have to keep learning new things.

ctx.s: 你们公司这几年没出新产品，是不是在{吃老本}？
ctx.en: Your company hasn't brought out a new product for years. Is it just coasting?

ctx.s: 我的日语是大学时候学的，现在全靠{吃老本}，好多词都忘了。
ctx.en: I learned my Japanese at university and I'm still living off that; I've forgotten lots of words.

ctx.s: 他靠十年前那部电影一直{吃老本}，再也没拍出好作品。
ctx.en: He has coasted on that film from ten years ago and never made anything good again.

ctx.s: 这家老字号光{吃老本}，不肯改进，客人越来越少。
ctx.en: This old brand just lives off its reputation and won't improve, so it has fewer and fewer customers.

ctx.s: 教练对冠军队员说：“去年的成绩不代表什么，别想着{吃老本}。”
ctx.en: The coach told the champions: "Last year's results mean nothing. Don't think you can rest on them."

bad.s: 他总是{吃老本}，真让人佩服。
bad.en: (meant: he always draws on his long experience, which is admirable)
bad.why: It is a criticism of coasting without new effort; it cannot be used to praise experience.

bad.s: 这个新同事刚来一周，就天天{吃老本}，不干活。
bad.en: (meant: this new colleague has been slacking every day since arriving last week)
bad.why: It needs a past success or store of skill to live off; a newcomer who is simply lazy is toulan, slacking.

cards.mean: to waste time through avoidable mistakes on the way
cards.lit: to take a winding, roundabout road

use.how: Verb-object phrase, often split: 少走弯路, 走了很多弯路. Said of detours and mistakes in study, work or life on the way to a goal.

near.diff: 走下坡路 is a steady decline; 走弯路 is a detour of avoidable mistakes on the way to a goal you may still reach.
