绕弯子 is talking around a point instead of saying it; 走弯路 is losing time through mistakes in what you do.

cards.cue: You spent two years learning piano with bad habits you then had to unlearn, and now you want your daughter to start with a good teacher so she avoids that. Why?

ctx.s: 有老师指导，你可以少{走弯路}。
ctx.en: With a teacher to guide you, you can avoid a lot of wasted effort.

ctx.s: 你当年创业的时候，{走过哪些弯路}？
ctx.en: When you started your business, what mistakes did you make along the way?

ctx.s: 我刚开始学吉他的时候{走了很多弯路}，练了半年还不会换和弦。
ctx.en: When I started learning guitar I went about it all wrong; after six months I still couldn't change chords.

ctx.s: 早知道有这个方法，我们就不用{走那么多弯路}了。
ctx.en: If we'd known about this method earlier, we wouldn't have wasted so much time.

ctx.s: 公司在海外市场{走了一段弯路}，后来才找到正确的方向。
ctx.en: The company took some wrong turns in overseas markets before it found the right direction.

ctx.s: 年轻人{走点弯路}也不是坏事，关键是要从中学到东西。
ctx.en: Making a few mistakes along the way isn't bad for young people; what matters is learning from them.

bad.s: 最近公司生意越来越差，一直在{走弯路}。
bad.en: (meant: business has been getting worse and worse lately)
bad.why: Steady decline is zou xiapo lu; this idiom is a detour of mistakes on the way to a goal.

bad.s: 他说话总是{走弯路}，从来不直接说。
bad.en: (meant: he always beats around the bush and never says things directly)
bad.why: Talking around the point is rao wanzi; this idiom is about wasting time through mistakes, not about speech.

cards.mean: to make a fool of oneself in front of others
cards.lit: to put on a 'foreign look': yangxiang has come to mean a ridiculous spectacle

use.how: Intransitive verb-object phrase, often split: 出了个大洋相, 出尽了洋相; make someone else do it with 让某人出洋相. Said of embarrassing, comic blunders in public.

near.diff: 丢人 is any shameful loss of face, even a serious one; 出洋相 is a comic, laughable blunder in front of others.

cards.cue: Walking onto the stage to collect your prize, you trip over the microphone cable and land flat in front of the whole school. What happened to you?

ctx.s: 我不会跳舞，别让我上去{出洋相}了。
ctx.en: I can't dance; don't make me go up there and embarrass myself.

ctx.s: 明天要用英语演讲，万一{出洋相}怎么办？
ctx.en: I have to give a speech in English tomorrow. What if I make a fool of myself?

ctx.s: 我第一次穿高跟鞋，在台上差点摔倒，{出了个大洋相}。
ctx.en: The first time I wore high heels I nearly fell over on stage. What an embarrassment!

ctx.s: 他喝多了，在婚礼上唱歌跑调，{出尽了洋相}。
ctx.en: He drank too much and sang off-key at the wedding, making a complete fool of himself.

ctx.s: 那位主持人把嘉宾的名字念错了，当场{出了洋相}。
ctx.en: The host mispronounced the guest's name and was embarrassed on the spot.

ctx.s: 有些人就喜欢看别人{出洋相}，这样很不好。
ctx.en: Some people just love watching others make fools of themselves, which isn't nice.

bad.s: 他去美国留学，在那儿{出洋相}了好几年。
bad.en: (meant: he studied in America and lived the foreign life there for years)
bad.why: Despite yang, 'foreign', it has nothing to do with going abroad; it means making a fool of yourself in public.

bad.s: 我在大家面前{出洋相}了他。
bad.en: (meant: I made him look a fool in front of everyone)
bad.why: It takes no object. To make someone else look foolish, use rang: make him look a fool (rang ta chu yangxiang).

cards.mean: to become popular or famous
cards.lit: to go red; red stands for popularity and good fortune

use.how: An intransitive verb, often with 在网上, 一夜之间, 迅速: 这首歌走红了. Said of performers, songs, places or products becoming widely known.

near.diff: 吃香 is being valued and sought after, said of skills, jobs or people; 走红 is becoming famous and talked about, said of stars, songs or places.

cards.cue: A street singer posts one video, and within a week millions have watched it and TV shows are calling her. What has happened to her?

ctx.s: 这首歌一夜之间在网上{走红}了。
ctx.en: This song became a hit online overnight.

ctx.s: 你知道这个小镇是怎么{走红}的吗？
ctx.en: Do you know how this little town became so famous?

ctx.s: 她因为一部电视剧{走红}，现在出门都要戴口罩。
ctx.en: She became famous through a TV series; now she has to wear a mask when she goes out.

ctx.s: 很多年轻人梦想当网红，可真正{走红}的没几个。
ctx.en: Lots of young people dream of being influencers, but very few actually make it big.

ctx.s: 这道家常菜去年突然{走红}，很多餐厅都加进了菜单。
ctx.en: This home-style dish suddenly took off last year, and many restaurants added it to their menus.

ctx.s: 他早年{走红}过一阵，后来就慢慢被人忘了。
ctx.en: He was famous for a while in his early years, then was gradually forgotten.

bad.s: 会说中文的人在外企很{走红}。
bad.en: (meant: people who speak Chinese are much in demand at foreign firms)
bad.why: Being in demand on the job market is chixiang; this idiom means becoming famous, which is not what is meant here.

bad.s: 他一害羞，脸就{走红}了。
bad.en: (meant: whenever he's shy, his face goes red)
bad.why: Blushing is lian hong; this idiom only means becoming popular or famous.

cards.mean: to be in high demand and much sought after
cards.lit: to eat something fragrant and tasty

use.how: Works like an adjective: 很吃香, 不太吃香, often with 在…: 在就业市场上很吃香. Said of skills, jobs, majors or people that are valued and wanted.

near.diff: 走红 is becoming famous and talked about; 吃香 is being valued and wanted, such as a skill employers look for.
吃得开 stresses a person getting on well and getting things done in some circle; 吃香 stresses being in demand and valued.

cards.cue: Every hospital in the city is short of experienced nurses, so they are offered jobs wherever they apply. How would you describe nurses on the job market?

ctx.s: 现在会编程的人特别{吃香}。
ctx.en: People who can code are in great demand these days.

ctx.s: 你觉得现在学什么专业最{吃香}？
ctx.en: Which university subject do you think is most sought after now?

ctx.s: 在我们村里，会修拖拉机的师傅最{吃香}。
ctx.en: In our village, mechanics who can fix tractors are the most in demand.

ctx.s: 以前当老师不太{吃香}，现在报考的人越来越多。
ctx.en: Teaching used to be not much sought after; now more and more people are applying.

ctx.s: 有经验的护士在各家医院都很{吃香}，根本不愁找工作。
ctx.en: Experienced nurses are in demand at every hospital; they never have to worry about finding work.

ctx.s: 既懂外语又懂技术的人才，到哪儿都{吃香}。
ctx.en: People who know both a foreign language and the technical side are in demand wherever they go.

bad.s: 这家餐厅的饭菜很{吃香}，我每次都吃很多。
bad.en: (meant: the food at this restaurant is delicious; I always eat a lot)
bad.why: It does not describe how food tastes; for that say haochi or hen xiang.

bad.s: 他面试很顺利，{吃香}了这份工作。
bad.en: (meant: his interview went well and he got the job)
bad.why: It takes no object and does not mean 'to get'; say he got (dedao) the job.

cards.mean: to have real skill and know what one is doing
cards.lit: to have a couple of moves: a few real blows or techniques up one's sleeve

use.how: Predicate after a person, often with 真, 还真, 确实 or 可: 你还真有两下子。 Praises skill someone has just shown; casual, so not for formal tributes.

near.diff: 小菜一碟 says a task is easy; 有两下子 praises the skill of the person who did it.

cards.cue: Your quiet new colleague fixes, in ten minutes, a printer the whole office had given up on. Impressed, you tell him he clearly knows his stuff.

ctx.s: 你还真{有两下子}，这么快就修好了！
ctx.en: You really know your stuff; you fixed it so fast!

ctx.s: 别看他年纪小，下棋可{有两下子}。
ctx.en: He may be young, but he's really good at chess.

ctx.s: 新来的同事做饭{有两下子}，聚餐时大家都抢着吃他做的菜。
ctx.en: Our new colleague can really cook; at the team dinner everyone fought over his dishes.

ctx.s: 能把这么乱的账理清楚，看来她确实{有两下子}。
ctx.en: She sorted out accounts in that state, so she clearly knows what she's doing.

ctx.s: “你会画画吗？”“会一点，画人像我还是{有两下子}的。”
ctx.en: "Can you draw?" "A bit. Portraits I'm actually pretty good at."

ctx.s: 他嘴上说自己不会打球，一上场大家才知道他{有两下子}。
ctx.en: He kept saying he couldn't play, but once he was on the court everyone saw how good he was.

bad.s: 这道数学题{有两下子}，我想了一个小时也不会做。
bad.en: (meant: this maths problem is tricky)
bad.why: It praises a person's skill; it cannot describe a problem as hard.

bad.s: 鲁迅先生在文学上{有两下子}，是现代文学的奠基人。
bad.en: (meant: Lu Xun was a towering literary figure)
bad.why: Far too casual for a great figure in formal writing; it sounds patronising, like praising a beginner.

cards.mean: a layman with no expertise in a field
cards.lit: a man outside the door: someone who has never stepped inside a craft or field

use.how: A noun, usually 是（个）门外汉 or 对……是门外汉. Most often said modestly of oneself; said of others it sounds dismissive.

near.diff: 外行 is the everyday word and can also be an adjective (这话很外行); 门外汉 is only a noun for a person.

cards.cue: At dinner your host asks what you think of an expensive wine, but you know nothing about wine. You modestly say you are no judge of it.

ctx.s: 我对音乐完全是个{门外汉}，听不出好坏。
ctx.en: I know nothing about music; I can't tell good from bad.

ctx.s: 说到投资，我就是个{门外汉}，你还是问别人吧。
ctx.en: When it comes to investing I'm a complete novice; you'd better ask someone else.

ctx.s: 这本书写得很浅显，连{门外汉}也能看懂。
ctx.en: This book is written so simply that even a layman can follow it.

ctx.s: “你觉得这个设计怎么样？”“我是{门外汉}，只能说说自己的感觉。”
ctx.en: "What do you think of this design?" "I'm no expert; I can only tell you my impression."

ctx.s: 三年前她还是摄影的{门外汉}，现在已经办了自己的影展。
ctx.en: Three years ago she knew nothing about photography; now she has held her own exhibition.

ctx.s: 他一个{门外汉}，凭什么对我们的方案指手画脚？
ctx.en: He knows nothing about this field; what gives him the right to tell us how to do our plan?

bad.s: 门口站着一个{门外汉}，好像在等人。
bad.en: (meant: a man is standing outside the door, waiting for someone)
bad.why: It is never literal; it only means a person with no knowledge of a field.

bad.s: 他对电脑很{门外汉}，连开机都不会。
bad.en: (meant: he is hopeless with computers)
bad.why: It is a noun and cannot follow hen (very); say he is a menwaihan when it comes to computers, or use waihang.

cards.mean: to take a chance and see whether luck is on one's side
cards.lit: to bump into luck: to try and see whether luck happens to be there

use.how: Verb-object, often reduplicated as 碰碰运气 after 去, 想 or 试着. Said of trying something with poor odds and no plan beyond hoping.

near.diff: 撞大运 means actually striking lucky by chance; 碰运气 is only the attempt, and it may well fail.

cards.cue: The concert is sold out, but you decide to go to the box office anyway in case someone returns a ticket. What are you doing?

ctx.s: 票早就卖完了，我们去门口{碰碰运气}吧。
ctx.en: The tickets sold out long ago, but let's try our luck at the door.

ctx.s: 这条河里鱼不多，来这儿钓鱼全凭{碰运气}。
ctx.en: There aren't many fish in this river; fishing here is down to luck.

ctx.s: 这次面试我没什么把握，就当是去{碰运气}。
ctx.en: I'm not confident about this interview; I'll treat it as taking a chance.

ctx.s: 考试一点都不复习，全靠{碰运气}，怎么可能及格？
ctx.en: You don't revise at all and just count on luck; how could you possibly pass?

ctx.s: 他把简历投给了几十家公司，想{碰碰运气}。
ctx.en: He sent his CV to dozens of companies, hoping to get lucky.

ctx.s: “你怎么知道这家店今天还开着？”“不知道，{碰运气}呗。”
ctx.en: "How do you know the shop is open today?" "I don't; I'm just trying my luck."

bad.s: 今天我很{碰运气}，在路上捡到了一百块钱。
bad.en: (meant: I was very lucky today and found a hundred yuan on the street)
bad.why: It is a verb phrase for trying one's luck, not an adjective for being lucky, so it cannot take hen; say wo yunqi hen hao.

bad.s: 明天你考试，祝你{碰运气}！
bad.en: (meant: good luck in your exam tomorrow!)
bad.why: It is not a wish; it suggests the person is just gambling. Say zhu ni haoyun (good luck) instead.

cards.mean: to produce a surprise upset, such as an underdog winning
cards.lit: to burst open the cold door: the choice few people back suddenly comes through

use.how: Verb-object, often split as 爆出冷门 or 爆了个大冷门. Said of sports, contests and awards when the unexpected side wins.

near.diff: 破天荒 is something happening for the very first time; 爆冷门 is an unexpected winner or result in a contest.

cards.cue: In the World Cup, a team ranked near the bottom beats the reigning champions. How does the sports news describe the result?

ctx.s: 昨晚的比赛{爆了个大冷门}，没人看好的小将赢了卫冕冠军。
ctx.en: Last night's match was a huge upset: a young player nobody rated beat the defending champion.

ctx.s: “你觉得今晚谁会赢？”“强队赢面大，不过也可能{爆冷门}。”
ctx.en: "Who do you think will win tonight?" "The stronger side should, but there could be an upset."

ctx.s: 这部小成本电影拿了最佳影片，算是{爆冷门}了。
ctx.en: This low-budget film winning best picture counts as a real surprise.

ctx.s: 排名最后的队把冠军队淘汰了，这算不算{爆冷门}？
ctx.en: The bottom-ranked team knocked out the champions; doesn't that count as an upset?

ctx.s: 赛前没人看好她，结果她拿了歌唱比赛第一名，{爆出了冷门}。
ctx.en: Nobody rated her before the contest, yet she won the singing competition: a real upset.

ctx.s: 这届运动会上，好几个项目都{爆出冷门}，老将纷纷落败。
ctx.en: At these games there were upsets in several events, with one veteran after another losing.

bad.s: 今天天气{爆冷门}，突然下雪了。
bad.en: (meant: the weather turned unexpectedly cold and it snowed)
bad.why: The 'cold' has nothing to do with temperature; it is about an unexpected result in a contest.

bad.s: 他是这次比赛最大的{爆冷门}。
bad.en: (meant: he is the biggest dark horse of the tournament)
bad.why: It is a verb phrase for the result, not a noun for a person; call him a heima (dark horse), or say that he bao le lengmen.

cards.mean: help that arrives just when it is most needed
cards.lit: timely rain: rain that falls just when the crops are dry

story.text: In the novel Water Margin, Song Jiang is a minor clerk in Yuncheng county who is famous for his generosity: he gives money and help freely to anyone in trouble. People everywhere call him by the nickname Timely Rain, because his help comes like rain falling on parched fields.

use.how: A noun: 是及时雨, 一场及时雨, 我的及时雨. Said of help, money or a person arriving at the very moment it was needed.

near.diff: 雪中送炭 is the act of helping someone in dire hardship; 及时雨 is the help itself, and stresses its perfect timing.

cards.cue: You are short of rent money with two days to go, and a friend unexpectedly repays a loan you had forgotten. What do you call that money?

ctx.s: 你这笔钱真是{及时雨}，我正愁交不起房租呢。
ctx.en: This money is a godsend; I was just worrying about paying the rent.

ctx.s: 考试前我忘了带计算器，同桌借给我一个，真是{及时雨}。
ctx.en: I forgot my calculator before the exam and my deskmate lent me one; perfect timing.

ctx.s: 正当我们人手不够的时候，他带着两个朋友来帮忙，简直是{及时雨}。
ctx.en: Just as we were short of hands, he turned up with two friends to help; a real lifesaver.

ctx.s: 这批订单对快撑不下去的小工厂来说，是一场{及时雨}。
ctx.en: For the small factory that was barely holding on, this batch of orders came just in time.

ctx.s: 新设的助学金，对家里困难的学生来说就像{及时雨}。
ctx.en: The new bursary is like timely rain for students from struggling families.

ctx.s: “我正愁找不到人翻译，你就来了！”“那我可是你的{及时雨}啊。”
ctx.en: "I was just fretting that I couldn't find a translator, and here you are!" "Then I'm your timely rescue."

bad.s: 他迟到了三个小时才来帮忙，真是{及时雨}。
bad.en: (meant: he came to help, three hours late)
bad.why: The whole point is perfect timing; help that comes too late is the opposite.

bad.s: 他每天都准时上班，是个{及时雨}。
bad.en: (meant: he is always punctual)
bad.why: It is not about punctuality; it is help that arrives when someone badly needs it.

cards.mean: something that sets one's mind at rest
cards.lit: a heart-steadying pill

use.how: A noun, usually with 吃: 吃了一颗定心丸, 给大家吃定心丸. Said of a promise, news or result that ends people's worry.

near.diff: 打包票 is the act of guaranteeing something; 定心丸 is the reassuring news or promise and its calming effect.
打预防针 warns people of bad news in advance; 定心丸 removes their worry.

cards.cue: Staff fear layoffs, and then the boss announces that nobody will lose their job this year. What has the announcement given them?

ctx.s: 医生说手术很成功，全家人像吃了一颗{定心丸}。
ctx.en: The doctor said the operation went well, and the whole family could finally relax.

ctx.s: 有你这句话，就等于给我吃了一颗{定心丸}。
ctx.en: Hearing you say that is all the reassurance I need.

ctx.s: 老板答应今年不裁员，等于给大家吃了{定心丸}。
ctx.en: The boss promised no layoffs this year, which put everyone's mind at ease.

ctx.s: 直到签了正式合同，房东才算给了我们一颗{定心丸}。
ctx.en: Only once the landlord signed the formal contract did we feel secure.

ctx.s: 上半场就领先三个球，这对球队来说是一颗{定心丸}。
ctx.en: Leading by three goals at half time gave the team real peace of mind.

ctx.s: “妈，我找到工作了。”“好啊，你这消息可让我吃了颗{定心丸}。”
ctx.en: "Mum, I've found a job." "Wonderful, that news takes a weight off my mind."

bad.s: 我晚上睡不着，医生给我开了几颗{定心丸}。
bad.en: (meant: I can't sleep, so the doctor prescribed some pills)
bad.why: In use it is figurative, never real medicine; sleeping pills are anmianyao.

bad.s: 他太紧张了，我们给他打了一个{定心丸}。
bad.en: (meant: we reassured him because he was so nervous)
bad.why: A pill is swallowed (chi), not injected; da goes with an injection (yufangzhen), not a pill.

cards.mean: to be on edge with worry for someone in a tight spot
cards.lit: to squeeze a handful of sweat: palms clenched and damp with tension

use.how: Verb phrase, usually 替/为某人捏一把汗 or 捏了/捏着一把汗. Said while watching someone face a risky or uncertain moment.

near.diff: 提心吊胆 is lasting fear and anxiety, often for oneself; 捏一把汗 is tense worry while watching someone else's risky moment.

cards.cue: Your friend, a beginner skier, heads straight down the steepest slope. Watching from below, you hold your breath for them.

ctx.s: 孩子第一次上台演讲，妈妈在下面替他{捏了一把汗}。
ctx.en: It was the boy's first speech on stage, and his mother sat below, tense with worry for him.

ctx.s: 看他在山路上开那么快，我真为他{捏一把汗}。
ctx.en: Watching him drive that fast on the mountain road, I was really on edge for him.

ctx.s: 比赛最后一分钟还是平局，球迷们都{捏着一把汗}。
ctx.en: With one minute left it was still level, and the fans were on the edge of their seats.

ctx.s: 你明天就要去面试了，我们都替你{捏着一把汗}呢。
ctx.en: You have your interview tomorrow; we're all nervous on your behalf.

ctx.s: 手术进行了六个小时，家属在门外一直{捏着一把汗}。
ctx.en: The operation lasted six hours, and the family waited outside, anxious the whole time.

ctx.s: 当时情况那么危险，现在想起来还替他{捏一把汗}。
ctx.en: It was so dangerous back then that even now, thinking about it, I feel nervous for him.

bad.s: 今天太热了，我走了几步就{捏了一把汗}。
bad.en: (meant: it was so hot that I was sweating after a few steps)
bad.why: It is never about real heat or sweating; it is tension while worrying for someone.

bad.s: 听说他升职了，我真替他{捏一把汗}。
bad.en: (meant: I'm really happy for him that he got promoted)
bad.why: It is anxious worry about a risky outcome, not joy; say wo zhen ti ta gaoxing (I'm so happy for him).

cards.mean: to lose one's nerve and back out of something midway
cards.lit: to beat the drum that closed a session in an old magistrate's court

use.how: Verb-object, often 想打退堂鼓, 打起了退堂鼓, 别打退堂鼓. Takes no object. Said of quitting something already begun because it looks hard.

near.diff: 掉链子 is failing others at the crucial moment; 打退堂鼓 is choosing to pull out because one has lost one's nerve.

cards.cue: You signed up for a marathon with friends, but after two weeks of training you tell them you want to pull out. What are they afraid you are doing?

ctx.s: 刚学了两天游泳，他就想{打退堂鼓}了。
ctx.en: He's only had two days of swimming lessons and already wants to quit.

ctx.s: 都已经报名了，你现在可不能{打退堂鼓}。
ctx.en: You've already signed up; you can't back out now.

ctx.s: 一听说要连续加班一个月，好几个人{打起了退堂鼓}。
ctx.en: As soon as they heard it meant a month of overtime, several people started getting cold feet.

ctx.s: 爬到半山腰，看到上面那么陡，我心里开始{打退堂鼓}。
ctx.en: Halfway up the mountain, seeing how steep it got, I began to lose my nerve.

ctx.s: “你不是说要跑马拉松吗？”“太累了，我还是{打退堂鼓}吧。”
ctx.en: "Weren't you going to run the marathon?" "It's too tiring; I think I'll back out."

ctx.s: 为了不让自己{打退堂鼓}，她把计划告诉了所有朋友。
ctx.en: So that she couldn't chicken out, she told all her friends about her plan.

bad.s: 电影结束了，我们{打退堂鼓}回家吧。
bad.en: (meant: the film's over, let's head home)
bad.why: It is not simply leaving; it means backing out of a commitment because one has lost one's nerve.

bad.s: 他{打退堂鼓}了这个项目。
bad.en: (meant: he pulled out of the project)
bad.why: It takes no direct object; the project must come before it, as in zai zhege xiangmu shang da le tuitanggu.

cards.r: bù guǎn sān qī èr shí yī
cards.mean: regardless of the consequences, without a second thought
cards.lit: never mind that three sevens make twenty-one: brushing all the calculations aside

use.how: An adverbial at the head of a clause, often followed by 就 or a comma: 他不管三七二十一就冲了进去。 Said of acting at once without weighing the consequences.

near.diff: 火烧眉毛 describes how urgent a situation is; 不管三七二十一 describes a person acting without weighing the consequences.

cards.cue: A child falls into a pond, and a passer-by jumps in at once without stopping to think whether they can swim well. How did they act?

ctx.s: 他{不管三七二十一}，拉起我就跑。
ctx.en: Without a second thought, he grabbed me and ran.

ctx.s: 饿了一整天，他{不管三七二十一}，抓起面包就吃。
ctx.en: Starving after a whole day, he grabbed the bread and ate it without a thought.

ctx.s: 你别{不管三七二十一}就签字，先把合同看清楚。
ctx.en: Don't just sign without thinking; read the contract carefully first.

ctx.s: 看到孩子掉进水里，他{不管三七二十一}就跳了下去。
ctx.en: Seeing the child fall into the water, he jumped straight in without hesitating.

ctx.s: “钱不够怎么办？”“{不管三七二十一}，先买了再说！”
ctx.en: "What if we don't have enough money?" "Forget all that, let's buy it first and worry later!"

ctx.s: 他做事总是{不管三七二十一}，结果经常出问题。
ctx.en: He always charges ahead without thinking, and things often go wrong as a result.

bad.s: {不管三七二十一}，他都考了第一名。
bad.en: (meant: whatever happened, he still came first)
bad.why: It is not 'no matter what'; it describes acting rashly. For 'in any case' say wulun ruhe or buguan zenyang.

bad.s: 经董事会研究，本公司决定{不管三七二十一}，下月起提高价格。
bad.en: (meant: the board has decided to raise prices from next month)
bad.why: It is casual speech and implies recklessness; it never belongs in a formal announcement.

cards.mean: very often, almost every other day
cards.lit: twice in three days: something comes round again every day or two

use.how: An adverbial before the verb: 三天两头生病, 三天两头往外跑. Says something keeps happening, usually with a note of complaint or worry.

near.diff: 时不时 is 'every now and then', a mild frequency; 三天两头 means so often that it is annoying or worrying.

cards.cue: Your new washing machine breaks down one week, then again the next, then again a few days later. How often does it go wrong?

ctx.s: 他{三天两头}感冒，身体太差了。
ctx.en: He catches a cold every few days; his health is really poor.

ctx.s: 这台洗衣机{三天两头}出毛病，还是换台新的吧。
ctx.en: This washing machine is forever breaking down; let's just get a new one.

ctx.s: 你怎么{三天两头}往我家跑？是不是有什么事？
ctx.en: Why do you keep coming round to my place? Is something up?

ctx.s: 楼上的邻居{三天两头}开派对，吵得我们睡不好觉。
ctx.en: The neighbours upstairs have parties all the time, and the noise keeps us awake.

ctx.s: 她刚搬到外地，{三天两头}给家里打电话。
ctx.en: She's just moved away, and she phones home every couple of days.

ctx.s: 小王{三天两头}请假，经理已经很不满意了。
ctx.en: Xiao Wang is always asking for time off, and the manager is getting fed up.

bad.s: 这次假期我出去玩，{三天两头}就回来了。
bad.en: (meant: on holiday I came back after just two or three days)
bad.why: It is about how often something happens, not how long something lasts.

bad.s: 他{三天两头}才来一次，我们很少见到他。
bad.en: (meant: he rarely comes, we hardly see him)
bad.why: It means very often, so it contradicts 'rarely'; for rare visits say hen shao lai.

cards.mean: hopelessly old and out of date
cards.lit: so old that its teeth have fallen out

use.how: An adjective: before 的 (老掉牙的笑话) or as a predicate (这手机太老掉牙了). Said of things, jokes, songs, ideas or methods, not of people.

near.diff: 过时 is a neutral word for out of fashion or no longer valid; 老掉牙 is colloquial and mocking, stressing that something is stale and very old.

cards.cue: Your uncle tells the same joke at every family dinner, and has done for twenty years. How do you describe the joke?

ctx.s: 这部手机太{老掉牙}了，连新软件都装不上。
ctx.en: This phone is ancient; it can't even install new apps.

ctx.s: 他每次聚会都讲那几个{老掉牙}的笑话。
ctx.en: At every party he tells the same few tired old jokes.

ctx.s: 别再用那套{老掉牙}的借口了，我不会信的。
ctx.en: Stop using that worn-out excuse; I'm not going to believe it.

ctx.s: 公司的电脑系统{老掉牙}了，经常死机，早该换了。
ctx.en: The company's computer system is hopelessly old and keeps crashing; it should have been replaced long ago.

ctx.s: 爷爷那台{老掉牙}的收音机，到现在还能响。
ctx.en: Grandpa's ancient old radio still works to this day.

ctx.s: 靠死记硬背学外语，这种方法早就{老掉牙}了。
ctx.en: Learning a foreign language by rote memorisation is a method that went out of date long ago.

bad.s: 我爸爸很{老掉牙}，晚上不让我出门。
bad.en: (meant: my dad is old-fashioned and won't let me go out at night)
bad.why: It describes outdated things, jokes and ideas, not a person's strict or conservative character.

bad.s: 这座寺庙是唐代建的，非常{老掉牙}，很有历史价值。
bad.en: (meant: the temple is ancient and historically valuable)
bad.why: It is a put-down for something stale and useless; it cannot praise great age or historical value.

cards.mean: happening for the very first time ever
cards.lit: to break open the never-tilled wasteland

story.text: In the Tang dynasty, Jingzhou sent candidates to the capital for the imperial examinations every year, but they almost never passed the highest degree, so its candidates were called 'tianhuang', wild land that had never been opened up. When Liu Tui of Jingzhou finally passed, people said he had 'broken the tianhuang'.

use.how: Mostly adverbial (破天荒地早到了, 破天荒头一回) or before 的. Marks a surprising first, often humorously about someone acting out of character.

near.diff: 史无前例 is formal and used of events on a historic scale; 破天荒 is lighter and fits personal firsts as well (他破天荒地洗了碗).
爆冷门 is an unexpected result, such as an underdog winning; 破天荒 is something that has simply never happened before.

cards.cue: Your brother, who has never once cooked in his life, makes dinner for the whole family tonight. How do you describe it?

ctx.s: 我哥哥今天{破天荒}地早起，还做了早饭。
ctx.en: My brother got up early today for once in his life, and even made breakfast.

ctx.s: 这是我们村{破天荒}头一回有人考上大学。
ctx.en: This is the very first time anyone from our village has got into university.

ctx.s: “你怎么{破天荒}请我吃饭了？”“今天发奖金嘛。”
ctx.en: "How come you're treating me to dinner, of all things?" "I got my bonus today."

ctx.s: 那位一向不爱说话的同事，{破天荒}地在会上发了言。
ctx.en: That colleague who never says a word spoke up at the meeting for the first time ever.

ctx.s: 这家百年老店{破天荒}地推出了外卖服务。
ctx.en: This century-old shop has launched a delivery service for the first time in its history.

ctx.s: 女性担任该校校长，在当时还是{破天荒}的事。
ctx.en: A woman serving as head of the school was, at the time, something that had never happened before.

bad.s: 我每天早上都{破天荒}地去跑步。
bad.en: (meant: I go running every morning)
bad.why: It marks a first, a break with all past habit, so it cannot describe something done every day.

bad.s: 这家餐厅的菜{破天荒}好吃。
bad.en: (meant: this restaurant's food is incredibly good)
bad.why: It means for the first time ever, not extremely; it is not an intensifier for adjectives.

cards.mean: (of rumours, ads etc.) to be found everywhere
cards.lit: flying all over the sky

use.how: A predicate after the thing that spreads: 谣言满天飞, 小广告满天飞. Suggests an uncontrolled, chaotic glut of something unwelcome.

near.diff: 铺天盖地 stresses overwhelming scale and can be neutral (铺天盖地的宣传); 满天飞 stresses that something is everywhere, unchecked and annoying.

cards.cue: After a celebrity's breakup, wild unverified stories pop up on every website and in every chat group. How do you describe the rumours?

ctx.s: 网上谣言{满天飞}，你别什么都信。
ctx.en: Rumours are flying all over the internet; don't believe everything you read.

ctx.s: 小区里小广告{满天飞}，墙上、电梯里到处都是。
ctx.en: Flyers are plastered all over our estate, on the walls and in the lifts.

ctx.s: “听说老板要辞职？”“别瞎说，最近这种消息{满天飞}。”
ctx.en: "I heard the boss is resigning?" "Don't talk nonsense; stories like that are going round everywhere lately."

ctx.s: 一到考试季，各种“押题秘籍”就{满天飞}。
ctx.en: As soon as exam season comes, 'guaranteed exam question' guides are everywhere.

ctx.s: 那几年，各种名目的收费{满天飞}，老百姓意见很大。
ctx.en: In those years fees of every description were being charged everywhere, and ordinary people were very unhappy.

ctx.s: 如今新概念{满天飞}，真正落地的项目却没几个。
ctx.en: These days new buzzwords are everywhere, but few projects actually get off the ground.

bad.s: 我把这个好消息{满天飞}了。
bad.en: (meant: I spread the good news everywhere)
bad.why: The subject must be the thing that is spreading, such as the news itself; it takes no object, so a person cannot do it to something.

bad.s: 老师的表扬{满天飞}，同学们都很受鼓励。
bad.en: (meant: the teacher's sincere praise encouraged everyone)
bad.why: It implies a cheap, chaotic glut, so it makes the praise sound worthless; it does not fit something you value.

cards.mean: to keep two options or partners going at once
cards.lit: standing with one foot in each of two boats

use.how: A predicate with no object: 他脚踩两只船. Said of someone secretly dating two people, or keeping in with two sides for their own advantage. Also 脚踏两只船.

near.diff: 三心二意 is being half-hearted or unable to make up one's mind; 脚踩两只船 is actively keeping two people or sides going behind their backs.

cards.cue: You discover that your friend's boyfriend has been secretly seeing another woman at the same time. What is he doing?

ctx.s: 原来他一直{脚踩两只船}，同时跟两个女孩交往。
ctx.en: So he'd been two-timing all along, seeing two girls at the same time.

ctx.s: 你要是{脚踩两只船}，迟早会被发现的。
ctx.en: If you play both sides like that, sooner or later you'll be found out.

ctx.s: “她同时跟两家公司谈合作，还瞒着对方？”“这不就是{脚踩两只船}吗？”
ctx.en: "She's negotiating with two companies at once and hiding it from each?" "Isn't that just playing both sides?"

ctx.s: 他白天在公司上班，晚上偷偷给竞争对手干活，{脚踩着两只船}。
ctx.en: He works at the company by day and secretly works for its rival at night, keeping a foot in both camps.

ctx.s: 做生意讲信用，{脚踩两只船}的合作伙伴谁都不敢要。
ctx.en: Business is built on trust; nobody wants a partner who plays both sides.

ctx.s: 他想{脚踩两只船}，结果两头都落空了。
ctx.en: He tried to keep both going and ended up losing both.

bad.s: 我会{脚踩两只船}，学习和工作都做得很好。
bad.en: (meant: I can balance study and work well)
bad.why: It condemns disloyal double-dealing; it is not praise for juggling two responsibilities.

bad.s: 他{脚踩两只船}了他女朋友。
bad.en: (meant: he cheated on his girlfriend)
bad.why: It takes no object, so the person being deceived cannot follow it; mention her before the phrase instead.

cards.mean: to be at odds and sulk with someone after a quarrel
cards.lit: to make a fuss of being awkward and contrary

use.how: A verb phrase, usually 跟某人闹别扭, and often split (闹了几天别扭, 闹什么别扭). Said of small, sulky fallings-out between people who are close.

near.diff: 吃醋 is feeling jealous; 闹别扭 is the sulking and cold shoulder after a small quarrel, whatever its cause.
闹矛盾 is a real conflict that may be serious; 闹别扭 is a petty, usually short-lived sulk.

cards.cue: Two roommates argued over whose turn it was to wash the dishes and have been giving each other the silent treatment ever since. What are they doing?

ctx.s: 这两天他跟女朋友{闹别扭}，谁也不理谁。
ctx.en: He's been sulking with his girlfriend for the past couple of days; neither is speaking to the other.

ctx.s: 你们俩又{闹什么别扭}了？
ctx.en: What are you two sulking about this time?

ctx.s: 小孩子{闹别扭}，过一会儿就好了。
ctx.en: When children fall out like that, they're fine again a little later.

ctx.s: “她怎么不跟你说话？”“昨天为了一点小事，我们{闹了点别扭}。”
ctx.en: "Why isn't she talking to you?" "We fell out a bit yesterday over some little thing."

ctx.s: 室友之间难免{闹别扭}，说开了就没事了。
ctx.en: Roommates are bound to fall out now and then; once you talk it through, it's fine.

ctx.s: 两个好朋友{闹了别扭}，在班上故意坐得远远的。
ctx.en: The two best friends had fallen out and deliberately sat far apart in class.

bad.s: 两家公司因为合同纠纷{闹别扭}，最后打起了官司。
bad.en: (meant: the two companies were in a dispute over the contract)
bad.why: It is a petty sulk between people who are close, far too light for a formal dispute between companies.

bad.s: 我昨天{闹别扭}了我妈妈。
bad.en: (meant: I fell out with my mother yesterday)
bad.why: It takes no object; the other person must be introduced before the phrase, as in 'fall out with someone'.

cards.mean: to step in and smooth over an awkward moment for others
cards.lit: to make an awkward scene round and whole again

use.how: A verb phrase, often 出来打圆场, 给某人打圆场, or split (打了个圆场). Said of someone using a joke or a few words to rescue an awkward or tense moment.

near.diff: 和稀泥 is criticism for blurring right and wrong to avoid conflict; 打圆场 is tactfully rescuing an awkward moment, usually seen as kind.

cards.cue: At dinner a guest makes a clumsy remark and the room goes silent; the host laughs it off and quickly changes the subject. What does the host do?

ctx.s: 气氛有点尴尬，主持人赶紧出来{打圆场}。
ctx.en: The atmosphere got a bit awkward, so the host quickly stepped in to smooth things over.

ctx.s: 他说错了话，幸好你帮他{打了个圆场}。
ctx.en: He said the wrong thing; luckily you covered for him.

ctx.s: 妈妈笑着{打圆场}：“孩子不懂事，您别往心里去。”
ctx.en: Mum smoothed it over with a smile: "He's only a child, please don't take it to heart."

ctx.s: 两位客户在饭桌上争了起来，经理连忙{打圆场}，把话题岔开了。
ctx.en: Two clients started arguing at the dinner table, and the manager hurried to smooth things over and changed the subject.

ctx.s: 每次开会吵起来，都是老李出来{打圆场}。
ctx.en: Whenever a meeting turns into a row, it's always Old Li who steps in to calm things down.

ctx.s: 他也觉得自己说过头了，想{打个圆场}，却越说越乱。
ctx.en: He knew he'd gone too far and tried to smooth it over, but the more he said, the worse it got.

bad.s: 比赛开始前，球员们先在场上{打圆场}热身。
bad.en: (meant: the players warmed up by running round the pitch)
bad.why: It has nothing to do with a sports ground; it means smoothing over an awkward social moment with words.

bad.s: 我{打圆场}了他们的矛盾。
bad.en: (meant: I smoothed over their disagreement)
bad.why: It takes no object; the person being helped is introduced before the phrase with the preposition meaning 'for'.

cards.mean: to make sarcastic remarks from the sidelines
cards.lit: to speak cool-breeze words, as someone sitting comfortably in the shade

use.how: A verb phrase, often split (说几句风凉话, 说什么风凉话). Said of an onlooker who mocks someone's trouble or effort instead of helping.

near.diff: 泼冷水 dampens someone's enthusiasm for a plan or hope; 说风凉话 mocks someone already struggling while the speaker does nothing.

cards.cue: You are struggling to change a flat tyre in the rain while a neighbour watches from his porch and jokes, 'Should've bought a better car.' What is he doing?

ctx.s: 别在旁边{说风凉话}了，过来帮忙吧！
ctx.en: Stop making snide remarks from over there and come and help!

ctx.s: 我考砸了，他不安慰我，反而{说风凉话}。
ctx.en: I failed my exam, and instead of comforting me he made sarcastic comments.

ctx.s: 我们搬家累得满头大汗，他却在一边{说风凉话}：“早该请搬家公司啊。”
ctx.en: We were drenched in sweat from moving, and he just stood there quipping, "Should have hired movers."

ctx.s: 你自己不出力，就少{说点风凉话}。
ctx.en: If you're not going to pitch in yourself, keep your sarcasm to yourself.

ctx.s: 大家加班加点想办法，他却在一旁{说风凉话}：“早知道会这样。”
ctx.en: Everyone was working overtime to find a solution, while he just sneered from the side: "I knew this would happen."

ctx.s: 看到别人创业失败，网上总有人{说风凉话}。
ctx.en: Whenever someone's start-up fails, there are always people online making snide remarks.

bad.s: 夏天太热了，我们去湖边{说风凉话}吧。
bad.en: (meant: let's go and chat somewhere cool by the lake)
bad.why: It is not about cool air or relaxed chat; it means mocking someone else's trouble.

bad.s: 朋友失业了，我{说了几句风凉话}安慰他。
bad.en: (meant: I said a few words to comfort my friend)
bad.why: These are mocking, unhelpful remarks, the opposite of words of comfort.

cards.mean: (of a secret or lie) to slip out and be exposed
cards.lit: the filling shows through, as when a dumpling's skin splits

use.how: An intransitive verb, usually 露馅了 or 露了馅; the subject is the liar or the lie (一开口就露馅了). Said of lies, pretences and surprises being given away by accident.

near.diff: 露出马脚 stresses a telltale clue that gives someone away and sounds more serious; 露馅 is the everyday word for a lie or surprise falling apart.

cards.cue: You tell your mum you spent the evening at the library, but your little brother mentions the film you both saw. What happened to your story?

ctx.s: 别说了，再说就{露馅}了！
ctx.en: Stop talking, any more and you'll give the game away!

ctx.s: 他说自己在加班，结果朋友圈的照片让他{露了馅}。
ctx.en: He said he was working late, but the photos he posted online gave him away.

ctx.s: 我们给妈妈准备的生日惊喜，被弟弟一句话说{露馅}了。
ctx.en: The birthday surprise we'd planned for Mum was given away by one remark from my little brother.

ctx.s: “你怎么知道是我拿的？”“你脸一红，就{露馅}了。”
ctx.en: "How did you know it was me who took it?" "The moment you blushed, you gave yourself away."

ctx.s: 他假装懂行，可是被问了两个专业问题就{露了馅}。
ctx.en: He pretended to be an expert, but a couple of technical questions exposed him.

ctx.s: 骗子编的故事漏洞太多，没过几天就{露馅}了。
ctx.en: The con man's story had too many holes in it, and within a few days it fell apart.

bad.s: 他在会上大胆地{露馅}了自己的新计划。
bad.en: (meant: he boldly unveiled his new plan at the meeting)
bad.why: It is the accidental exposure of something hidden and takes no object; it cannot mean announcing a plan on purpose.

bad.s: 警察很快就{露馅}了他的谎言。
bad.en: (meant: the police soon exposed his lie)
bad.why: It is intransitive: the lie or the liar is the subject. Someone else exposing the lie needs a different verb.

cards.r: qì bù dǎ yī chù lái
cards.mean: to be filled with anger at the very thought of it
cards.lit: anger comes not from one place alone, but from every side

use.how: A clause, often 一想到/一看到…就气不打一处来, or with 就 inside (气就不打一处来). The speaker's own anger at something seen, heard or remembered.

near.diff: 火冒三丈 describes a sudden, visible explosion of rage; 气不打一处来 is anger welling up at the sight or memory of something that already annoys you.

cards.cue: Every time you remember how a coworker took credit for your work last year, you feel furious all over again. How do you describe it?

ctx.s: 一想到他骗了我，我就{气不打一处来}。
ctx.en: Just thinking about how he lied to me makes my blood boil.

ctx.s: 看到儿子又在打游戏，妈妈{气不打一处来}。
ctx.en: Seeing her son playing video games yet again, the mother was furious.

ctx.s: 你还提那件事？我一听就{气不打一处来}！
ctx.en: You're bringing that up again? Just hearing it makes me livid!

ctx.s: 加班到半夜，回家又发现忘带钥匙，他真是{气不打一处来}。
ctx.en: After working till midnight he got home and found he'd forgotten his keys; he was furious.

ctx.s: 每次看到楼道里堆满别人家的杂物，我{气就不打一处来}。
ctx.en: Every time I see the stairwell piled with other people's junk, I get angry.

ctx.s: 老王拿着那张不合理的罚单，{气不打一处来}，当场就去找人理论。
ctx.en: Holding that unfair fine, Old Wang was seething, and went straight off to argue his case.

bad.s: 我考试得了满分，今天{气不打一处来}。
bad.en: (meant: I got full marks and I'm thrilled today)
bad.why: Qi here is anger; the phrase only describes being furious, never excitement or good spirits.

bad.s: 他总迟到，真让我{气不打一处来}他。
bad.en: (meant: his lateness makes me furious with him)
bad.why: It takes no object; the angry person is the subject, and the cause comes before it in its own clause.

cards.mean: a person one detests and wants out of the way
cards.lit: a nail in one's eye

story.text: In the Five Dynasties period, the military governor Zhao Zaili squeezed the people of Songzhou with heavy levies. When he was moved away, people rejoiced, saying it was like having a nail pulled from their eyes. Soon he was sent back to Songzhou for another year, and he made every person in his territory pay a thousand cash, which he called 'nail-pulling money'.

use.how: A noun, mostly 是某人的眼中钉 or 把某人当成/视为眼中钉; often extended as 眼中钉、肉中刺. Said of a rival or nuisance someone hates and wants removed.

near.diff: 绊脚石 is any obstacle in the way of progress, not necessarily hated; 眼中钉 is someone you loathe and want to get rid of.

cards.cue: The new manager can't stand one outspoken employee who keeps pointing out his mistakes, and is looking for a way to get rid of him. What is that employee to the manager?

ctx.s: 他总跟经理唱反调，早就成了经理的{眼中钉}。
ctx.en: He's always contradicting the manager and has long been a thorn in the manager's side.

ctx.s: 新来的同事业绩太好，被几个老员工当成了{眼中钉}。
ctx.en: The new colleague's results were so good that some of the old hands came to hate her.

ctx.s: 你为什么老针对我？难道我是你的{眼中钉}吗？
ctx.en: Why do you keep picking on me? Am I some thorn in your side?

ctx.s: 那家小店抢走了不少顾客，对面的大超市把它当成{眼中钉}，恨不得它马上关门。
ctx.en: That little shop took a lot of customers, so the big supermarket opposite sees it as a thorn in its side and wishes it would close down at once.

ctx.s: 两家公司竞争多年，早就把对方视为{眼中钉}、肉中刺。
ctx.en: After years of rivalry, the two companies have long regarded each other as a thorn in their flesh.

ctx.s: 那位记者揭露了不少黑幕，一些人把他视为{眼中钉}，恨不得让他闭嘴。
ctx.en: That journalist exposed a great deal of wrongdoing; certain people regard him as a thorn in their side and would love to silence him.

bad.s: 她是我的{眼中钉}，我每天都想见到她。
bad.en: (meant: she is the apple of my eye)
bad.why: It is the opposite of 'apple of my eye': it names a person you hate and want gone, not one you treasure.

bad.s: 这道数学题是我的{眼中钉}，怎么也做不出来。
bad.en: (meant: this maths problem is my nemesis; I just can't solve it)
bad.why: It names a person or rival one hates and wants removed, not a difficulty one cannot overcome.

cards.mean: to drag up old grievances during an argument
cards.lit: to leaf back through the old account books

use.how: Verb-object phrase, often after 别、又、老; can split (翻什么旧账, 翻起旧账来). Said of bringing up past wrongs in a quarrel, mostly between couples, family or friends.

near.diff: 揭短 exposes someone's faults or secrets, often in front of others; 翻旧账 brings up old wrongs that were supposed to be settled.

cards.cue: In the middle of a row about the washing-up, your partner starts listing every mistake you made over the last five years. What are they doing?

ctx.s: 吵架归吵架，别老是{翻旧账}。
ctx.en: Argue if you must, but stop dragging up the past.

ctx.s: 我不过是忘了倒垃圾，她就{翻起旧账}来，从结婚那年说起。
ctx.en: I only forgot to take out the rubbish, and she started raking up old grievances, going right back to the year we married.

ctx.s: “上次你也迟到了！”“都过去半年了，你还{翻什么旧账}？”
ctx.en: "You were late last time too!" "That was six months ago, why are you bringing it up again?"

ctx.s: 今天开会是讨论下一步怎么办，不是来{翻旧账}的。
ctx.en: This meeting is about what to do next, not about raking over old grievances.

ctx.s: 两个人本来已经和好了，结果一喝酒又开始{翻旧账}。
ctx.en: The two of them had already made up, but as soon as they had a drink they started dredging up the past again.

ctx.s: 夫妻之间最伤感情的，就是吵架时{翻旧账}。
ctx.en: Nothing hurts a marriage more than dragging up old grievances in an argument.

bad.s: 周末我们一起{翻旧账}，看了很多小时候的照片。
bad.en: (meant: at the weekend we reminisced and looked at childhood photos)
bad.why: It means raking up old grievances in a quarrel, not fond reminiscing; for that say huiyi guoqu (recall the past).

bad.s: 他昨天又{翻旧账}我了。
bad.en: (meant: he brought up my past mistakes again yesterday)
bad.why: It is already verb plus object and takes no further object; say gen wo fan jiuzhang or fan wo de jiuzhang.

cards.mean: a person who always makes others laugh and cheer up
cards.lit: the pistachio, literally 'happy-heart nut': the word for the nut also names a cheerful person

use.how: A noun, usually 是……的开心果 or 一个开心果. Said warmly of a person (sometimes a pet or child) who keeps a group in good spirits.

near.diff: 活宝 is a funny, often silly character, sometimes said with mild teasing; 开心果 stresses that they lift everyone's mood.

cards.cue: Every office has one person who tells jokes, remembers birthdays and lightens the mood when things get tense. What do you call her?

ctx.s: 她是我们班的{开心果}，大家都喜欢她。
ctx.en: She's the one who keeps our class cheerful; everyone likes her.

ctx.s: 有他在，聚会从来不冷场，他简直是个{开心果}。
ctx.en: When he's around, a party never goes flat; he's a real ray of sunshine.

ctx.s: 自从小狗来了，它就成了我们全家的{开心果}。
ctx.en: Since the puppy arrived, it has become the joy of the whole family.

ctx.s: 爷爷住院时，小孙女天天去讲笑话，成了病房里的{开心果}。
ctx.en: While Grandpa was in hospital, his little granddaughter went every day to tell jokes and cheered up the whole ward.

ctx.s: 你们部门谁是{开心果}？年会想请他来当主持人。
ctx.en: Who's the joker in your department? We'd like them to host the annual party.

ctx.s: 他平时是大家的{开心果}，没想到自己心里也有这么多烦恼。
ctx.en: He's usually the one who cheers everyone up; who'd have thought he had so many worries of his own?

bad.s: 今天考试通过了，我是{开心果}！
bad.en: (meant: I passed my exam today and I'm so happy)
bad.why: It names someone who cheers other people up, not your own happiness; just say wo hen kaixin.

bad.s: 他很{开心果}，总是笑嘻嘻的。
bad.en: (meant: he's very cheerful and always smiling)
bad.why: It is a noun and cannot follow hen like an adjective; say ta shi ge kaixinguo, or ta hen kailang (cheerful).

cards.mean: to join in where there is fun or a crowd
cards.lit: to draw close to where it is hot and noisy

use.how: Verb phrase: 去凑热闹, 凑个热闹, 凑凑热闹. Said of joining a lively scene for fun; 别来凑热闹 can also mean 'don't butt in and add to the trouble'.

cards.cue: You know nothing about football, but the whole town is watching the final in the square, so you go along for the atmosphere. What are you doing?

ctx.s: 广场上在放烟花，我们也去{凑热闹}吧！
ctx.en: They're setting off fireworks in the square; let's go and join the fun!

ctx.s: 我不太懂足球，就是跟朋友去{凑个热闹}。
ctx.en: I don't really understand football; I just went along with my friends for the atmosphere.

ctx.s: 新店开张排了长队，很多人其实只是来{凑热闹}的。
ctx.en: There was a long queue when the new shop opened; a lot of people only came because of the crowd.

ctx.s: “你也报名跑马拉松了？”“我肯定跑不完，就是{凑凑热闹}。”
ctx.en: "You've signed up for the marathon too?" "I'll never finish it; I'm just joining in for fun."

ctx.s: 我这边已经忙不过来了，你就别来{凑热闹}了。
ctx.en: I'm already swamped here; please don't come and add to the chaos.

ctx.s: 庙会那天，全村老少都出来{凑热闹}，街上挤得水泄不通。
ctx.en: On the day of the temple fair, the whole village, young and old, came out to join the fun, and the streets were packed.

bad.s: 这个城市晚上很{凑热闹}。
bad.en: (meant: this city is very lively at night)
bad.why: It is a verb phrase for going to join the fun, not an adjective for a lively place; say hen renao.

bad.s: 听说邻居家着火了，我们赶紧跑去{凑热闹}，帮忙灭火。
bad.en: (meant: we heard the neighbours' house was on fire and rushed over to help put it out)
bad.why: It means going along for the fun or the spectacle; said of a fire it sounds like gawking, not helping. Say qu bangmang.

cards.mean: to take a setback too hard and be unable to let it go
cards.lit: to think and not be able to open up: the mind stays shut around the hurt

use.how: Potential complement used as predicate, often in 别想不开 or 一直想不开; opposite 想得开. Said with concern; 一时想不开 can hint at fear of self-harm, so it is not a light word.

near.diff: 钻牛角尖 is stubbornly fixing on a narrow or pointless question; 想不开 is being unable to get over an emotional blow.

cards.cue: Your friend failed one job interview and has been miserable for a week, saying it proves she's useless. What do you tell her not to do?

ctx.s: 不就是一次考试没考好吗？哭一场就过去了，别{想不开}。
ctx.en: It's only one exam that went badly; have a good cry and move on, don't take it so hard.

ctx.s: 他被女朋友甩了以后一直{想不开}，天天喝闷酒。
ctx.en: Ever since his girlfriend dumped him he hasn't been able to get over it, and he drinks alone every day.

ctx.s: 被老板说了两句就难过了好几天，你怎么就{想不开}呢？
ctx.en: The boss criticised you a little and you've been upset for days; why can't you let it go?

ctx.s: 妈妈退休以后总觉得自己没用了，有点{想不开}。
ctx.en: Since retiring, Mum keeps feeling she's useless and is taking it rather hard.

ctx.s: “比赛输了，他把自己关在房间里。”“你去陪陪他，别让他{想不开}。”
ctx.en: "He lost the match and has shut himself in his room." "Go and keep him company; don't let him brood over it."

ctx.s: 遇到挫折总是{想不开}，最后苦的只是自己。
ctx.en: If you always take setbacks so hard, in the end the only one who suffers is you.

bad.s: 这道数学题太难了，我{想不开}。
bad.en: (meant: this maths problem is too hard, I can't work it out)
bad.why: It means being unable to get over something upsetting, not failing to solve a problem; say wo xiang bu chulai.

bad.s: 我一直{想不开}，他为什么突然辞职了。
bad.en: (meant: I still can't understand why he suddenly quit)
bad.why: Being puzzled is xiang bu tong; this phrase is about your own grief or resentment, not about understanding someone else.

cards.mean: an obstacle that stands in the way of progress
cards.lit: a stone that trips your feet

use.how: A noun, usually in 是/成为……的绊脚石. Said of a habit, problem or person that blocks progress; contrasts with 垫脚石, a stepping stone.

near.diff: 拖后腿 is a verb: someone holds a person or team back; 绊脚石 is a noun naming the obstacle itself.

cards.cue: A good student keeps losing marks through careless mistakes, and the teacher wants to name that one habit as what's blocking her. What does the teacher call it?

ctx.s: 粗心是你学习上最大的{绊脚石}。
ctx.en: Carelessness is the biggest obstacle in your studies.

ctx.s: 骄傲往往会成为进步的{绊脚石}。
ctx.en: Arrogance often becomes a stumbling block to progress.

ctx.s: 对很多外国人来说，声调是学中文的第一块{绊脚石}。
ctx.en: For many foreigners, tones are the first stumbling block in learning Chinese.

ctx.s: 你觉得公司发展最大的{绊脚石}是什么？
ctx.en: What do you think is the biggest obstacle to the company's growth?

ctx.s: 他一直觉得，父母的反对是自己追求梦想路上的{绊脚石}。
ctx.en: He always felt his parents' opposition was what stood in the way of his dream.

ctx.s: 别让一次失败成为你前进的{绊脚石}，要把它变成垫脚石。
ctx.en: Don't let one failure become a stumbling block; turn it into a stepping stone.

bad.s: 他{绊脚石}了我的计划。
bad.en: (meant: he got in the way of my plan)
bad.why: It is a noun, not a verb; say ta cheng le wo jihua de banjiaoshi, or ta zu'ai le wo de jihua.

bad.s: 老师是我成功的{绊脚石}，帮了我很多。
bad.en: (meant: my teacher helped me a lot on my way to success)
bad.why: It means an obstacle, the opposite of help; for someone who helped you on your way say yinluren or guiren.

cards.mean: to force someone to do what they are not able to do
cards.lit: to drive ducks up onto a perch: ducks cannot climb up and roost the way chickens do

use.how: Predicate, often 是/被赶鸭子上架 or 这不是赶鸭子上架吗. Often said wryly of oneself when pushed into a task beyond one's skill, or as a complaint on someone's behalf.

near.diff: 强人所难 is any unreasonable demand, more formal; 赶鸭子上架 stresses that the person simply lacks the skill, and is often self-mocking.

cards.cue: You have never spoken in public, but the host fell ill and you were pushed onto the stage to run the company party. How do you describe your situation?

ctx.s: 我从来没主持过晚会，这次完全是{赶鸭子上架}。
ctx.en: I'd never hosted a show before; I was completely thrown in at the deep end.

ctx.s: 老板让我这个新人去谈合同，真是{赶鸭子上架}。
ctx.en: The boss sent me, a newcomer, to negotiate the contract; talk about being pushed into something beyond me.

ctx.s: “你唱得不错啊，以前学过？”“哪儿啊，今天是被{赶鸭子上架}的。”
ctx.en: "You sang well! Have you had lessons?" "Not at all, I was dragged up there against my will today."

ctx.s: 孩子五音不全，你非让他去参加唱歌比赛，这不是{赶鸭子上架}吗？
ctx.en: The child can't carry a tune, yet you insist he enter a singing contest; isn't that forcing him into something he can't do?

ctx.s: 学校缺数学老师，就让体育老师顶上，这不是{赶鸭子上架}嘛。
ctx.en: The school is short of maths teachers, so they had the PE teacher fill in; that's asking him to do something he's not cut out for.

ctx.s: 妻子出差那几天，从不下厨的他只好被{赶鸭子上架}，天天给孩子做饭。
ctx.en: While his wife was away on business, he, who never cooks, had no choice but to struggle through making the kids' meals every day.

bad.s: 我快迟到了，只好{赶鸭子上架}，一路跑到车站。
bad.en: (meant: I was nearly late, so I rushed all the way to the station)
bad.why: Here gan means to drive or herd, not to hurry; the phrase is about being forced into a task beyond one's ability.

bad.s: 他是专业厨师，让他做菜真是{赶鸭子上架}。
bad.en: (meant: he is a professional chef, so asking him to cook is a natural fit)
bad.why: It only fits when the person lacks the ability; for a chef cooking, it is the opposite of the meaning.

cards.mean: to warn someone in advance so they are prepared
cards.lit: to give a vaccination: an injection that protects you before the illness arrives

use.how: Verb-object, in 给某人打（个）预防针; can split (打了个预防针). Said of preparing someone mentally for bad news or a disappointment before it comes.

near.diff: 打招呼 can mean giving a quiet heads-up or asking for a favour; 打预防针 is preparing someone for something unwelcome.

cards.cue: Before the exam results come out, a teacher tells her class the paper was marked very strictly this year, so they won't be shocked. What is she doing?

ctx.s: 我先给你{打个预防针}：这次考试特别难。
ctx.en: Let me warn you in advance: this exam is especially hard.

ctx.s: 项目可能会延期，我得提前给客户{打打预防针}。
ctx.en: The project may be delayed, so I need to prepare the client for it ahead of time.

ctx.s: 面试前，师兄给我{打了预防针}：那位面试官说话非常直接。
ctx.en: Before the interview, a senior student warned me that the interviewer is very blunt.

ctx.s: 涨价的事，你跟顾客{打过预防针}没有？
ctx.en: Have you given customers advance warning about the price rise?

ctx.s: 搬家前，妈妈就给孩子{打了预防针}，说刚到新学校可能会有点孤单。
ctx.en: Before the move, Mum prepared the child, saying it might be a bit lonely at first at the new school.

ctx.s: 经理开会时早就{打过预防针}，所以名单公布后，大家并不太意外。
ctx.en: The manager had warned everyone at the meeting, so when the list came out, nobody was very surprised.

bad.s: 会议结束后，他才给我们{打预防针}，说方案已经被否了。
bad.en: (meant: after the meeting he told us the plan had been rejected)
bad.why: It is a warning given before the bad news lands; telling people afterwards is simply informing them (gaosu).

bad.s: 我昨天{打预防针}他了。
bad.en: (meant: I warned him in advance yesterday)
bad.why: It is verb plus object and cannot take a person as object; say wo zuotian gei ta da le yufangzhen.

cards.mean: to hold back some of one's skill or plans just in case
cards.lit: to keep one move back: not show your whole hand

use.how: Verb phrase, often 留了一手 or 总爱留一手. Said of teachers or rivals not showing all they know (a complaint), or of keeping a fallback (prudence).

near.diff: 卖关子 is deliberately keeping listeners in suspense at the key point of a story; 留一手 is keeping back skill or resources for oneself.

cards.cue: Your aunt taught you her famous dumpling recipe, but yours never taste the same and you suspect she left out one secret step. What do you accuse her of?

ctx.s: 你教我做菜是不是{留了一手}？我做的怎么没你的好吃？
ctx.en: Did you hold something back when you taught me that dish? Why doesn't mine taste as good as yours?

ctx.s: 跟他谈判要小心，这个人做事总爱{留一手}。
ctx.en: Be careful negotiating with him; he always keeps something up his sleeve.

ctx.s: 做生意得{留一手}，不能把所有的钱都投进去。
ctx.en: In business you have to keep something in reserve; you can't put all your money in.

ctx.s: “你怎么把最好的方案留到最后才拿出来？”“谈判嘛，总得{留一手}。”
ctx.en: "Why did you only bring out your best proposal at the very end?" "It's a negotiation; you always keep something in reserve."

ctx.s: 以前有的老师傅教徒弟时{留一手}，怕徒弟以后超过自己。
ctx.en: In the past some old craftsmen held back part of their skill from apprentices, afraid of being surpassed.

ctx.s: 原来他前几轮都{留了一手}，到决赛才拿出真本事。
ctx.en: It turned out he'd been holding back in the early rounds and only showed what he could really do in the final.

bad.s: 他对我很好，吃饭时总给我{留一手}。
bad.en: (meant: he's good to me and always saves me some food)
bad.why: It is about holding back skill or keeping a fallback, not saving food for someone; say gei wo liu yi fen.

bad.s: 这个箱子太重了，你能{留一手}帮我抬一下吗？
bad.en: (meant: this box is too heavy, can you lend me a hand?)
bad.why: Liu means to keep back, the opposite of helping; to lend a hand is da ba shou or bang ge mang.

cards.mean: to turn the clock back and reverse progress
cards.lit: to drive the car in reverse

use.how: Predicate, often 是在开倒车 or the set phrase 开历史的倒车. Criticises a policy, rule or practice that deliberately goes back to an older, worse way.

near.diff: 走下坡路 is a gradual decline that just happens; 开倒车 is a deliberate step backwards that someone chooses.

cards.cue: A company that switched to online forms years ago suddenly orders everyone back to paper forms signed in triplicate. What do the staff say management is doing?

ctx.s: 现在还要用纸质表格登记，简直是在{开倒车}。
ctx.en: Still making people register on paper forms these days is really turning the clock back.

ctx.s: 这项新规定取消了员工的带薪假，被很多人批评是{开倒车}。
ctx.en: The new rule abolished staff paid leave, and many criticised it as a step backwards.

ctx.s: 别的学校都在减轻学生负担，我们反而增加考试，这不是{开倒车}吗？
ctx.en: Other schools are lightening students' workload while we're adding more exams; isn't that going backwards?

ctx.s: “新经理把以前的审批流程又恢复了。”“唉，又在{开倒车}。”
ctx.en: "The new manager has brought back the old approval process." "Sigh, turning the clock back again."

ctx.s: 这个城市拆掉了自行车道，重新扩建停车场，有人说这是在{开倒车}。
ctx.en: The city tore up its cycle lanes to build more car parks, and some say that's reversing progress.

ctx.s: 在环保问题上{开历史的倒车}，只会让后代付出代价。
ctx.en: Turning back the clock on environmental protection will only make future generations pay.

bad.s: 爷爷最近身体越来越差，健康在{开倒车}。
bad.en: (meant: Grandpa's health has been getting worse lately)
bad.why: It criticises a chosen step backwards in policy or practice; for health gradually declining use zou xiapo lu.

bad.s: 我们{开倒车}一下，再讨论一遍第一个问题吧。
bad.en: (meant: let's go back and discuss the first point again)
bad.why: It is a criticism of reversing progress, not a neutral 'go back'; say huidao di yi ge wenti.

cards.mean: to go downhill and steadily decline
cards.lit: to walk the downhill road

use.how: Predicate, often 开始走下坡路, 一直在走下坡路 or 走上了下坡路. Said of health, business, careers, grades or teams declining over time.

near.diff: 开倒车 accuses someone of deliberately reversing progress; 走下坡路 simply describes a gradual decline.

cards.cue: A once-popular restaurant has had fewer customers every year since its famous chef left. How would you describe its business?

ctx.s: 爷爷年纪大了，身体开始{走下坡路}了。
ctx.en: Grandpa is getting old, and his health has started to go downhill.

ctx.s: 这家老字号自从换了老板，生意就一直在{走下坡路}。
ctx.en: Ever since this old shop changed hands, its business has been going steadily downhill.

ctx.s: 你最近成绩怎么{走下坡路}了？是不是游戏玩得太多了？
ctx.en: Why have your grades been slipping lately? Have you been playing too many games?

ctx.s: 球队连输了好几场，球迷都担心球队要{走下坡路}了。
ctx.en: The team has lost several games in a row, and the fans are worried it's starting to decline.

ctx.s: “那个牌子以前很火啊。”“早就{走下坡路}了，现在没什么人买。”
ctx.en: "That brand used to be really popular." "It's been in decline for ages; hardly anyone buys it now."

ctx.s: 随着网购兴起，许多实体书店都{走上了下坡路}。
ctx.en: With the rise of online shopping, many bricks-and-mortar bookshops have gone into decline.

bad.s: 他的病{走下坡路}了，很快就能出院。
bad.en: (meant: his illness is easing and he'll soon leave hospital)
bad.why: Going downhill means getting worse, not the illness going away; for recovery say bingqing haozhuan le.

bad.s: 新校长故意{走下坡路}，把以前的改革全取消了。
bad.en: (meant: the new head deliberately undid all the earlier reforms)
bad.why: It describes a decline that happens over time, not a deliberate choice; for undoing progress use kai daoche.

cards.mean: enthusiasm that fades almost as soon as it starts
cards.lit: three minutes' worth of heat

use.how: Noun phrase, usually after 是、只有、就是 or 又是: 他学什么都是三分钟热度。 Said of a person's short-lived keenness for a hobby, plan or resolution.

near.diff: 虎头蛇尾 is a strong start and a weak finish of one task; 三分钟热度 is a person's habit of losing interest quickly.

cards.cue: Your friend buys a guitar, a gym card and a set of paints in one month, and has given up on all of them by the next. What do you say about her?

ctx.s: 他学什么都是{三分钟热度}，从来坚持不下去。
ctx.en: Whatever he takes up, his enthusiasm dies in no time; he never sticks with anything.

ctx.s: 你上个月说要学日语，现在书都不翻了，又是{三分钟热度}吧？
ctx.en: Last month you said you'd learn Japanese and now you don't even open the book. Lost interest already?

ctx.s: 孩子想学钢琴，我们怕他只有{三分钟热度}，先租了一台试试。
ctx.en: Our son wants to learn the piano; we were afraid his keenness wouldn't last, so we rented one to try first.

ctx.s: “这次我一定每天跑步！”“得了吧，你就是{三分钟热度}。”
ctx.en: "This time I'll definitely run every day!" "Oh, come on, you'll lose interest in a few days."

ctx.s: 很多人新年定了计划，可惜大多是{三分钟热度}，二月就忘了。
ctx.en: Lots of people make New Year resolutions, but most of that enthusiasm fizzles out and is forgotten by February.

ctx.s: 网上的热点来得快去得也快，大家对什么都只有{三分钟的热度}。
ctx.en: Online trends come and go fast; people never stay interested in anything for long.

bad.s: 他对工作很有{三分钟热度}，每天都加班。
bad.en: (meant: he is very passionate about his work and works overtime every day)
bad.why: It does not mean passion; it says the enthusiasm will not last, so it cannot describe steady dedication.

bad.s: 微波炉{三分钟热度}，饭就热好了。
bad.en: (meant: three minutes in the microwave and the food is hot)
bad.why: It is only used figuratively about a person's interest fading, never about heating something for three minutes.

cards.mean: very nearly right, pretty close to the truth
cards.lit: eight or nine, not far from ten

use.how: Predicate or complement after a verb of guessing or judging: 你猜得八九不离十。 Said of a guess, estimate or account that is close to the facts.

near.diff: 差不多 is a general 'about the same, roughly'; 八九不离十 says a guess or judgement is close to the real answer.

cards.cue: Without being told anything, your friend works out almost exactly why you and your boss fell out. How do you admit she has got it about right?

ctx.s: 你猜得{八九不离十}，我确实是想换工作了。
ctx.en: You've guessed pretty much right: I am thinking of changing jobs.

ctx.s: 看他那个表情，我心里就猜了个{八九不离十}：他肯定没考好。
ctx.en: From the look on his face I had a pretty good guess: he hadn't done well in the exam.

ctx.s: “这个包大概多少钱？”“我估计三千块，{八九不离十}。”
ctx.en: "Roughly how much is this bag?" "I'd guess three thousand, give or take."

ctx.s: 他讲的经过虽然有点夸张，但大体上{八九不离十}。
ctx.en: His account of what happened was a bit exaggerated, but broadly it was close to the truth.

ctx.s: 天气预报说明天下雨，最近报得挺准，应该{八九不离十}。
ctx.en: The forecast says rain tomorrow; it's been accurate lately, so it's probably about right.

ctx.s: 警察听完邻居的描述，对嫌疑人身份的判断已经{八九不离十}了。
ctx.en: After hearing the neighbour's description, the police were already close to the truth about who the suspect was.

bad.s: 我们班{八九不离十}的同学都去参加了比赛。
bad.en: (meant: about ninety per cent of our class took part in the contest)
bad.why: It does not mean 'about ninety per cent of'; it judges whether a guess or account is close to the truth.

bad.s: 他{八九不离十}每天都迟到。
bad.en: (meant: he is late almost every day)
bad.why: It is not an adverb of frequency; for 'almost every day' say jihu meitian.

cards.r: dāo zi zuǐ dòu fu xīn
cards.mean: sharp-tongued but soft-hearted underneath
cards.lit: a mouth like a knife and a heart like tofu

use.how: Describes a person, after 是 or as an attributive with 的: 我妈是刀子嘴豆腐心。 Usually said to excuse or explain someone's harsh words.

cards.cue: Your grandmother scolds you loudly for coming home late, then quietly heats up dinner and sits with you while you eat. How do you describe her?

ctx.s: 我妈是{刀子嘴豆腐心}，骂完我又给我煮面。
ctx.en: My mum's bark is worse than her bite: after telling me off she made me noodles.

ctx.s: 别生王老师的气，她就是{刀子嘴豆腐心}。
ctx.en: Don't be angry with Ms Wang; she talks tough, but she has a soft heart.

ctx.s: 老板说话很冲，可大家都知道他{刀子嘴豆腐心}，谁有困难他都帮。
ctx.en: The boss is blunt, but everyone knows he's soft underneath; he helps anyone who's in trouble.

ctx.s: “你奶奶刚才那么凶！”“她{刀子嘴豆腐心}，过一会儿就好了。”
ctx.en: "Your grandma was so fierce just now!" "She sounds harsh but she doesn't mean it; she'll be fine in a minute."

ctx.s: 像他这种{刀子嘴豆腐心}的人，最容易被人误会。
ctx.en: People like him, sharp-tongued but kind at heart, are the easiest to misunderstand.

ctx.s: 爸爸嘴上说不管我了，第二天还是帮我交了房租，真是{刀子嘴豆腐心}。
ctx.en: Dad said he was done with me, but the next day he paid my rent anyway. All talk, soft heart.

bad.s: 他当面对你笑，背后却害你，真是{刀子嘴豆腐心}。
bad.en: (meant: he smiles to your face but stabs you in the back)
bad.why: It is the other way round: harsh words with a kind heart. A sweet face over bad intentions is xiao li cang dao.

bad.s: 她说话总是轻声细语，心地又好，是个{刀子嘴豆腐心}的人。
bad.en: (meant: she is soft-spoken and kind-hearted)
bad.why: The first half needs a sharp tongue; someone gentle in speech and heart is simply kind, not sharp-tongued.

cards.mean: a change in name or form but not in substance
cards.lit: to change the broth but not the medicine in it, as in a herbal decoction

use.how: Predicate, often after 只是、不过是、还是: 新规定不过是换汤不换药。 Criticises reforms, products or plans that look new but are the same.

near.diff: 炒冷饭 repeats old material with nothing new; 换汤不换药 dresses up the old thing to look like a change.

cards.cue: The company renames its overtime policy 'flexible commitment hours', but the hours and pay are exactly the same. What do the staff call it?

ctx.s: 这个新规定只是改了个名字，其实是{换汤不换药}。
ctx.en: The new rule just has a new name; nothing has really changed.

ctx.s: 手机外壳换了个颜色就叫新款，这不是{换汤不换药}吗？
ctx.en: They change the colour of the case and call it a new model. Isn't that the same old thing?

ctx.s: 经理换了三个，管理方式还是老一套，{换汤不换药}。
ctx.en: They've been through three managers, but the management style is the same old stuff: new faces, same thing.

ctx.s: 学校说要减轻学生负担，结果作业从本子上换到了手机上，{换汤不换药}。
ctx.en: The school promised to lighten the students' load, but the homework just moved from exercise books to phones.

ctx.s: 如果只换个口号，制度一点不变，这样的改革就是{换汤不换药}。
ctx.en: If you only swap the slogan and leave the system exactly as it is, the reform is a change in name only.

ctx.s: 这家店重新装修后菜单一点没变，价格倒涨了，顾客都说{换了汤没换药}。
ctx.en: After the refit the menu was exactly the same, only dearer, and customers said it was the same old stuff in new wrapping.

bad.s: 公司彻底改革了管理制度，真是{换汤不换药}，效果非常好！
bad.en: (meant: the company thoroughly reformed its system and it worked very well)
bad.why: It says nothing real has changed, so it cannot describe a thorough reform, and it is always critical.

bad.s: 老店装修得很漂亮，但味道一点没变，{换汤不换药}，太好了！
bad.en: (meant: the old shop got a nice refit and, happily, the food tastes the same)
bad.why: It is a complaint that the change is only on the surface, not praise for keeping what is good.

cards.r: zhēng yī zhī yǎn bì yī zhī yǎn
cards.mean: to turn a blind eye and let something pass
cards.lit: to keep one eye open and one eye shut

use.how: Verb phrase, often 对……睁一只眼闭一只眼. Said of someone who notices a minor fault or rule-breaking and deliberately lets it go.

near.diff: 视而不见 is failing or refusing to see at all; 睁一只眼闭一只眼 is knowing and choosing to let a small thing slide.

cards.cue: The dorm forbids cooking, but the warden knows a student makes noodles in his room every night and never says a word. What is the warden doing?

ctx.s: 小事情就{睁一只眼闭一只眼}吧，别太较真。
ctx.en: Let the little things slide; don't be so strict.

ctx.s: 宿舍不让做饭，可管理员一直对我们{睁一只眼闭一只眼}。
ctx.en: Cooking isn't allowed in the dorm, but the warden has always turned a blind eye to us.

ctx.s: 孩子偶尔多玩一会儿游戏，我也就{睁一只眼闭一只眼}了。
ctx.en: If the kids play video games a bit longer now and then, I just let it go.

ctx.s: “他上班老是晚到十分钟，你不管吗？”“他活干得好，我就{睁只眼闭只眼}。”
ctx.en: "He's always ten minutes late. Aren't you going to do anything?" "His work is good, so I let it pass."

ctx.s: 安全问题不能{睁一只眼闭一只眼}，出了事谁负责？
ctx.en: You can't turn a blind eye to safety problems. If something happens, who'll take responsibility?

ctx.s: 有些地方对小摊小贩{睁一只眼闭一只眼}，反而方便了居民。
ctx.en: Some places look the other way about street stalls, which actually makes life easier for residents.

bad.s: 我当时在看手机，没注意到他进来，{睁一只眼闭一只眼}。
bad.en: (meant: I was on my phone and didn't notice him come in)
bad.why: It means seeing something and choosing to ignore it, not failing to notice it by accident.

bad.s: 监考老师考试时{睁一只眼闭一只眼}，盯得特别紧，谁也别想作弊。
bad.en: (meant: the invigilator watched very closely so no one could cheat)
bad.why: It means the opposite of watching closely: an invigilator who did this would be letting cheating go.

cards.r: bā zì hái méi yī piě
cards.mean: nothing is settled yet, things have barely begun
cards.lit: the character for eight (ba) does not even have its first stroke yet

use.how: Clause, usually 这事八字还没一撇呢. Said to brush off people who talk about a plan, deal or romance as if it were already certain.

cards.cue: You have had one coffee with someone, and your mother is already asking when the wedding is. How do you tell her to calm down?

ctx.s: 结婚？{八字还没一撇}呢，我们才认识一个月。
ctx.en: Getting married? Nothing's settled yet; we've only known each other a month.

ctx.s: 这份工作{八字还没一撇}，你先别告诉别人。
ctx.en: Nothing's certain about this job yet, so don't tell anyone for now.

ctx.s: 项目{八字还没一撇}，他就开始讨论怎么分奖金了。
ctx.en: The project hasn't even got off the ground and he's already talking about how to split the bonus.

ctx.s: “听说你要去国外读书了？”“哪儿啊，申请都没交，{八字还没一撇}。”
ctx.en: "I hear you're going to study abroad?" "Where did you hear that? I haven't even applied. It's nowhere near settled."

ctx.s: 房子的事{八字还没一撇}，装修的样子你倒已经想好了。
ctx.en: Nothing about the flat is settled yet, and you've already planned how to decorate it.

ctx.s: 两家公司合作的事{八字还没一撇}，媒体就已经报道出来了。
ctx.en: Nothing at all had been agreed between the two companies, yet the media was already reporting the partnership.

bad.s: 房子马上就装修好了，{八字还没一撇}。
bad.en: (meant: the flat is almost finished being decorated)
bad.why: It says a matter has barely begun and nothing is settled, the opposite of nearly finished.

bad.s: 人能长生不老吗？我看{八字还没一撇}。
bad.en: (meant: can people live for ever? I think it is impossible)
bad.why: It is about a concrete plan that has not started yet, not about something that can never happen.

cards.r: jī dàn lǐ tiāo gǔ tou
cards.mean: to find fault where there is none
cards.lit: to pick bones out of an egg

use.how: Verb phrase, often 这不是鸡蛋里挑骨头吗 or 专门/故意鸡蛋里挑骨头. Said of someone who invents faults in work or behaviour that is fine.

near.diff: 抬杠 is arguing for the sake of it; 鸡蛋里挑骨头 is inventing faults in something that is fine.

cards.cue: Your report has no errors, so your manager complains that the font looks 'a bit too serious'. What is she doing?

ctx.s: 这篇作文已经很好了，你别{鸡蛋里挑骨头}。
ctx.en: This essay is already very good; stop looking for faults that aren't there.

ctx.s: 新来的主管专门{鸡蛋里挑骨头}，大家都怕交报告给他。
ctx.en: The new supervisor goes out of his way to find fault, so everyone dreads handing him reports.

ctx.s: 菜做得好好的，他非说盘子颜色不对，这不是{鸡蛋里挑骨头}吗？
ctx.en: The food was perfectly good and he insisted the plates were the wrong colour. Isn't that nitpicking for nothing?

ctx.s: “这条裙子的扣子好像有点歪。”“哪儿歪了？你就是在{鸡蛋里挑骨头}。”
ctx.en: "The buttons on this dress look a bit crooked." "Crooked where? You're just looking for something to complain about."

ctx.s: 婆婆看她什么都不顺眼，连她叠衣服的方法都要{鸡蛋里挑出骨头}来。
ctx.en: Her mother-in-law disapproves of everything she does and even finds fault with the way she folds clothes.

ctx.s: 审稿要认真，但也不能{鸡蛋里挑骨头}，把作者的风格都改没了。
ctx.en: Editing should be careful, but you shouldn't invent faults and edit the author's style out of existence.

bad.s: 报告里错字很多，经理{鸡蛋里挑骨头}，把它们都找了出来。
bad.en: (meant: the report had many typos and the manager found them all)
bad.why: It means finding faults that do not exist; pointing out real errors is just careful checking.

bad.s: 我弟弟吃饭{鸡蛋里挑骨头}，这个不吃那个也不吃。
bad.en: (meant: my brother is a picky eater)
bad.why: It is about inventing criticism, not about food; a picky eater is tiaoshi.

cards.r: dǎ kāi tiān chuāng shuō liàng huà
cards.mean: to speak frankly and openly, hiding nothing
cards.lit: to open the skylight and speak in the light

use.how: Said by the speaker before getting blunt, often 咱们打开天窗说亮话吧 or 我就打开天窗说亮话了. Signals dropping politeness to say what both sides really think.

near.diff: 开门见山 is getting straight to the point in speech or writing; 打开天窗说亮话 is dropping pretence in a tense conversation.

cards.cue: After an hour of polite hints in a pay negotiation, you decide to stop pretending and tell the other side your real bottom line. What do you say first?

ctx.s: 咱们{打开天窗说亮话}吧，你到底想要多少钱？
ctx.en: Let's be frank: exactly how much money do you want?

ctx.s: 既然你问了，那我就{打开天窗说亮话}，这个方案我不同意。
ctx.en: Since you ask, I'll be blunt: I don't agree with this plan.

ctx.s: 都是老朋友了，有什么不满就{打开天窗说亮话}，别憋在心里。
ctx.en: We're old friends; if something's bothering you, out with it, don't keep it bottled up.

ctx.s: “您的意思是……”“我{打开天窗说亮话}，公司今年不打算给你升职。”
ctx.en: "So what you mean is..." "I'll put it plainly: the company doesn't plan to promote you this year."

ctx.s: 谈判拖了一上午，最后双方决定{打开天窗说亮话}，很快就签了合同。
ctx.en: The talks dragged on all morning; in the end both sides decided to lay their cards on the table and soon signed.

ctx.s: 与其互相猜来猜去，不如{打开天窗说亮话}，把问题解决了。
ctx.en: Rather than second-guessing each other, we'd do better to speak openly and sort the problem out.

bad.s: 后面的同学听不清，请你{打开天窗说亮话}。
bad.en: (meant: the students at the back can't hear, please speak up)
bad.why: It is about speaking frankly, not loudly; to ask someone to speak up say da sheng dian.

bad.s: 她{打开天窗说亮话}，把好朋友的秘密告诉了全班。
bad.en: (meant: she blurted out her best friend's secret to the whole class)
bad.why: It is candour between the speaker and listener about their own matter, not leaking someone else's secret.

cards.r: guà yáng tóu mài gǒu ròu
cards.mean: to pass off something inferior under a respectable label
cards.lit: to hang up a sheep's head and sell dog meat

story.text: Duke Ling of Qi liked the women of his palace to dress as men. The fashion spread through the state, so he banned it outside the palace, but the ban did not work. His minister Yanzi told him: you let them do it inside and forbid it outside; that is like hanging an ox head at the door and selling horse meat inside. Stop it in the palace and no one outside will dare. The Duke did, and the fashion ended. Later the saying took its present form, with a sheep's head and dog meat.

use.how: Predicate or attributive: 这家公司挂羊头卖狗肉。 Exposes businesses, organisations or people that use a good name to sell or do something quite different and worse.

near.diff: 换汤不换药 is a cosmetic change to the same old thing; 挂羊头卖狗肉 is a respectable front hiding something worse.

cards.cue: A shop advertised as a 'health and wellness centre' turns out to be selling dubious pills at huge prices to elderly people. How do you expose it?

ctx.s: 这家店说卖进口牛肉，其实是便宜货，{挂羊头卖狗肉}。
ctx.en: This shop claims to sell imported beef, but it's cheap stuff: a classic bait and switch.

ctx.s: 那个所谓的英语培训班根本不上课，就是{挂羊头卖狗肉}，推销保健品。
ctx.en: That so-called English course never holds classes; it's just a front for selling health supplements.

ctx.s: 有些网站{挂着学术的羊头卖广告的狗肉}，读者要小心。
ctx.en: Some websites put on an academic front but are really selling ads, so readers should be careful.

ctx.s: “这个纪录片怎么全是产品介绍？”“它就是{挂羊头卖狗肉}的广告。”
ctx.en: "Why is this documentary all product plugs?" "It's an advert dressed up as something respectable."

ctx.s: 记者调查发现，这家“养老服务中心”{挂羊头卖狗肉}，专门骗老人买高价药。
ctx.en: Reporters found that this 'elderly care centre' was a front, set up to trick old people into buying overpriced medicine.

ctx.s: 做生意要讲诚信，{挂羊头卖狗肉}的做法早晚会被发现。
ctx.en: Business needs honesty; passing off rubbish under a good name will be found out sooner or later.

bad.s: 这家店{挂羊头卖狗肉}，卖的都是正宗的新疆羊肉，很好吃。
bad.en: (meant: this shop sells genuine, delicious Xinjiang lamb)
bad.why: It accuses a seller of deceiving customers, so it cannot praise a shop that sells exactly what it advertises.

bad.s: 这家饭馆{挂羊头卖狗肉}，菜单上什么肉都有，选择很多。
bad.en: (meant: this restaurant serves all kinds of meat and has a wide choice)
bad.why: It is only figurative, about a fake front hiding something worse, never a description of a varied menu.

cards.r: bān qǐ shí tou zá zì jǐ de jiǎo
cards.mean: to have a scheme aimed at others backfire on oneself
cards.lit: to lift up a rock and drop it on your own foot

use.how: Predicate, often after 结果、真是、小心; the past form is 搬起石头砸了自己的脚. Said of a plan or trick meant to harm others or gain an edge that ends up hurting its author.

near.diff: 自作自受 is any suffering one brings on oneself; 搬起石头砸自己的脚 stresses a scheme aimed at someone else that turns back on its maker.

cards.cue: A shop owner spreads rumours about the shop next door; the rumours are traced back to him and his own customers leave. What has he done?

ctx.s: 他想在背后陷害同事，结果{搬起石头砸了自己的脚}。
ctx.en: He tried to frame a colleague behind his back and ended up hurting only himself.

ctx.s: 你在网上骂老板，小心{搬起石头砸自己的脚}。
ctx.en: You're slagging off the boss online; careful it doesn't come back to bite you.

ctx.s: 那家公司为了挤走对手恶意降价，最后自己亏得最惨，真是{搬起石头砸了自己的脚}。
ctx.en: That company slashed prices to drive out its rivals and lost more than anyone; a real own goal.

ctx.s: 他在简历上造假想多拿工资，被查出来后直接被开除，这不是{搬起石头砸自己的脚}吗？
ctx.en: He faked his CV to get a higher salary and was fired as soon as it was found out. Isn't that shooting himself in the foot?

ctx.s: 她故意把错误的考试范围告诉同学，结果自己也没复习对，{搬起石头砸了自己的脚}。
ctx.en: She deliberately told her classmates the wrong exam topics, then revised the wrong ones herself; the trick backfired on her.

ctx.s: 散布谣言的人，往往会{搬起石头砸自己的脚}。
ctx.en: People who spread rumours often end up being the ones who get hurt.

bad.s: 我不小心{搬起石头砸了自己的脚}，把手机掉进了水里。
bad.en: (meant: I clumsily dropped my phone in the water)
bad.why: It is about a plan or trick that backfires on its author, not about an ordinary accident or bad luck.

bad.s: 他为了帮朋友{搬起石头砸自己的脚}，真让人感动。
bad.en: (meant: he sacrificed himself to help a friend, which is moving)
bad.why: It mocks a self-defeating scheme; it cannot describe a generous sacrifice or be used as praise.

cards.mean: to be unable to cope with or stand any more of it
cards.lit: to eat something and be unable to digest it

use.how: Predicate, usually after the person or body: 身体吃不消, 我可吃不消. Said of workload, tiredness, cost or a demanding person that exceeds what one can bear. Positive: 吃得消.

near.diff: 受不了 also covers emotional annoyance (我受不了他); 吃不消 is mainly about strength, money or stamina being overloaded.

cards.cue: After three weeks of night shifts and weekend overtime, your body is giving out. How do you tell your boss you can't keep this up?

ctx.s: 每天加班到半夜，身体真的{吃不消}。
ctx.en: Working overtime till midnight every day, my body really can't take it.

ctx.s: 这么贵的房租，我一个人可{吃不消}。
ctx.en: I can't manage rent this high on my own.

ctx.s: 你要是{吃不消}就早点说，我们停下来休息一会儿。
ctx.en: If it gets too much for you, say so and we'll stop for a rest.

ctx.s: 老人家年纪大了，坐这么久的长途车怕是{吃不消}。
ctx.en: Grandad is getting on; a long coach ride like that may be too much for him.

ctx.s: 他一个人干三个人的活，时间长了谁都{吃不消}。
ctx.en: He's doing the work of three people; nobody could keep that up for long.

ctx.s: 新老师布置的作业太多，学生们纷纷表示{吃不消}。
ctx.en: The new teacher sets so much homework that one student after another says they can't cope.

bad.s: 这块肉已经坏了，{吃不消}，扔了吧。
bad.en: (meant: this meat has gone off and can't be eaten, throw it away)
bad.why: It does not mean inedible; it says a person cannot bear a burden. For food that has gone off say bu neng chi le.

bad.s: 这家店的菜太好吃了，我天天吃都{吃不消}。
bad.en: (meant: the food here is so good I can never get enough of it)
bad.why: It says something is too much to bear, not that one wants more; for never tiring of food say chi bu gou or chi bu ni.

cards.mean: to try to help but only make things worse
cards.lit: to give help that runs the wrong way round

use.how: Verb-object phrase, often after 别、尽、又; can split: 帮了倒忙, 帮了个倒忙. Said of well-meant help that causes more trouble, often teasingly.

near.diff: 添乱 is any trouble-making, with or without good intentions; 帮倒忙 is specifically sincere help that backfires.

cards.cue: Your little brother insists on helping you pack, then breaks two plates and mixes up all the boxes. What has he done?

ctx.s: 你别进厨房{帮倒忙}了，去客厅坐着吧。
ctx.en: Stop getting in the way in the kitchen; go and sit in the living room.

ctx.s: 弟弟想帮我收拾房间，结果把东西放得到处都是，真是{帮倒忙}。
ctx.en: My brother tried to tidy my room for me and left things everywhere; some help that was.

ctx.s: “我帮你把旧文件都删了，电脑快多了！”“你这是{帮倒忙}啊，那些文件我还要用！”
ctx.en: "I deleted all your old files for you, the computer's much faster!" "That's not helping, I still need those files!"

ctx.s: 他好心替同事回了客户的邮件，却写错了价格，害得同事还得去道歉，等于{帮了个倒忙}。
ctx.en: He kindly answered a client's email for a colleague but quoted the wrong price, so the colleague had to apologise; his help only made things worse.

ctx.s: 新来的实习生很热情，可总是{帮倒忙}，大家只好让他先在旁边看着。
ctx.en: The new intern is keen, but his help always makes things worse, so everyone has him watch for now.

ctx.s: 家长替孩子包办一切，其实是在{帮倒忙}。
ctx.en: Parents who do everything for their children are really doing them a disservice.

bad.s: 谢谢你昨天{帮倒忙}，我的问题全解决了。
bad.en: (meant: thanks for helping me yesterday, my problem is solved)
bad.why: It means the help made things worse, so it cannot thank someone for help that worked.

bad.s: 他昨天{帮倒忙}我搬家，把我的花瓶打碎了。
bad.en: (meant: he helped me move yesterday and only made it worse by breaking my vase)
bad.why: It is verb-object and takes no object after it; say gei wo bang dao mang, or bang wo banjia, jieguo bang le dao mang.

cards.mean: to be left embarrassed in public with no graceful way out
cards.lit: to be stuck on the stage, unable to get down
