use.how: Predicate, very often 让/叫/弄得某人下不来台; variant 下不了台. Said of being put on the spot in front of others, usually by someone else's words.

near.diff: 丢面子 is losing face in general; 下不来台 is the awkward moment in front of others when one cannot save face or escape it.

cards.cue: At a family dinner, your aunt loudly asks your cousin in front of everyone why he failed his exam again; he sits there red-faced, lost for words.

ctx.s: 他当场被问住了，一时{下不来台}。
ctx.en: He was stumped on the spot and, for a moment, had no way to save face.

ctx.s: 有话私下说，别当着客户的面让经理{下不来台}。
ctx.en: Say it in private; don't embarrass the manager in front of the client.

ctx.s: “你刚才为什么那样说？”“我就是要让他{下不来台}，谁让他先骗我。”
ctx.en: "Why did you say that just now?" "I wanted to put him on the spot; he lied to me first."

ctx.s: 主持人及时开了个玩笑，给了嘉宾一个台阶，免得他{下不来台}。
ctx.en: The host quickly made a joke and gave the guest a way out, so he wasn't left stranded.

ctx.s: 老师那句话让他当众{下不来台}，从那以后他再也不举手了。
ctx.en: That remark from the teacher humiliated him in front of the class, and he never raised his hand again.

ctx.s: 她在婚礼上提起新郎的前女友，弄得一家人都{下不来台}。
ctx.en: She brought up the groom's ex at the wedding and left the whole family squirming.

bad.s: 演出结束了，观众一直鼓掌，他{下不来台}。
bad.en: (meant: the audience kept clapping, so he couldn't leave the stage)
bad.why: It is figurative public embarrassment, not literally staying on stage because the audience wants more.

bad.s: 我一个人在家打碎了杯子，真{下不来台}。
bad.en: (meant: I broke a cup at home alone, how embarrassing)
bad.why: It needs an audience: it is about embarrassment in front of others, not a private mishap.

cards.mean: to do something out of respect so that a person keeps face
cards.lit: to give someone face

use.how: Verb-object phrase; the person goes inside: 给他面子, 给我个面子, 不给面子. Said of accepting an invitation, complying or holding back criticism out of regard for someone.

near.diff: 爱面子 is caring too much about one's own image; 给面子 is acting to protect someone else's.

cards.cue: Your boss invites the team to her birthday dinner. You're exhausted, but you go anyway so she isn't left with empty seats. Why did you go?

ctx.s: 今晚我请客，你可一定要{给面子}啊。
ctx.en: Dinner's on me tonight; you really must come, for my sake.

ctx.s: 大家都{给他面子}，没有当场指出他的错误。
ctx.en: Out of respect for him, nobody pointed out his mistake there and then.

ctx.s: 老同学请你吃饭你都不来，也太不{给面子}了吧？
ctx.en: An old classmate invites you to dinner and you don't even show up? That's a bit of a snub, isn't it?

ctx.s: 看在老朋友的份上，你就{给我个面子}，原谅他这一次吧。
ctx.en: For old times' sake, do it for me and forgive him just this once.

ctx.s: 领导讲的笑话并不好笑，但大家还是很{给面子}地笑了。
ctx.en: The boss's joke wasn't funny, but everyone politely laughed anyway.

ctx.s: 老板听说我们是他朋友介绍来的，很{给面子}，给我们打了八折。
ctx.en: When the owner heard his friend had sent us, he did us the honour of a twenty percent discount.

bad.s: 你应该{给面子}他，别跟他吵了。
bad.en: (meant: you should let him save face and stop arguing)
bad.why: The person goes between gei and mianzi: say gei ta mianzi, never put the person after the whole phrase.

bad.s: 他很{给面子}，从来不愿意在别人面前认错。
bad.en: (meant: he cares about his image and never admits mistakes in front of others)
bad.why: That is ai mianzi, caring about one's own face; gei mianzi is showing regard for someone else.

cards.mean: petty and easily offended
cards.lit: a small mind, with no room in it to let things go

use.how: Adjective or noun: 他很小心眼, 别那么小心眼; in the north often 小心眼儿. Said of people who take small slights to heart and hold grudges.

near.diff: 小气 is mainly stingy with money or things; 小心眼 is touchy and grudging about small offences.

cards.cue: Your friend refuses to speak to you for a week because you forgot to like her photo online. What is she being?

ctx.s: 别那么{小心眼}，他只是开个玩笑。
ctx.en: Don't be so touchy; he was only joking.

ctx.s: 我就是没回她的消息，她就三天不理我，真{小心眼}。
ctx.en: I just didn't answer her message and she ignored me for three days. How petty.

ctx.s: “你是不是还在生我的气？”“我才没那么{小心眼}呢。”
ctx.en: "Are you still angry with me?" "I'm not that petty."

ctx.s: 他这个人有点{小心眼}，谁说了他一句不好，他能记一年。
ctx.en: He's a bit petty; say one bad word about him and he'll remember it for a year.

ctx.s: 输了比赛就不跟对手握手，这也太{小心眼}了吧？
ctx.en: Refusing to shake the opponent's hand just because you lost? Isn't that rather small-minded?

ctx.s: 当领导的不能{小心眼}，要听得进不同意见。
ctx.en: A leader can't be thin-skinned; they have to be able to hear disagreement.

bad.s: 她做事非常{小心眼}，从来没出过错。
bad.en: (meant: she is very careful in her work and never makes mistakes)
bad.why: It does not mean careful (that is xiaoxin or zixi); it criticises pettiness.

bad.s: 我很喜欢他的{小心眼}，他总是记得我的生日。
bad.en: (meant: I love how attentive he is, he always remembers my birthday)
bad.why: It is criticism of touchiness, never praise for attentiveness; for that say xin xi or tiexin.

cards.mean: to seek the limelight and show off
cards.lit: to bring out one's fengtou, the 'wind-head': prominence, being in the public eye

use.how: Verb-object phrase, often 爱出风头, 想出风头; can split: 出尽了风头, 出这个风头. Usually criticises attention-seeking; 出尽风头 can simply mean stealing the show.

near.diff: 抢风头 is taking the attention away from someone else who should have it; 出风头 is putting oneself in the spotlight.

cards.cue: At every party your cousin grabs the microphone, tells the loudest stories and makes sure all eyes are on him. What does he love to do?

ctx.s: 他这个人就爱{出风头}，什么场合都想站在中间。
ctx.en: He just loves the limelight; whatever the occasion, he wants to be centre stage.

ctx.s: 开会时她抢着发言，大家都觉得她是想{出风头}。
ctx.en: She kept jumping in to speak at the meeting, and everyone thought she was showing off.

ctx.s: 这次运动会，我们班的小王拿了三个第一，{出尽了风头}。
ctx.en: At this sports day, Xiao Wang from our class won three events and stole the show.

ctx.s: “你为什么不上台唱一首？”“我可不想{出这个风头}。”
ctx.en: "Why don't you get up and sing one?" "I don't want to make a spectacle of myself."

ctx.s: 新人刚进公司，最好低调一点，别急着{出风头}。
ctx.en: When you're new at a company, it's best to keep a low profile and not rush to grab attention.

ctx.s: 他在朋友圈发了一堆和明星的合影，就是想{出出风头}。
ctx.en: He posted a pile of photos with celebrities on his feed just to show off a bit.

bad.s: 今天外面{出风头}了，记得多穿点衣服。
bad.en: (meant: it's windy outside today, wrap up warm)
bad.why: It has nothing to do with weather; for wind say gua feng le.

bad.s: 他默默帮助别人，从来不说，真爱{出风头}。
bad.en: (meant: he quietly helps others and never mentions it, so modest)
bad.why: It means seeking attention, the opposite of quiet modesty, and it is not praise.

cards.mean: to take something for granted without checking
cards.lit: to think that it must be so

story.text: After Cao Cao took the city of Ye, his son Cao Pi married the wife of the defeated Yuan Xi. Kong Rong wrote to Cao Cao that when King Wu of Zhou conquered the Shang, he gave the tyrant's consort Daji to the Duke of Zhou. Cao Cao later asked which book recorded this. Kong Rong answered that, judging by what happens today, he had supposed it must have been so.

use.how: Often adverbial (想当然地以为) or after 凭、不能、别: 做事不能想当然. Criticises judging by assumption instead of finding out.

near.diff: 理所当然 means naturally, as it should be, with no criticism; 想当然 criticises assuming something without checking.

cards.cue: Your colleague books an outdoor team lunch without looking at the forecast, sure it will be sunny because it usually is. It pours. What was his mistake?

ctx.s: 做事要先调查清楚，不能{想当然}。
ctx.en: Find out the facts first; you can't just assume.

ctx.s: 我{想当然}地以为他会来，结果他根本不知道今天开会。
ctx.en: I took it for granted he would come, but he didn't even know there was a meeting today.

ctx.s: “你怎么不先打电话问问商店开没开门？”“是我{想当然}了，以为周末也开。”
ctx.en: "Why didn't you ring first to check the shop was open?" "I just assumed it; I thought it would be open at the weekend."

ctx.s: 很多人{想当然}地认为，外国人都不会用筷子。
ctx.en: Many people simply assume that foreigners can't use chopsticks.

ctx.s: 这份报告里的数字都是凭{想当然}写的，根本经不起检查。
ctx.en: The figures in this report are pure guesswork and won't stand up to any checking.

ctx.s: 做科研最怕{想当然}，每个结论都要有证据。
ctx.en: The worst thing in research is assuming; every conclusion needs evidence.

bad.s: 他帮了你，你谢谢他是{想当然}的。
bad.en: (meant: he helped you, so naturally you should thank him)
bad.why: That is lisuo dangran, naturally so; xiang dangran criticises assuming without checking.

bad.s: 我调查了半年，终于{想当然}地得出了结论。
bad.en: (meant: after six months of research I confidently reached a conclusion)
bad.why: It means reaching a view without checking, so it contradicts careful research.

cards.mean: the thing one does best, one's speciality
cards.lit: the play a performer handles best, the one they are known for

use.how: Noun, usually 是某人的拿手好戏 or 表演/拿出拿手好戏. Said of a skill one is known for; used ironically for a habitual trick (迟到是他的拿手好戏).

near.diff: 看家本领 is the core skill one relies on, often for a living; 拿手好戏 is what one is known to do best, and can be light or ironic.

cards.cue: At every family gathering your uncle is asked to do magic tricks, because nobody does them better. What are magic tricks to him?

ctx.s: 做红烧肉是我妈妈的{拿手好戏}。
ctx.en: Red-braised pork is my mum's signature dish.

ctx.s: 讲笑话是他的{拿手好戏}，每次聚会他都是主角。
ctx.en: Telling jokes is his forte; he's the star of every party.

ctx.s: 晚会上，她表演了自己的{拿手好戏}，边弹钢琴边唱歌。
ctx.en: At the party she did her party piece, singing while playing the piano.

ctx.s: “你会修自行车吗？”“当然，这可是我的{拿手好戏}！”
ctx.en: "Can you fix bikes?" "Of course, that's my speciality!"

ctx.s: 一到考试前就喊肚子疼，这是他的{拿手好戏}了。
ctx.en: Getting a stomach ache right before every exam is his old trick.

ctx.s: 把复杂的技术做成简单好用的产品，是这家公司的{拿手好戏}。
ctx.en: Turning complex technology into simple, easy products is what this company does best.

bad.s: 我的{拿手好戏}是一部老电影，我已经看了十遍。
bad.en: (meant: my favourite film is an old one I've seen ten times)
bad.why: It means what one does best oneself, not a favourite film or show that one watches.

bad.s: 我刚学了一个星期吉他，还弹得不太好，这是我的{拿手好戏}。
bad.en: (meant: I've just taken up guitar, my new hobby, and I'm not good yet)
bad.why: It names a proven strong skill, so it cannot describe a new hobby one is still bad at.

cards.mean: to pass a problem back and forth, each refusing to handle it
cards.lit: to kick a ball back and forth to each other

use.how: Predicate, often 互相踢皮球; can split: 踢了半年皮球. Said of offices, departments or people passing a matter on so that nobody deals with it.

near.diff: 推卸责任 is shifting responsibility onto someone; 踢皮球 is two or more parties passing a matter back and forth.

cards.cue: You call the bank about a wrong charge; the bank says ask the shop, the shop says ask the bank, and nobody fixes it. What are they doing?

ctx.s: 出了问题就从这个部门推到那个部门，互相{踢皮球}，没有人愿意管。
ctx.en: When something goes wrong it gets pushed from one department to the next; they bat it back and forth and nobody will deal with it.

ctx.s: 我去办手续，几个部门互相{踢皮球}，跑了一整天也没办成。
ctx.en: I went to sort out the paperwork; the departments kept sending me to each other, and after a whole day it still wasn't done.

ctx.s: 物业让我来找你们，你们又让我去找物业，这不是{踢皮球}吗？
ctx.en: The management office sent me to you, and you're sending me back to them. Isn't that just passing the buck?

ctx.s: 客户投诉了三次，客服和售后一直在{踢皮球}。
ctx.en: The customer has complained three times, and customer service and after-sales keep pushing it onto each other.

ctx.s: 新规定要求每项业务都指定一个部门负责，不许再互相{踢皮球}。
ctx.en: The new rules assign every kind of request to one department, so they can no longer pass it back and forth.

ctx.s: 学校和家长为了谁负责接送孩子，{踢了半年皮球}，问题还是没解决。
ctx.en: The school and the parents have been batting the question of who takes the children to and from school back and forth for six months, and it's still not solved.

bad.s: 他工作特别负责，问题一来就马上{踢皮球}。
bad.en: (meant: he is very responsible and deals with problems at once)
bad.why: It means passing a problem on to avoid it, the opposite of dealing with it responsibly.

bad.s: 经理把这个责任{踢皮球}给了我。
bad.en: (meant: the manager passed this responsibility to me)
bad.why: It is a verb-object phrase that takes no further object or gei; say ba zeren tui gei wo le.

cards.mean: to apply one rule to every case, ignoring differences
cards.lit: to cut everything with one stroke of the knife, so every piece comes out the same

use.how: Used as a verb (不能一刀切, 搞一刀切), an adverb (一刀切地禁止) or before 的. Said of rules, policies and management that ignore real differences.

near.diff: 一视同仁 is praise for treating everyone equally and fairly; 一刀切 criticises a rule applied rigidly to cases that differ.
一概而论 is judging or talking about different things as if they were the same; 一刀切 is acting on them with one rule.

cards.cue: The new rule says every employee must arrive at nine, whether they live next door or two hours away, and nobody can ask for an exception. What do the staff complain about?

ctx.s: 每个学生的情况都不一样，管理上不能{一刀切}。
ctx.en: Every student's situation is different, so you can't manage them all with one rule.

ctx.s: 公司要求所有人九点到岗，不管住多远，这种{一刀切}的做法引起了不满。
ctx.en: The company requires everyone to be at work by nine however far away they live, and this one-size-fits-all approach has caused resentment.

ctx.s: 小区突然禁止所有电动车进门，住户问：“这样{一刀切}，腿脚不好的老人怎么办？”
ctx.en: The estate suddenly banned all e-bikes from the gate, and residents asked: "If you ban them across the board, what about elderly people who can't walk well?"

ctx.s: 治理污染不能简单地{一刀切}，把所有小工厂都关掉。
ctx.en: Tackling pollution can't simply mean applying one blanket rule and shutting down every small factory.

ctx.s: 专家建议，孩子用手机应该按年龄管理，而不是{一刀切}地全面禁止。
ctx.en: Experts suggest that children's phone use should be managed by age rather than banned outright for everyone.

ctx.s: 新政策没有搞{一刀切}，而是给了各地一定的灵活性。
ctx.en: The new policy doesn't impose one rule on everyone; it gives each region some flexibility.

bad.s: 王老师对每个学生都{一刀切}，大家都很喜欢她。
bad.en: (meant: Ms Wang treats every student equally, and everyone likes her)
bad.why: It criticises a rigid rule that ignores differences; praise for treating people fairly and equally is yi shi tong ren.

bad.s: 他做事很{一刀切}，从来不拖泥带水。
bad.en: (meant: he is decisive and never dithers)
bad.why: It is not about being decisive; a person who acts quickly and cleanly is gan cui li luo (crisp and decisive).

cards.mean: to rehash old material with nothing new added
cards.lit: to stir-fry yesterday's cold rice and serve it up again

use.how: A verb-object phrase, often split (炒了不少冷饭). Said of films, songs, books, talks or ideas that serve up old content again as if it were new.

near.diff: 老生常谈 is a familiar, trite remark everyone has heard; 炒冷饭 is offering old work or content again as something new.
换汤不换药 is a change of name or form with no change in substance; 炒冷饭 is serving up the same old content again.

cards.cue: A famous writer's "new" book turns out to be essays he already published years ago, put together again. What do readers say he is doing?

ctx.s: 这部电影又是{炒冷饭}，一点新意都没有。
ctx.en: This film is just a rehash again, with nothing fresh in it at all.

ctx.s: 新专辑里一半是老歌重新录的，粉丝说他在{炒冷饭}。
ctx.en: Half of the new album is old songs re-recorded, and fans say he is just recycling old material.

ctx.s: 老板看完方案说：“这些点子去年都用过了，别再{炒冷饭}了。”
ctx.en: After reading the proposal the boss said: "We used all these ideas last year, stop serving up the same old stuff."

ctx.s: 这本书不就是把他以前的文章重新编了一下吗？是不是在{炒冷饭}？
ctx.en: Isn't this book just his old articles re-edited? Isn't he simply rehashing old material?

ctx.s: 游戏公司这几年{炒了不少冷饭}，老游戏换个画面就重新卖。
ctx.en: In recent years the game company has done a lot of rehashing, putting new graphics on old games and selling them again.

ctx.s: 他的讲座每年内容都一样，学生们私下说他年年{炒冷饭}。
ctx.en: His lecture has the same content every year, and students say privately that he serves up the same old stuff year after year.

bad.s: 考试前我要把学过的课文{炒冷饭}，好好复习一遍。
bad.en: (meant: before the exam I'm going to go over the texts I've studied)
bad.why: Going over old lessons for yourself is fuxi (revise); this idiom criticises presenting old content to others as if it were new.

bad.s: 博物馆把这幅古画修复得跟原来一样，真是{炒冷饭}的好手艺。
bad.en: (meant: the museum restored the old painting perfectly, what fine craftsmanship)
bad.why: It is a criticism of stale repetition and cannot praise careful restoration of something old.

cards.mean: a successful start right at the beginning
cards.lit: red as the door opens: red, the colour of good fortune, on the very first day

use.how: A noun, usually after 取得, 实现, 迎来 or 来个: 新年开门红. Said of a good result at the start of a year, season, match series or new venture.

near.diff: 旗开得胜 is winning the very first battle or contest and is more bookish; 开门红 is a good start to a period such as a year, season or new business.

cards.cue: On the first working day of the new year, your sales team closes the biggest deal it has had in months. How do you describe the start of the year?

ctx.s: 新年第一天就签了大单，真是{开门红}！
ctx.en: We signed a big deal on the very first day of the new year, what a great start!

ctx.s: 中国队首场比赛三比零获胜，取得了{开门红}。
ctx.en: The Chinese team won their first match three-nil, getting off to a winning start.

ctx.s: 新店开业第一天就排起了长队，老板笑着说这是个{开门红}。
ctx.en: On the new shop's opening day there was a long queue, and the owner said with a smile that it was a great start.

ctx.s: 朋友问他新工作怎么样，他说：“第一周就完成了两个项目，算是{开门红}吧。”
ctx.en: A friend asked how the new job was going, and he said: "I finished two projects in the first week, so it's off to a good start."

ctx.s: 今年一月份公司销售额大幅增长，实现了{开门红}。
ctx.en: The company's sales rose sharply this January, giving the year a strong start.

ctx.s: 新学期第一次考试，希望大家都能来个{开门红}。
ctx.en: It's the first test of the new term, and I hope everyone gets off to a flying start.

bad.s: 比赛最后一分钟他踢进了决胜球，真是{开门红}！
bad.en: (meant: he scored the winner in the last minute, what a finish!)
bad.why: It is only for a good result at the very beginning, never for a win at the end.

bad.s: 他一进门就害羞得满脸通红，真是{开门红}。
bad.en: (meant: he went red in the face with shyness as soon as he came in)
bad.why: It is a fixed phrase for a lucky good start, not a description of someone blushing at a door.

cards.mean: everyone rushing to do the same thing at once
cards.lit: a whole nest of bees pouring out together

use.how: Mostly used as an adverb (一窝蜂地挤进去, 一窝蜂似的) or before 的. Describes a crowd surging at once, and often mildly mocks everyone copying a trend.

near.diff: 蜂拥而至 is a written phrase that only describes crowds arriving; 一窝蜂 is colloquial and also mocks people all following the same trend.

cards.cue: A few people made money opening bubble-tea shops, and suddenly everyone in town opened one too, so most went bust within a year. How did people rush into the business?

ctx.s: 下课铃一响，孩子们{一窝蜂}地跑向食堂。
ctx.en: As soon as the bell rang, the children all rushed off to the canteen at once.

ctx.s: 商场的门一开，顾客{一窝蜂}地挤了进去。
ctx.en: The moment the mall doors opened, the shoppers all crowded in together.

ctx.s: 前几年大家{一窝蜂}地去开奶茶店，现在很多都关门了。
ctx.en: A few years ago everyone rushed to open bubble-tea shops, and now many have closed down.

ctx.s: 选专业要看自己的兴趣，别看见什么热门就{一窝蜂}地去报。
ctx.en: Choose your major by your own interests; don't all pile into whatever is popular.

ctx.s: 听说超市鸡蛋打折，大爷大妈们{一窝蜂}似的赶了过去。
ctx.en: Hearing that the supermarket had eggs on sale, the old folks all swarmed over there at once.

ctx.s: 这种{一窝蜂}的投资方式风险很大，最后亏的往往是普通人。
ctx.en: This kind of herd investing is very risky, and it's usually ordinary people who end up losing.

bad.s: 他一个人{一窝蜂}地冲进了办公室。
bad.en: (meant: he rushed into the office on his own)
bad.why: It describes a whole crowd moving at once, so it cannot be said of one person.

bad.s: 我们组很团结，大家做事都{一窝蜂}，配合得特别好。
bad.en: (meant: our group is united and everyone works together really well)
bad.why: It pictures a disorderly crowd rushing or copying others, not well-coordinated teamwork, and is never praise.

cards.mean: to suffer a humbling setback through a mistake
cards.lit: to trip and fall flat, head over heels

use.how: An intransitive verb phrase, often split: 栽了个大跟头, 栽过跟头. Said of a person or company that fails through carelessness, pride or misjudgment.

near.diff: 碰钉子 is being flatly turned down when you ask for something; 栽跟头 is failing badly because of your own mistake.

cards.cue: A star salesman who boasted he never needed to prepare lost the company's biggest client because he skipped the homework. What happened to him?

ctx.s: 他太骄傲了，早晚会{栽跟头}。
ctx.en: He is far too proud; sooner or later he'll come a cropper.

ctx.s: 这次考试我{栽了个大跟头}，数学没及格。
ctx.en: I really came unstuck in this exam: I failed maths.

ctx.s: 年轻人做生意{栽几个跟头}不要紧，关键是吸取教训。
ctx.en: It doesn't matter if young people take a few falls in business; what counts is learning the lesson.

ctx.s: 这家老牌公司就是因为忽视网上销售才{栽了跟头}。
ctx.en: This long-established company came to grief precisely because it ignored online sales.

ctx.s: 爸爸提醒他：“轻敌最容易{栽跟头}，比赛时认真点。”
ctx.en: His dad reminded him: "Underestimating your opponent is the easiest way to come a cropper, so take the match seriously."

ctx.s: 你在同一个问题上已经{栽过两次跟头}了，怎么还不长记性？
ctx.en: You've already been tripped up twice over the same thing; why haven't you learned?

bad.s: 今天出门被雨淋湿了，真是{栽跟头}。
bad.en: (meant: I got caught in the rain today, how unlucky)
bad.why: It is a real failure, usually from one's own mistake, not a small piece of bad luck like getting wet.

bad.s: 他在背后使坏，{栽跟头}了我。
bad.en: (meant: he worked against me behind my back and tripped me up)
bad.why: It is intransitive and cannot take a person as object; the one who fails must be the subject, as in rang wo zai le gen tou.

cards.mean: to cause trouble through a careless blunder
cards.lit: to poke a hole: jab at something and make a breach that others must patch

use.how: A verb-object phrase, often split: 捅了个大娄子, 捅出娄子, 他捅的娄子. Takes no object; said of someone whose blunder lands others in trouble.

near.diff: 闯祸 is the everyday word for causing an accident or trouble of any size; 捅娄子 is more colloquial and pictures a careless blunder that others must fix.
烂摊子 is the mess that is left behind; 捅娄子 is the act of causing the trouble.

cards.cue: On their first day the new intern runs the wrong command and wipes half the client database, and now the whole team must stay late to fix it. What has the intern done?

ctx.s: 看你这副表情，是不是又{捅娄子}了？
ctx.en: Judging by that look on your face, have you gone and caused trouble again?

ctx.s: 他把合同上的价格写错了，{捅了个大娄子}。
ctx.en: He wrote the wrong price on the contract and landed us in big trouble.

ctx.s: 新来的实习生第一天就{捅了娄子}，把系统数据删了一半。
ctx.en: The new intern caused trouble on the very first day by deleting half of the system's data.

ctx.s: 你少说两句吧，别再{捅出什么娄子}来。
ctx.en: Say less, will you? Don't go stirring up any more trouble.

ctx.s: 妈妈出门前嘱咐：“在家老实待着，别给我{捅娄子}。”
ctx.en: Before going out, Mum said: "Behave yourself at home and don't get into any trouble."

ctx.s: 要不是经理及时发现，小王这回{捅的娄子}可就大了。
ctx.en: If the manager hadn't spotted it in time, the trouble Xiao Wang caused this time would have been serious.

bad.s: 他故意在背后{捅娄子}，想让同事丢掉工作。
bad.en: (meant: he deliberately sabotaged his colleague behind his back to get him fired)
bad.why: It is trouble caused by a careless blunder, not a deliberate plot against someone; that is shi huai (playing dirty).

bad.s: 小偷用刀{捅娄子}了他。
bad.en: (meant: the thief stabbed him with a knife)
bad.why: Tong alone means to stab; this idiom means causing trouble and cannot take a person as object.

cards.mean: a mess left behind for someone else to sort out
cards.lit: a broken-down, rotten market stall that someone has to take over

use.how: A noun, usually with 收拾, 接手, 留下 or 接: 收拾烂摊子. Said of a failing business, project or situation that someone else has to put right.

near.diff: 捅娄子 is the act of causing trouble; 烂摊子 is the messy situation left for someone else to deal with.

cards.cue: Your predecessor quit suddenly, leaving unpaid bills, angry clients and missing records, and now it's all on your desk. What did they leave you?

ctx.s: 他说辞职就辞职，留下一个{烂摊子}给我。
ctx.en: He just quit out of the blue and left me with a mess to sort out.

ctx.s: 每次你闯了祸，都是我来收拾{烂摊子}。
ctx.en: Every time you get into trouble, I'm the one who has to clean up the mess.

ctx.s: 这个项目都快黄了，谁愿意接这个{烂摊子}？
ctx.en: This project is about to collapse; who would want to take over a mess like that?

ctx.s: 新经理接手的是一个{烂摊子}：欠债多，客户少，员工人心涣散。
ctx.en: The new manager inherited a mess: lots of debt, few customers and staff with no morale.

ctx.s: 同事抱怨：“前任把账目弄得一团糟，这种{烂摊子}谁都不想管。”
ctx.en: A colleague complained: "The last person made a total mess of the accounts, and nobody wants to deal with that kind of mess."

ctx.s: 老板退休后，女儿接下了工厂这个{烂摊子}，没想到三年就扭亏为盈了。
ctx.en: After the owner retired, the owner's daughter took over the failing factory and, surprisingly, turned it into a profit within three years.

bad.s: 他是个{烂摊子}，什么事都做不好。
bad.en: (meant: he is useless and can't do anything right)
bad.why: It is a messy situation left to others, not a word for a useless person.

bad.s: 对不起，我把公司的事{烂摊子}了。
bad.en: (meant: sorry, I messed up the company's business)
bad.why: It is a noun, not a verb; say gao za le (messed it up) or use it as an object of liu xia (left behind).

cards.mean: a long-standing problem nobody has managed to solve
cards.lit: old, big and hard: a problem that is long-standing, serious and difficult all at once

use.how: A noun or before 问题: 停车难是个老大难问题. Said of chronic problems in a city, workplace or community. It is also used of people who have long stayed single, but take care with that.

near.diff: 绊脚石 is anything or anyone that blocks progress; 老大难 is a problem that has dragged on for years without being solved.

cards.cue: For twenty years residents of an old neighbourhood have complained there's nowhere to park, and every new committee promises to fix it but never does. What kind of problem is it?

ctx.s: 停车难是这个小区的{老大难}问题。
ctx.en: The lack of parking is this estate's long-standing problem.

ctx.s: 堵车一直是这座城市的{老大难}，修了地铁才好一点。
ctx.en: Traffic jams have long been this city's chronic problem, and things only got a bit better once the metro was built.

ctx.s: 老旧小区装电梯，为什么一直是个{老大难}？
ctx.en: Why has installing lifts in old housing estates remained such an intractable problem?

ctx.s: 经理在会上说：“客户投诉回复慢是我们部门多年的{老大难}，今年必须解决。”
ctx.en: The manager said at the meeting: "Slow replies to customer complaints have been our department's chronic problem for years, and this year we must fix it."

ctx.s: 新校长上任才三个月，就解决了食堂这个{老大难}。
ctx.en: Just three months after taking office, the new head teacher solved the canteen problem that had dragged on for years.

ctx.s: 村里的饮水问题拖了二十年，一直是个{老大难}，直到去年才通上自来水。
ctx.en: The village's water supply problem dragged on for twenty years, and only last year did running water finally arrive.

bad.s: 这道数学题太{老大难}了，我做不出来。
bad.en: (meant: this maths problem is too hard, I can't do it)
bad.why: It is a noun for a problem that has dragged on for years, not an adjective for something hard; a hard exercise is just hen nan (very hard).

bad.s: 他是我们公司的{老大难}，什么事都由他决定。
bad.en: (meant: he is the top boss of our company and decides everything)
bad.why: Laoda alone can mean boss, but this idiom is a chronic problem; the person in charge is yi ba shou.

cards.mean: to fall out openly, dropping all pretence of goodwill
cards.lit: to tear the face: rip away the polite mask people keep up with each other

use.how: A verb phrase, also 撕破脸皮 or split as 撕破了脸; often 跟某人撕破脸, 不想撕破脸. Said when two parties drop politeness and the conflict becomes open.

near.diff: 翻脸 is suddenly turning angry or hostile; 撕破脸 stresses that all politeness is gone and the conflict is now in the open.
闹别扭 is a passing sulk between people who are still close; 撕破脸 is an open break with no pretence left.

cards.cue: For years two business partners stayed polite despite their quarrels, but now they insult each other in public and talk only through lawyers. What has happened between them?

ctx.s: 大家以后还要一起工作，别为这点小事{撕破脸}。
ctx.en: We all still have to work together, so don't fall out openly over something this small.

ctx.s: 为了遗产，兄弟俩最后{撕破了脸}，闹上了法庭。
ctx.en: Over the inheritance, the two brothers finally fell out openly and ended up in court.

ctx.s: 两家公司合作多年，这次因为合同纠纷彻底{撕破脸}了。
ctx.en: The two companies had worked together for years, but this contract dispute has turned them into open enemies.

ctx.s: 他欠钱一直不还，你还不好意思跟他{撕破脸}吗？
ctx.en: He has never paid back what he owes; are you still too embarrassed to have it out with him openly?

ctx.s: 她心里很不满，但表面上还客客气气的，不想跟对方{撕破脸}。
ctx.en: She was very unhappy inside, but stayed polite on the surface because she didn't want an open break.

ctx.s: 事情闹到{撕破脸}的地步，以后很难再合作了。
ctx.en: Now that things have come to an open break, it will be hard to work together again.

bad.s: 他在会上说错了话，觉得特别{撕破脸}。
bad.en: (meant: he said the wrong thing in the meeting and felt really humiliated)
bad.why: Feeling embarrassed is diu lian (lose face); this idiom is an open break between two parties, not a feeling.

bad.s: 小两口昨天为谁洗碗{撕破脸}了，今天早上就和好了。
bad.en: (meant: the young couple had a little spat about the dishes yesterday and made up this morning)
bad.why: It means a serious, open break in a relationship, not a small quarrel that is mended the next morning.

cards.mean: to go to any length, even at great risk, to help a friend
cards.lit: to have knives thrust into both sides of one's ribs for someone's sake

use.how: A verb phrase, usually 为朋友两肋插刀, or before 的 (两肋插刀的兄弟). Said of loyalty between friends that will take real risk or sacrifice.

near.diff: 雪中送炭 is timely help to someone in need; 两肋插刀 is loyalty so great that one would risk oneself for a friend.
赴汤蹈火 is braving any danger for a cause or a person and is more formal; 两肋插刀 is specifically loyalty to a friend.

cards.cue: An old friend is in serious trouble, and you tell him you will stand by him even if it costs you your job and your savings. What are you ready to do for him?

ctx.s: 他是那种能为朋友{两肋插刀}的人。
ctx.en: He is the kind of man who would do anything, whatever the risk, for a friend.

ctx.s: 只要你一句话，兄弟我{两肋插刀}，在所不辞！
ctx.en: Just say the word, and I'll go through fire for you, no questions asked!

ctx.s: 当年他被人冤枉，只有老同学冒着得罪老板的风险站出来替他作证，这才叫{两肋插刀}。
ctx.en: When he was falsely accused back then, only an old classmate risked angering the boss to stand up and testify for him; that is what real loyalty to a friend looks like.

ctx.s: 嘴上说讲义气的人很多，可真遇到事，有几个肯{两肋插刀}？
ctx.en: Lots of people talk about loyalty, but when trouble really comes, how many will stick their neck out for you?

ctx.s: 为朋友{两肋插刀}是好事，但帮他做违法的事就不是义气了。
ctx.en: Going to any length for a friend is good, but helping him break the law is not loyalty.

ctx.s: 这部小说里的两个主人公是{两肋插刀}的好兄弟。
ctx.en: The two heroes of this novel are sworn friends who would risk anything for each other.

bad.s: 他对公司{两肋插刀}，十年来从来没迟到过。
bad.en: (meant: he is devoted to the company and hasn't been late once in ten years)
bad.why: It is loyalty between friends at great personal risk, not diligence or devotion to an employer.

bad.s: 同学忘带笔了，我{两肋插刀}借了他一支。
bad.en: (meant: a classmate forgot his pen, so I lent him one)
bad.why: It is for great risk or sacrifice; used for lending a pen it can only sound sarcastic.

cards.mean: an ingrate who repays kindness with betrayal
cards.lit: a white-eyed wolf

use.how: Noun, usually 是个白眼狼 or 骂他白眼狼. A harsh insult for someone who turns on the person who raised, fed or helped them.

near.diff: 忘恩负义 is a four-character phrase naming the act, at home in writing; 白眼狼 is a blunt spoken insult for the person.
墙头草 switches to whichever side is stronger; 白眼狼 turns on the very person who helped them.

cards.cue: Your nephew lived with you rent-free for three years, then sued you over the flat as soon as he moved out. What do you call him?

ctx.s: 我把他当亲弟弟一样照顾，没想到他是个{白眼狼}。
ctx.en: I looked after him like my own brother; I never thought he would turn out to be such an ingrate.

ctx.s: 爸妈辛辛苦苦供你上大学，你现在连电话都不打，真是个{白眼狼}！
ctx.en: Mum and Dad worked themselves to the bone to put you through university, and now you don't even call. What an ungrateful wretch!

ctx.s: 当初是我借钱帮他渡过难关，现在他却到处说我坏话，你说他是不是{白眼狼}？
ctx.en: I lent him money to get through hard times, and now he badmouths me everywhere. Tell me, isn't that the height of ingratitude?

ctx.s: “老板培养了他五年，他一跳槽就把客户全带走了。”“这种{白眼狼}，谁还敢用？”
ctx.en: "The boss trained him for five years, and the moment he changed jobs he took all the clients with him." "Who would dare hire an ingrate like that?"

ctx.s: 老人收养的孩子长大后卷走了家里的钱，村里人都骂他{白眼狼}。
ctx.en: The boy the old man had adopted ran off with the family's money when he grew up, and the whole village cursed him as an ingrate.

ctx.s: 帮人之前最好看清楚，别好心养出个{白眼狼}来。
ctx.en: Look carefully before you help someone, or your kindness may just raise a wolf that bites you.

bad.s: 我跟他打招呼，他理都不理，真是个{白眼狼}。
bad.en: (meant: I said hello and he ignored me, how rude)
bad.why: It is for someone who betrays a benefactor; a person who is merely cold or rude and owes you nothing is not one.

bad.s: 那个陌生人在网上骗了我的钱，真是个{白眼狼}。
bad.en: (meant: that stranger who conned me online is a crook)
bad.why: A swindler you never helped is a pianzi (cheat); this insult needs kindness given first and betrayal in return.

cards.r: gē bo zhǒu wǎng wài guǎi
cards.mean: to side with outsiders against one's own people
cards.lit: the elbow bends outwards, away from one's own body

use.how: Predicate, often in reproach: 你怎么胳膊肘往外拐？ Said of family, friends or teammates who take an outsider's side, often half-jokingly.

near.diff: 吃里扒外 is living off your own side while secretly helping outsiders, a real betrayal; 胳膊肘往外拐 is just taking the outsider's side.

cards.cue: Your brother is arguing with a shop assistant, and you tell him the assistant is right. He turns and glares at you. What does he accuse you of?

ctx.s: 你是我妹妹，怎么{胳膊肘往外拐}，帮着外人说话？
ctx.en: You're my sister. How can you take an outsider's side against me?

ctx.s: 我跟同学打架，妈妈却先批评我，我觉得她{胳膊肘往外拐}。
ctx.en: I got into a fight with a classmate, but Mum told me off first. I felt she had taken the other side.

ctx.s: “这次比赛对手确实比我们强。”“你一个队长，怎么也{胳膊肘往外拐}了？”
ctx.en: "The other team really was better than us this time." "You're the captain! How can you be on their side too?"

ctx.s: 他在谈判桌上处处替对方着想，老板怀疑他{胳膊肘往外拐}。
ctx.en: At the negotiating table he kept looking out for the other party, and his boss began to suspect he was on their side.

ctx.s: 球迷骂主场解说员{胳膊肘往外拐}，整场比赛都在夸客队。
ctx.en: Fans accused the home commentator of switching sides, since he praised the away team all match long.

ctx.s: 身为公司员工，却到处推荐对手的产品，你这{胳膊肘也往外拐}得太厉害了吧。
ctx.en: You work for this company, yet you go around recommending our rival's products. Aren't you taking their side a bit too far?

bad.s: 法官{胳膊肘往外拐}，对双方一视同仁，大家都很佩服。
bad.en: (meant: the judge was impartial and everyone admired him)
bad.why: It reproaches disloyalty to one's own side and is never praise; for even-handedness between parties use yi wan shui duan ping.

bad.s: 他不管谁对谁错，总是护着自己家里人，真是{胳膊肘往外拐}。
bad.en: (meant: he always defends his own family, right or wrong)
bad.why: It is the opposite: it reproaches siding with outsiders. Always backing your own people is huduan or bang qin bu bang li.

cards.mean: to treat everyone fairly and favour no one
cards.lit: to carry a bowl of water level, so none spills to either side

use.how: Predicate, often after 要、得、没、做不到: 父母要一碗水端平。 Said of parents, teachers or bosses dealing with two or more parties.

near.diff: 一视同仁 is a more formal phrase for treating everyone alike; 一碗水端平 is everyday speech and stresses not favouring one rival over another.

cards.cue: Your two children both want the bigger bedroom, and each is watching to see whether you favour the other. What must you do?

ctx.s: 家里有两个孩子，父母一定要{一碗水端平}。
ctx.en: When there are two children in the family, the parents must treat them exactly alike.

ctx.s: 老师只批评我，不批评他，明明{一碗水没端平}嘛！
ctx.en: The teacher only told me off and not him. That's obviously not fair!

ctx.s: “奶奶给哥哥买了新手机，给我买什么？”“别急，奶奶向来{一碗水端平}。”
ctx.en: "Grandma bought my brother a new phone, so what's she getting me?" "Don't worry, Grandma never plays favourites."

ctx.s: 当领导最难的，就是在几个部门之间{一碗水端平}。
ctx.en: The hardest part of being a manager is being even-handed between the different departments.

ctx.s: 分奖金的时候，经理完全按业绩算，{一碗水端得很平}，没人有意见。
ctx.en: When the bonuses were shared out, the manager went strictly by performance and was perfectly fair, so nobody complained.

ctx.s: 婆媳之间闹矛盾，夹在中间的丈夫很难做到{一碗水端平}。
ctx.en: When a wife and her mother-in-law fall out, the husband caught in the middle finds it very hard not to favour one of them.

bad.s: 我对女朋友一直{一碗水端平}，她要什么我都给。
bad.en: (meant: I have always treated my girlfriend well and given her whatever she wants)
bad.why: It needs two or more parties to be fair between; for treating one person well just say dui ta hen hao.

bad.s: 遇到再大的困难，他也能{一碗水端平}，一点都不慌。
bad.en: (meant: however hard things get, he stays steady and calm)
bad.why: The level bowl is about fairness between people, not about keeping calm; for composure say chen de zhu qi.

cards.mean: a group with no unity or cohesion at all
cards.lit: a tray of loose sand that cannot be held together

use.how: Noun phrase, mostly 像一盘散沙 or 成了一盘散沙. Said of teams, classes, companies or communities whose members do not pull together.

near.diff: 乌合之众 is a scornful term for a disorderly rabble; 一盘散沙 says a group that ought to be united has no cohesion.

cards.cue: Since the coach left, every player does their own thing: nobody passes, nobody turns up to training on time. What has the team become?

ctx.s: 这个班以前像{一盘散沙}，新班主任来了以后才团结起来。
ctx.en: This class used to have no unity at all; it only pulled together after the new form teacher arrived.

ctx.s: 公司没有统一的目标，各部门各干各的，简直是{一盘散沙}。
ctx.en: The company has no common goal and every department goes its own way. It's completely disjointed.

ctx.s: “我们队人人都是高手，为什么老输？”“因为大家是{一盘散沙}，没人配合。”
ctx.en: "Everyone on our team is a top player, so why do we keep losing?" "Because there's no teamwork. Nobody plays together."

ctx.s: 小区业主想一起跟物业交涉，可是意见始终统一不了，还是{一盘散沙}。
ctx.en: The residents wanted to take on the property management together, but they could never agree and stayed hopelessly divided.

ctx.s: 一个团队如果没有核心人物，人再多也只是{一盘散沙}。
ctx.en: Without someone at its centre, a team is just loose sand, however many people it has.

ctx.s: 志愿者来了不少，但没人组织分工，大家各忙各的，像{一盘散沙}。
ctx.en: Plenty of volunteers turned up, but nobody organised them, so everyone did their own thing with no coordination.

bad.s: 他房间里书和衣服到处都是，像{一盘散沙}。
bad.en: (meant: his room is a mess, with books and clothes everywhere)
bad.why: It describes people who do not unite, not a messy pile of things; for a mess say luanqibazao.

bad.s: 他这个人做事没计划，是{一盘散沙}。
bad.en: (meant: he is a disorganised person who never plans)
bad.why: Only a group can lack cohesion; for one disorganised person say zuoshi mei tiaoli or hen sanman.

cards.mean: to tell tales about others to a superior
cards.lit: to file a little report behind someone's back

use.how: Verb-object phrase: 向老师打小报告, 打他的小报告. Said of secretly telling a teacher or boss about a classmate's or colleague's faults, often to curry favour.

near.diff: 告状 is complaining to someone in authority, often openly and with good cause; 打小报告 is sneaky tale-telling behind someone's back.

cards.cue: A coworker notices you leave twenty minutes early and quietly emails the manager about it. What did the coworker do?

ctx.s: 小明又向老师{打小报告}了，说同桌上课吃零食。
ctx.en: Xiao Ming went telling tales to the teacher again, saying his deskmate was eating snacks in class.

ctx.s: 你迟到的事，是不是有人跟经理{打了小报告}？
ctx.en: About you being late: did someone go and tell on you to the manager?

ctx.s: 有意见就当面说，别在背后{打我的小报告}。
ctx.en: If you have a problem with me, say it to my face. Don't go telling tales about me behind my back.

ctx.s: 办公室里谁都提防她，因为她最爱{打小报告}。
ctx.en: Everyone in the office is on guard around her, because she loves nothing more than snitching to the boss.

ctx.s: 小时候我{打过哥哥的小报告}，结果被他记恨了好久。
ctx.en: When I was little I told on my big brother once, and he held it against me for ages.

ctx.s: 为了升职，他经常偷偷给领导{打小报告}，同事们都很看不起他。
ctx.en: He was always secretly reporting on people to the boss to get promoted, and his colleagues despised him for it.

bad.s: 下午我要给经理{打小报告}，汇报一下项目进度。
bad.en: (meant: this afternoon I will give the manager a short progress report)
bad.why: It means sneaky tale-telling, not a short work report; for reporting progress say huibao.

bad.s: 市民勇敢地{打小报告}，帮警察抓住了小偷。
bad.en: (meant: a brave citizen reported it and helped the police catch the thief)
bad.why: It is always contemptuous and cannot praise anyone; for public-spirited reporting say jubao or baojing.

cards.mean: to argue just for the sake of arguing
cards.lit: to carry a pole together on the shoulders

use.how: Verb, usually 跟某人抬杠, 爱抬杠, 抬什么杠; takes no object. Said of contradicting someone over small points just to keep arguing.

near.diff: 唱反调 is taking the opposite stand against a plan or view; 抬杠 is quibbling back and forth in conversation for the sake of it.

cards.cue: Whatever you say at dinner, your uncle insists on the opposite, then argues about that too, just to keep it going. What does he love to do?

ctx.s: 我说一句他顶一句，就爱跟我{抬杠}。
ctx.en: Every time I say something he comes back at me. He just loves arguing with me.

ctx.s: 你明知道我说的是对的，还{抬什么杠}？
ctx.en: You know perfectly well I'm right, so why are you arguing?

ctx.s: 我不是跟你{抬杠}，可是这个数字真的不对。
ctx.en: I'm not trying to pick an argument, but this figure really is wrong.

ctx.s: “今天好热啊。”“夏天哪有不热的？”“你能不能别{抬杠}了！”
ctx.en: "It's so hot today." "When is summer ever not hot?" "Can you stop contradicting me for once!"

ctx.s: 两兄弟一见面就{抬起杠}来，从球赛一直争到天气。
ctx.en: The moment the two brothers meet they start bickering, from football all the way to the weather.

ctx.s: 网上有些人专门在评论区挑字眼，就是为了{抬杠}。
ctx.en: Some people online nitpick every word in the comments, just to start an argument.

bad.s: 两位科学家在会议上{抬杠}，提出了很多有价值的观点。
bad.en: (meant: the two scientists debated at the conference and raised many valuable points)
bad.why: It is pointless contrarian bickering; a serious, productive exchange of views is bianlun or taolun.

bad.s: 他总是{抬杠}我，真烦人。
bad.en: (meant: he always argues with me, it's so annoying)
bad.why: It takes no object; the person goes before it with gen: ta zongshi gen wo taigang.

cards.mean: to make promises one has no means or intention to keep
cards.lit: to write a cheque that the account cannot cover

use.how: Verb-object, often split: 开了不少空头支票, 别给我开空头支票. Said of promises made to win someone over, with no real plan to keep them.

near.diff: 画大饼 paints a vague rosy future to keep staff working; 开空头支票 is a definite promise, of money, a trip or a favour, that is never kept.
打包票 is confidently guaranteeing something; 开空头支票 is promising what will never be delivered.

cards.cue: Your flatmate has promised for months to pay back what he owes next week, and every week he says it again. What does he keep doing?

ctx.s: 说到就要做到，别{开空头支票}。
ctx.en: If you say you'll do it, do it. Don't make empty promises.

ctx.s: 爸爸说暑假带我们去海边，结果又{开了空头支票}。
ctx.en: Dad said he'd take us to the seaside in the summer holidays, but it was another empty promise.

ctx.s: 这家商店{开了一张空头支票}，承诺的免费维修根本没兑现。
ctx.en: The shop made a promise it never meant to keep: the free repairs it offered never happened.

ctx.s: “下次一定请你吃饭！”“你都{开过多少次空头支票}了？”
ctx.en: "Next time dinner's definitely on me!" "How many times have you promised that already?"

ctx.s: 新来的物业经理说一个月内修好电梯，大家担心他只是在{开空头支票}。
ctx.en: The new property manager has promised to fix the lift within a month, and people worry it is just an empty promise.

ctx.s: 与其{开空头支票}，不如老老实实告诉客户什么时候能交货。
ctx.en: Rather than make promises you can't keep, just tell the customer honestly when you can deliver.

bad.s: 他给孩子{开了空头支票}，周末真的带他们去了动物园。
bad.en: (meant: he promised the children a trip and really took them to the zoo at the weekend)
bad.why: It means a promise that is never kept; for a kept promise say shuohua suanhua or shuodao zuodao.

bad.s: 我向你{开空头支票}：明天一定按时交稿。
bad.en: (meant: I promise you I will hand in the draft on time tomorrow)
bad.why: It is an accusation; nobody uses it for their own sincere promise. Say wo xiang ni baozheng.

cards.mean: (of a boss) to dangle a rosy future that never arrives
cards.lit: to draw a big flatbread that no one can eat

use.how: Verb-object, often 给员工画大饼, 又在画大饼. Mostly said of bosses or companies offering bright prospects, such as promotion or shares, instead of real rewards.

near.diff: 开空头支票 is breaking a definite promise; 画大饼 is painting a vague, grand future to keep people motivated now.

cards.cue: Your manager can't give you a raise, but says that once the company goes public in a few years you'll all be rich. What is he doing?

ctx.s: 老板又在会上{画大饼}了，说明年人人都能升职。
ctx.en: The boss is dangling the dream again at the meeting, saying everyone will be promoted next year.

ctx.s: 别给我{画大饼}了，先把这个月的工资发了吧。
ctx.en: Spare me the grand vision. Just pay this month's wages first.

ctx.s: 面试时公司{画了一个大饼}，入职后才发现什么都没有。
ctx.en: At the interview the company promised a bright future, but once I started I found there was nothing behind it.

ctx.s: “老板说公司上市后我们都能分股票。”“他那是{画大饼}，你也信？”
ctx.en: "The boss says we'll all get shares once the company lists." "That's pie in the sky. You actually believe him?"

ctx.s: 有的创业者靠{画大饼}招人，员工一年拿不到奖金，很快就走光了。
ctx.en: Some founders recruit by selling dreams, and when staff go a year without a bonus they all leave.

ctx.s: 好的领导会把现实困难讲清楚，而不是一味地{画大饼}。
ctx.en: A good leader explains the real difficulties clearly instead of just promising a rosy future.

bad.s: 经理{画了大饼}，把下周每个人的任务都安排得清清楚楚。
bad.en: (meant: the manager made a plan, setting out everyone's tasks for next week clearly)
bad.why: It means empty promises of a bright future, not concrete planning; for that say zuo jihua or anpai renwu.

bad.s: 妈妈在厨房{画大饼}，准备做晚饭。
bad.en: (meant: Mum is making flatbread in the kitchen for dinner)
bad.why: Making real flatbread is lao da bing; with hua (draw) it only means empty promises.

cards.mean: the person in overall charge, the top boss
cards.lit: the number-one hand, the first in line

use.how: Noun, often 公司的一把手, 单位一把手. Names whoever holds top authority in an organisation; used about someone, not as a form of address.

near.diff: 一把好手 is someone very good at something (做饭是一把好手); 一把手 today normally means the person in charge.
挑大梁 is carrying the main load of a job; 一把手 is the top position itself.

cards.cue: A department head says she can't approve your request herself: only the person at the very top of the organisation can. Who must decide?

ctx.s: 这件事太大了，得{一把手}亲自决定。
ctx.en: This matter is too big; the top boss will have to decide personally.

ctx.s: 她三十多岁就当上了医院的{一把手}。
ctx.en: She became head of the hospital while still in her thirties.

ctx.s: “你们公司谁说了算？”“当然是{一把手}张总。”
ctx.en: "Who calls the shots at your company?" "Mr Zhang, the boss, of course."

ctx.s: 很多问题拖了好几年，换了{一把手}以后很快就解决了。
ctx.en: Many problems had dragged on for years, but they were quickly sorted out once there was a new person at the top.

ctx.s: 作为单位的{一把手}，他要为这次安全事故负主要责任。
ctx.en: As head of the organisation, he bears the main responsibility for this safety accident.

ctx.s: 公司的{一把手}和二把手意见不合，下面的人很难办事。
ctx.en: The company's number one and number two don't see eye to eye, which makes it hard for everyone below them to get anything done.

bad.s: 他在这次数学比赛中得了第一名，成了全校的{一把手}。
bad.en: (meant: he won first place in the maths contest and became the school's top student)
bad.why: It is the person who leads an organisation, not the winner of a contest; for that say diyiming or guanjun.

bad.s: 见到经理时，他说：“{一把手}，早上好！”
bad.en: (meant: he greeted the manager, "Good morning, boss!")
bad.why: It describes someone's position and is not used to address them; greet them by surname and title, as in Wang zong hao.

cards.mean: to dawdle over work on purpose and drag it out
cards.lit: to grind away at foreign (hired) work, making the job last

use.how: Verb-object, can split: 磨了一下午洋工, 磨什么洋工. Said of workers, students or contractors who stretch out work on purpose.

near.diff: 开小差 is letting your mind wander or slipping away from duty; 磨洋工 is staying at the job but working slowly on purpose.

cards.cue: The decorators are paid by the day, and a job that should take a week has stretched to a month, with a tea break every hour. What are they doing?

ctx.s: 这点活儿半天就能干完，别{磨洋工}了！
ctx.en: This is half a day's work at most. Stop dragging it out!

ctx.s: 这些装修工人按天算钱，所以故意{磨洋工}。
ctx.en: These decorators are paid by the day, so they deliberately drag the job out.

ctx.s: 儿子写作业{磨了一晚上洋工}，才写了两道题。
ctx.en: My son dawdled over his homework all evening and only did two questions.

ctx.s: “这份报告怎么还没交？”“他整天在{磨洋工}，你还指望他？”
ctx.en: "Why hasn't this report been handed in yet?" "He spends all day spinning things out. You were counting on him?"

ctx.s: 加班按小时算钱，有些员工白天就开始{磨洋工}，把活儿留到晚上。
ctx.en: Overtime is paid by the hour, so some employees start going slow during the day and leave the work for the evening.

ctx.s: 项目进度这么慢，到底是真遇到了困难，还是有人在{磨洋工}？
ctx.en: The project is moving so slowly. Have we really hit problems, or is someone dragging their feet on purpose?

bad.s: 他刚学开车，开得很慢，是在{磨洋工}。
bad.en: (meant: he has just learned to drive, so he drives slowly)
bad.why: It means slowing down on purpose to drag out work, not slowness from inexperience.

bad.s: 老师傅慢慢{磨洋工}，做出了一套精美的家具。
bad.en: (meant: the old craftsman worked patiently and made a beautiful set of furniture)
bad.why: It is criticism and cannot praise patient, careful work; for that say man gong chu xi huo.

cards.mean: to shoulder the key role or main responsibility
cards.lit: to carry the main roof beam on one's shoulders

use.how: Verb-object phrase, often split as 挑起大梁 or 挑起了…的大梁. Said of a person or group taking the central role in a team, project or performance.

near.diff: 一把手 is the person in the top post; 挑大梁 is whoever actually carries the main load, whatever their title.
跑龙套 is the opposite: having only a small part that anyone could fill.

cards.cue: The star striker is injured, and a nineteen-year-old suddenly becomes the player the whole team relies on to win. What has he done?

ctx.s: 老师傅退休了，现在由小王{挑大梁}。
ctx.en: The old master has retired, and now Xiao Wang carries the main load.

ctx.s: 这次项目是你第一次{挑大梁}，紧张吗？
ctx.en: This project is the first time you've taken the lead role. Nervous?

ctx.s: 主力队员受伤以后，这个十九岁的新人{挑起了大梁}。
ctx.en: After the key players were injured, this nineteen-year-old newcomer took on the team's main burden.

ctx.s: 公司现在缺的不是普通员工，而是能{挑大梁}的人。
ctx.en: What the company lacks now is not ordinary staff but people who can shoulder the key responsibilities.

ctx.s: “这部戏谁演主角？”“这回让年轻演员{挑大梁}。”
ctx.en: "Who's playing the lead in this play?" "This time we're letting a young actor carry the show."

ctx.s: 经过几年锻炼，这批年轻人已经能在单位里{挑起大梁}了。
ctx.en: After a few years of experience, this group of young people can now shoulder the main work of the organisation.

bad.s: 搬家那天，他一个人{挑大梁}，把冰箱扛上了五楼。
bad.en: (meant: on moving day he carried the fridge up to the fifth floor by himself)
bad.why: It is figurative: taking the central role in work, a team or a show, not physically carrying something heavy.

bad.s: 他{挑大梁}了这个项目。
bad.en: (meant: he took the lead on this project)
bad.why: It is already verb plus object and takes no further object; say zai zhege xiangmu li tiao daliang (take the lead in this project).

cards.mean: to play only a minor, supporting part
cards.lit: to run about the stage in the dragon-patterned extras' costume

story.text: In traditional Chinese opera, the extras who play soldiers, guards and attendants wear a standard costume embroidered with dragons, called a longtao. They come on in a group, run across the stage, stand in formation around the main characters and run off again, usually without lines of their own. Running in the longtao came to mean having only a small part in anything.
story.source: Stage term of traditional Chinese opera (京剧 and other 戏曲)

use.how: Verb-object phrase, often as 跑龙套的 (an extra) or split as 跑了几年龙套. Said of oneself or others having only a minor role, often modestly or wryly.

near.diff: 挑大梁 is carrying the main role; 跑龙套 is the opposite, a small supporting part.

cards.cue: Asked about his part in an award-winning project, a junior designer shrugs and says he only fetched files and booked meeting rooms. How does he describe his role?

ctx.s: 我在这部电影里只是{跑龙套}的，镜头不到一分钟。
ctx.en: I'm only an extra in this film; I'm on screen for less than a minute.

ctx.s: 他在剧组{跑了五年龙套}，才演上第一个有台词的角色。
ctx.en: He played bit parts for five years before he got his first role with lines.

ctx.s: “这次活动你负责什么？”“我就是{跑跑龙套}，帮忙搬搬东西。”
ctx.en: "What are you in charge of at this event?" "I'm just helping out on the side, carrying things around."

ctx.s: 别看他现在是大明星，当年也是从{跑龙套}开始的。
ctx.en: He may be a big star now, but he started out as an extra.

ctx.s: 这个项目我们部门只是{跑龙套}，主要工作都是总部做的。
ctx.en: Our department only played a supporting part in this project; headquarters did the main work.

ctx.s: 他不甘心一辈子在公司里{跑龙套}，决定出去自己创业。
ctx.en: Unwilling to spend his whole career in minor roles at the company, he decided to leave and start his own business.

bad.s: 他是我们公司的总经理，每天都在{跑龙套}。
bad.en: (meant: he is our general manager and rushes about busily every day)
bad.why: It does not mean rushing about busily; it means having a minor, unimportant part, so it cannot describe the boss's busy day.

bad.s: 我想{跑龙套}这个角色。
bad.en: (meant: I want to play this small role)
bad.why: It is already verb plus object and takes no further object; say zai zhe bu xi li pao longtao (play a bit part in this show).

cards.mean: to give someone special extra attention or coaching
cards.lit: to fire up a small stove: cook a separate, better meal apart from the big communal kitchen

use.how: Verb-object phrase, usually 给某人开小灶 or 开个小灶. Said of extra one-to-one help or special treatment from a teacher, coach or boss; can hint at favouritism.

near.diff: 走后门 is getting an advantage through connections, usually improperly; 开小灶 is someone in charge giving one person extra help or better treatment.

cards.cue: A student keeps failing maths, so her teacher stays after school every Thursday to go through problems with her alone. What is the teacher doing?

ctx.s: 考试前，老师每天放学后给我{开小灶}。
ctx.en: Before the exam, the teacher gave me extra one-to-one coaching every day after school.

ctx.s: 这个新人学得慢，师傅专门给他{开了小灶}。
ctx.en: The new apprentice was a slow learner, so the master gave him special extra lessons.

ctx.s: “教练，下课后能不能给我{开个小灶}？我的发球太差了。”
ctx.en: "Coach, could you give me some extra practice after class? My serve is terrible."

ctx.s: 同学们抱怨，班主任总是给成绩好的学生{开小灶}。
ctx.en: The students complain that the form teacher always gives the top students special attention.

ctx.s: 公司给重点项目{开小灶}，资金和人手都优先安排。
ctx.en: The company gives its priority projects special treatment: they get money and staff first.

ctx.s: 同样是新员工，经理凭什么只给他一个人{开小灶}？
ctx.en: We're all new staff, so why does the manager give him alone special one-to-one coaching?

bad.s: 我家厨房太小，所以我们{开小灶}。
bad.en: (meant: our kitchen is small, so we cook on a small stove)
bad.why: It is figurative: extra help or special treatment given to someone, not literally cooking in a small kitchen.

bad.s: 老师上课的时候给全班同学{开小灶}。
bad.en: (meant: the teacher taught the whole class in the lesson)
bad.why: It means attention singled out for one person or a few, beyond the normal routine; a regular lesson for the whole class is the opposite.

cards.mean: to make an outrageous demand, such as a sky-high price
cards.lit: the lion opens its mouth wide

use.how: Used as a predicate or after 是、简直是, about someone asking an outrageous price, salary or compensation: 房东狮子大开口，要涨一倍。

near.diff: 冤大头 is the person who ends up paying too much; 狮子大开口 is what the one demanding too much does.

cards.cue: At the airport, a driver sees you are a tourist and asks ten times the normal fare for a short ride into town. What is he doing?

ctx.s: 一碗面要两百块？你这是{狮子大开口}啊！
ctx.en: Two hundred yuan for a bowl of noodles? That's daylight robbery!

ctx.s: 房东{狮子大开口}，房租一下子要涨一倍。
ctx.en: The landlord is making an outrageous demand: he wants to double the rent in one go.

ctx.s: 对方{狮子大开口}，要我们赔一百万，我们当然不能答应。
ctx.en: The other side made an absurd demand for a million in compensation, which of course we can't accept.

ctx.s: 刚毕业就要求月薪五万，是不是有点{狮子大开口}了？
ctx.en: Asking for fifty thousand a month straight out of university: isn't that asking a bit much?

ctx.s: 谈判时，对方一上来就{狮子大开口}，后来才一点点让步。
ctx.en: In the negotiations, they opened with a sky-high demand and only gave ground bit by bit.

ctx.s: 有些景区趁节假日{狮子大开口}，一瓶水卖到二十块。
ctx.en: Some tourist sites take advantage of the holidays to charge absurd prices, twenty yuan for a bottle of water.

bad.s: 他饿坏了，{狮子大开口}，一口吃了半个汉堡。
bad.en: (meant: he was starving and ate half a burger in one big bite)
bad.why: It is about outrageous demands, usually for money, not about eating with a big mouthful.

bad.s: 老板很大方，{狮子大开口}给我们每人发了奖金。
bad.en: (meant: the boss was generous and gave each of us a bonus)
bad.why: It criticises someone who demands far too much; it never describes generous giving.

cards.mean: a sucker who pays far more than they should
cards.lit: a hard-done-by 'big head': the dupe left footing the bill

use.how: A noun, mostly in 当冤大头 or 把…当冤大头: 别把我当冤大头。 Said of someone tricked or pressured into paying too much, often of oneself in rueful self-mockery.

near.diff: 狮子大开口 is what the seller or claimant does in demanding too much; 冤大头 is the person who pays it.

cards.cue: You paid three times the going price for a phone case at a tourist market, then saw the same one for sale round the corner. What were you?

ctx.s: 这件衣服我花了八百，网上才两百，我真是个{冤大头}。
ctx.en: I paid eight hundred for this jacket and it's two hundred online. What a sucker I am.

ctx.s: 他们看你是外地人，把你当{冤大头}了。
ctx.en: They saw you were from out of town and took you for a mug.

ctx.s: 修个水龙头要五百？我可不当这个{冤大头}。
ctx.en: Five hundred to fix a tap? I'm not going to be the sucker who pays that.

ctx.s: 每次聚餐都是他买单，大家早就把他当成{冤大头}了。
ctx.en: He pays every time they eat out; everyone has long since treated him as the one who foots the bill.

ctx.s: 有些商家专门找不懂行情的顾客当{冤大头}。
ctx.en: Some shops specifically target customers who don't know the going rate and overcharge them.

ctx.s: 买房的时候一定要多比较，别做了{冤大头}还不知道。
ctx.en: When buying a flat, compare a lot of offers, or you may end up overpaying without even knowing it.

bad.s: 他头很大，大家都叫他{冤大头}。
bad.en: (meant: he has a big head, so everyone calls him 'big head')
bad.why: It says nothing about the size of anyone's head; it is the person who gets tricked into paying too much.

bad.s: 谢谢你请客，你真是个{冤大头}！
bad.en: (meant: thanks for treating us, you're so generous!)
bad.why: It mocks someone as a gullible sucker; said as thanks for a treat it is an insult, not praise.

cards.r: dǎ zhǒng liǎn chōng pàng zi
cards.mean: to keep up a show beyond one's means just to save face
cards.lit: to slap your own face until it swells, so you look plump and well fed

use.how: Used as a predicate, often in advice with 别、何必: 没钱就别打肿脸充胖子。 Said of spending or promising beyond one's real means to look rich or capable.

near.diff: 爱面子 is caring about face in general; 打肿脸充胖子 is the specific act of pretending to money or ability you lack, at your own cost.

cards.cue: A friend on a modest salary insists on paying for a lavish banquet for ten people, then lives on instant noodles for the rest of the month. What did he do?

ctx.s: 没钱就说没钱，别{打肿脸充胖子}。
ctx.en: If you don't have the money, just say so. Don't pretend you can afford it.

ctx.s: 他工资不高，却非要买名牌包送女朋友，这不是{打肿脸充胖子}吗？
ctx.en: He doesn't earn much, yet he insists on buying his girlfriend a designer bag. Isn't that living beyond his means just for show?

ctx.s: 为了在同学会上有面子，他借钱租了一辆豪车，真是{打肿脸充胖子}。
ctx.en: To look good at the class reunion he borrowed money to rent a luxury car, a show he couldn't really afford.

ctx.s: 这么难的活儿你干不了就直说，何必{打肿脸充胖子}？
ctx.en: If a job this hard is beyond you, just say so. Why pretend you can do it?

ctx.s: 我们公司规模小，展会上没必要{打肿脸充胖子}，租那么大的展位。
ctx.en: We're a small company; there's no need to put on a show at the trade fair by renting such a big stand.

ctx.s: 婚礼办得那么排场，其实是{打肿脸充胖子}，到现在还在还债。
ctx.en: The wedding was so lavish, but it was all for show: they're still paying off the debts.

bad.s: 他最近吃得太多，{打肿脸充胖子}了。
bad.en: (meant: he has been eating too much lately and put on weight)
bad.why: It has nothing to do with gaining weight; it means pretending to be richer or more capable than you are.

bad.s: 他很有钱，所以请大家吃饭就是{打肿脸充胖子}。
bad.en: (meant: being rich, he showed off by treating everyone to dinner)
bad.why: It only applies when someone acts beyond their real means; a rich man treating his friends is not straining to keep up a show.

cards.mean: to suffer a loss one cannot complain about
cards.lit: to swallow a loss in silence, unable to speak of it

use.how: Verb-object phrase, often 吃了个哑巴亏 or 只能吃哑巴亏. Said of a loss you cannot complain about or claim back: no proof, no recourse, or partly your own fault.

near.diff: 背黑锅 is taking the blame for someone else's fault; 吃哑巴亏 is suffering a loss you are in no position to protest.

cards.cue: You paid a deposit in cash with no receipt, and now the landlord denies ever receiving it. There is nothing you can prove or do. What has happened to you?

ctx.s: 没签合同，钱要不回来，只能{吃哑巴亏}了。
ctx.en: There was no contract, so I can't get the money back. I just have to swallow the loss.

ctx.s: 网上买的东西是假的，店铺已经关了，我{吃了个哑巴亏}。
ctx.en: What I bought online was fake and the shop has already closed. I've been cheated with no comeback.

ctx.s: 这件事你一定要留好证据，别到时候{吃哑巴亏}。
ctx.en: Make sure you keep evidence of this, or you'll end up taking a loss you can't do anything about.

ctx.s: 他明知道功劳被同事抢了，可又说不出口，只好{吃了这个哑巴亏}。
ctx.en: He knew his colleague had taken the credit, but he couldn't bring himself to say so and had to swallow it.

ctx.s: “你为什么不去投诉？”“当初是我自己没看清条款，只能{吃这个哑巴亏}。”
ctx.en: "Why don't you complain?" "I didn't read the terms properly myself, so I just have to take the loss."

ctx.s: 小企业被大客户拖欠货款，往往{吃了哑巴亏}也不敢声张。
ctx.en: When big clients pay small firms late, the small firms often suffer in silence and don't dare make a fuss.

bad.s: 他被骗了以后马上报警，还上了新闻，真是{吃了哑巴亏}。
bad.en: (meant: after being cheated he went to the police and was on the news; what a loss)
bad.why: The point is that you cannot speak up or seek redress; someone who went to the police and the press did not suffer in silence.

bad.s: 他{吃哑巴亏}了我。
bad.en: (meant: he made me suffer a loss I couldn't complain about)
bad.why: The subject is the one who suffers, and it takes no object; say ta rang wo chile ge yaba kui (he left me with a loss I couldn't protest).

cards.mean: to switch to a new field late, without formal training
cards.lit: to leave home to become a monk halfway along life's road

story.text: Chujia, 'leaving home', is the Buddhist term for giving up family life to become a monk or nun. Someone who took this step as an adult, after years of ordinary life, rather than entering a temple young, was said to have left home halfway along the road. The phrase was later applied to anyone who takes up a trade or field late, without a grounding in it from the start.
story.source: From the Buddhist term 出家 (to become a monk or nun)

use.how: Used as a predicate or adverbial: 我是半路出家, 半路出家学画画. Said of someone who came to a field late, often modestly about oneself.

near.diff: 门外汉 is an outsider who knows little of the field; 半路出家 is someone now working in it who simply started late, without formal training.

cards.cue: A successful pastry chef explains that she trained as an accountant and only started baking at thirty-five, teaching herself from videos. How does she describe her path?

ctx.s: 我是{半路出家}，以前是学会计的，现在做设计。
ctx.en: I came to this late; I studied accounting and now I work in design.

ctx.s: 他三十多岁才{半路出家}学编程，现在已经是技术骨干了。
ctx.en: He only switched to programming in his thirties, and now he's one of the key engineers.

ctx.s: 别看她是{半路出家}，画得比科班出身的还好。
ctx.en: She may have taken up painting late, but she paints better than people who trained at art school.

ctx.s: “您是专业学音乐的吗？”“不是，我是{半路出家}，自己摸索着学的。”
ctx.en: "Did you study music professionally?" "No, I came to it late and taught myself."

ctx.s: 很多优秀的作家都是{半路出家}，原来的职业五花八门。
ctx.en: Many fine writers came to writing late; their earlier jobs were all kinds of things.

ctx.s: 他知道{半路出家}的人基础不扎实，所以每天都比别人多练两个小时。
ctx.en: He knew that those who switch late lack a solid grounding, so every day he practised two hours more than everyone else.

bad.s: 我们开车去旅游，车坏了，只好{半路出家}。
bad.en: (meant: we were driving on holiday, the car broke down and we had to turn back halfway)
bad.why: It is not about a journey; it means taking up a field or trade late, without formal training.

bad.s: 他从小就学钢琴，后来成了钢琴家，是{半路出家}。
bad.en: (meant: he learned the piano from childhood and became a pianist)
bad.why: It only fits someone who came to the field late; a pianist trained from childhood is the opposite: keban chushen (professionally trained).

cards.mean: to have high standards but little ability to meet them
cards.lit: the eyes are high, the hands are low

use.how: Used as a predicate: 他这个人眼高手低, 有点眼高手低. Criticises someone, often a beginner, who judges or aims high and looks down on modest work but cannot deliver themselves.

near.diff: 好高骛远 is aiming at goals far beyond reach; 眼高手低 stresses the gap between one's judgement and one's actual skill.

cards.cue: A new graduate criticises every report the team writes and turns down simple tasks, but his own first report is full of mistakes. What is his problem?

ctx.s: 他评论别人头头是道，自己一做就错，真是{眼高手低}。
ctx.en: He criticises others very convincingly, but the moment he does it himself he gets it wrong. Great standards, no skill.

ctx.s: 有些刚毕业的学生{眼高手低}，小事不愿做，大事又做不好。
ctx.en: Some new graduates aim too high for their ability: they won't do small jobs and can't do big ones well.

ctx.s: 我学画画的时候也{眼高手低}，看得出好坏，就是画不出来。
ctx.en: When I was learning to paint I had the same problem: I could tell good from bad, I just couldn't paint it.

ctx.s: 面试官最怕招到{眼高手低}的人。
ctx.en: What interviewers fear most is hiring someone whose standards outrun their ability.

ctx.s: “新来的小李怎么样？”“人挺聪明，就是有点{眼高手低}，得让他从基础做起。”
ctx.en: "How's the new guy, Xiao Li?" "Bright enough, but his ambitions outrun his skills. He needs to start from the basics."

ctx.s: 写作要多动笔，光看不练，就容易{眼高手低}。
ctx.en: To write well you have to write a lot; if you only read and never practise, your judgement will outstrip your skill.

bad.s: 他眼光很好，挑的东西都很漂亮，真是{眼高手低}。
bad.en: (meant: he has excellent taste and everything he picks is lovely)
bad.why: It is criticism: high standards with poor ability to meet them, not praise for good taste.

bad.s: 他{眼高手低}了这项工作。
bad.en: (meant: he looked down on this task and did it badly)
bad.why: It describes a person's failing and takes no object; use it of the person: ta zhege ren yan gao shou di.

cards.mean: a hard worker who toils on without complaint
cards.lit: the old yellow ox, the draught animal that ploughs the fields year after year

use.how: A noun: 是…的老黄牛, 像老黄牛一样, also 老黄牛精神. Praises someone, often long-serving, who works hard and steadily without complaint or seeking credit.

near.diff: 挑大梁 is taking the central role; 老黄牛 is the steady, uncomplaining worker, who need not be in charge or in the spotlight.

cards.cue: At a retirement party, a manager praises a clerk who for thirty years came in early, took on every dull job and never once asked for promotion. What was the clerk?

ctx.s: 张师傅是我们厂里的{老黄牛}，三十年没请过一天假。
ctx.en: Master Zhang is our factory's faithful workhorse; he hasn't taken a day off in thirty years.

ctx.s: 我爸一辈子像{老黄牛}一样干活，从来不喊累。
ctx.en: My dad worked like an ox all his life and never once complained of being tired.

ctx.s: 他不爱说话，也不争名利，大家都说他是个{老黄牛}。
ctx.en: He doesn't say much and never chases fame or gain; everyone says he's a real workhorse.

ctx.s: 公司不能只靠几个{老黄牛}撑着，也得给他们涨工资啊。
ctx.en: The company can't just rely on a few uncomplaining hard workers to keep it going; it has to give them a raise too.

ctx.s: “这次评优秀员工，你推荐谁？”“我推荐老刘，他是部门里真正的{老黄牛}。”
ctx.en: "Who do you recommend for employee of the year?" "Lao Liu. He's the one in our department who really keeps quietly working."

ctx.s: 这种埋头苦干、任劳任怨的{老黄牛}精神，值得我们学习。
ctx.en: This spirit of the patient ox, working hard without complaint, is something we should all learn from.

bad.s: 他每天上班都偷懒，真是个{老黄牛}。
bad.en: (meant: he slacks off at work every day, slow as an ox)
bad.why: It praises a hard, uncomplaining worker; for dawdling at work use mo yanggong.

bad.s: 我爷爷已经九十岁了，是个{老黄牛}。
bad.en: (meant: my grandfather is ninety, a very old man)
bad.why: Lao here is part of the image, not a comment on age; it praises tireless work, not being old.

cards.mean: someone who always sides with whoever is stronger
cards.lit: grass growing on top of a wall, bending whichever way the wind blows

use.how: Noun, usually after 是、当、做 or 像: 他就是个墙头草。 Said of someone with no stand of their own who follows whoever has power or is winning.

near.diff: 脚踩两只船 secretly keeps two options open at once, often in love; 墙头草 openly switches to whichever side is stronger.

cards.cue: In every office dispute Lao Zhang agrees with whoever seems to be winning, and changes his view the moment the boss's mood changes. What is he?

ctx.s: 他就是个{墙头草}，谁有权就听谁的。
ctx.en: He just goes whichever way the wind blows; he listens to whoever has the power.

ctx.s: 经理一换人，他马上就改口了，真是{墙头草}。
ctx.en: As soon as the manager was replaced he changed his tune. What a weathervane.

ctx.s: “你到底支持哪一边？”“我不想当{墙头草}，我只支持我认为对的。”
ctx.en: "Which side are you actually on?" "I don't want to be a turncoat; I'll back whatever I think is right."

ctx.s: 开会时谁的声音大，小王就跟着谁说，活像一棵{墙头草}。
ctx.en: In meetings Xiao Wang echoes whoever is loudest, just like grass bending in the wind.

ctx.s: 做人要有自己的立场，别做{墙头草}。
ctx.en: You should have a position of your own; don't just side with whoever is winning.

ctx.s: 那些{墙头草}，你得势时围着你转，你一失势就全跑了。
ctx.en: Those fair-weather types swarm round you while you're on top and vanish the moment you fall.

bad.s: 我在公司只是个{墙头草}，没人注意我。
bad.en: (meant: I'm a nobody at the company; no one notices me)
bad.why: It does not mean an insignificant person; it means someone who sways to whichever side is stronger.

bad.s: 他总是{墙头草}老板。
bad.en: (meant: he always sides with the boss)
bad.why: It is a noun and cannot take an object like a verb; say ta shi ge qiangtoucao, or ta zong gen zhe laoban shuo.

cards.mean: someone with a friendly smile and a vicious heart
cards.lit: a tiger with a smiling face

use.how: Noun, usually 是个笑面虎. Said of a person who is all smiles and politeness to your face but schemes against you behind your back.

near.diff: 白眼狼 is someone who repays kindness with ingratitude; 笑面虎 hides hostility behind a pleasant smile.

cards.cue: Your new manager smiles and praises you in every meeting, but you later learn he has been quietly running you down to the director. What is he?

ctx.s: 别看他整天笑眯眯的，其实是个{笑面虎}。
ctx.en: Don't be fooled by his constant smile; underneath he's a wolf in sheep's clothing.

ctx.s: 跟{笑面虎}打交道，千万别把心里话都说出来。
ctx.en: When you deal with someone who smiles but means you harm, never tell them what you really think.

ctx.s: “新来的主任人挺好的吧？”“小心点，听说是个{笑面虎}。”
ctx.en: "The new director seems nice, doesn't he?" "Be careful, I hear he's all smiles and knives."

ctx.s: 他当面夸我方案做得好，背后却跟老板说我能力不行，真是只{笑面虎}。
ctx.en: To my face he praised my proposal, behind my back he told the boss I wasn't up to it. A real smiling tiger.

ctx.s: 有些{笑面虎}比当面骂你的人可怕多了。
ctx.en: Some people who smile while they plot against you are far scarier than those who shout at you openly.

ctx.s: 小说里的反派是个{笑面虎}，对谁都客客气气，暗地里却害了好几个人。
ctx.en: The villain of the novel smiles politely at everyone while secretly destroying several people.

bad.s: 我奶奶是个{笑面虎}，总是笑着给我们做好吃的。
bad.en: (meant: my grandma is always smiling and cooking for us)
bad.why: It is an insult for someone whose smile hides malice, not a word for a cheerful, kind person.

bad.s: 他平时很凶，可是一看到孩子就变成了{笑面虎}。
bad.en: (meant: he is usually fierce but turns gentle around children)
bad.why: It does not mean a tough person turning soft; it means someone friendly on the outside and vicious inside.

cards.mean: to smooth over a dispute without regard to who is right
cards.lit: to stir watery mud, mixing everything into one soft mess

use.how: Verb-object phrase, often after 别、只会、不能; can split (和了半天稀泥). Criticises a mediator, often a superior, who glosses over a conflict instead of judging it.

near.diff: 打圆场 eases an awkward moment so nobody loses face, usually a kindness; 和稀泥 dodges the question of who is right in a real dispute.

cards.cue: One employee took credit for another's work. The manager just says 'you're both valuable, let's all get along' and refuses to look into what happened. What is he doing?

ctx.s: 这件事谁对谁错很清楚，你别{和稀泥}。
ctx.en: It's obvious who is right and who is wrong here, so don't try to fudge it.

ctx.s: 两个人吵到经理那儿，经理却只会{和稀泥}，谁也不得罪。
ctx.en: The two of them took their quarrel to the manager, but all he did was paper over it so as not to offend anyone.

ctx.s: “你们俩都有错，各退一步吧。”“明明是他先动手的，你这不是{和稀泥}吗？”
ctx.en: "You're both at fault, meet each other halfway." "He clearly hit me first. Aren't you just glossing over it?"

ctx.s: 遇到原则问题，当领导的不能{和稀泥}。
ctx.en: When a matter of principle comes up, a leader can't just smooth it over.

ctx.s: 老师{和了半天稀泥}，最后欺负人的同学连句道歉都没说。
ctx.en: The teacher spent ages smoothing things over, and in the end the bully didn't even say sorry.

ctx.s: 邻居之间的纠纷，居委会总是{和稀泥}，问题一直没解决。
ctx.en: The neighbourhood committee always fudges disputes between neighbours, so the problem never gets solved.

bad.s: 聚会的气氛很尴尬，我讲了个笑话{和稀泥}，大家都笑了。
bad.en: (meant: the party was awkward, so I told a joke to ease the tension)
bad.why: Kindly easing an awkward moment is da yuanchang; this idiom criticises glossing over who is right in a real dispute.

bad.s: 他是个很会{和稀泥}的好法官，大家都佩服他。
bad.en: (meant: he is a fair judge, good at settling disputes, and everyone admires him)
bad.why: It is always criticism of avoiding right and wrong, never praise; a judge admired for fairness keeps yi wan shui duan ping.

cards.r: bù shì shěng yóu de dēng
cards.mean: a troublesome person who is not easy to deal with
cards.lit: not a lamp that is sparing with its oil

use.how: Predicate about a person, usually with 可、也、都 or 什么: 他可不是省油的灯。 A warning that someone makes trouble or is a tough opponent who won't be pushed around.

near.diff: 有两下子 admires real skill; 不是省油的灯 warns that someone is a handful or hard to get the better of.

cards.cue: You warn a colleague about a new client: he argues over every clause, goes over people's heads to complain and never lets anything drop. What do you say about him?

ctx.s: 这孩子可{不是省油的灯}，一天到晚惹事。
ctx.en: This kid is a real handful; he's in trouble from morning to night.

ctx.s: 小心点，对方的律师也{不是省油的灯}。
ctx.en: Watch out, the other side's lawyer is no pushover either.

ctx.s: “她会乖乖听你的？”“想得美，她可{不是什么省油的灯}。”
ctx.en: "She'll just do as you say?" "Dream on. She's anything but easy to handle."

ctx.s: 这次的几个竞争对手都{不是省油的灯}，我们得好好准备。
ctx.en: None of our rivals this time are easy opponents, so we need to prepare properly.

ctx.s: 新来的那位客户{不是省油的灯}，合同改了七八遍还不满意。
ctx.en: That new client is hard work: the contract has been revised seven or eight times and he's still not happy.

ctx.s: 别以为他老实好欺负，真闹起来，他也{不是省油的灯}。
ctx.en: Don't think he's a soft touch because he's quiet; once things kick off he's no easy customer.

bad.s: 她工作又认真又能干，真{不是省油的灯}！
bad.en: (meant: she is so conscientious and capable, a real asset!)
bad.why: It warns that someone is troublesome or hard to handle; to praise ability say you liang xiazi or hen nenggan.

bad.s: 他花钱大手大脚，{不是省油的灯}。
bad.en: (meant: he spends money freely)
bad.why: Despite the image it is not about spending or wasting money; it describes a person who causes trouble or is hard to deal with.

cards.r: rè guō shàng de mǎ yǐ
cards.mean: frantic with anxiety and not knowing what to do
cards.lit: ants running about on a hot wok

use.how: A comparison, usually 急得像热锅上的蚂蚁 or 跟热锅上的蚂蚁似的. Describes a person pacing and fretting helplessly in a crisis.

near.diff: 火烧眉毛 says the situation is desperately urgent; 热锅上的蚂蚁 describes the person's frantic, helpless state.

cards.cue: Your flight leaves in an hour and your passport is missing. You keep pacing the flat and opening the same drawers again and again. What are you like?

ctx.s: 孩子找不到了，她急得像{热锅上的蚂蚁}。
ctx.en: Her child had gone missing and she was beside herself with worry.

ctx.s: 考试快开始了，准考证还没找到，我简直成了{热锅上的蚂蚁}。
ctx.en: The exam was about to start and I still couldn't find my admission ticket. I was frantic.

ctx.s: “你怎么在门口走来走去的？”“手术还没结束，我心里跟{热锅上的蚂蚁}似的。”
ctx.en: "Why are you pacing by the door?" "The operation still isn't over. I'm going out of my mind."

ctx.s: 资金一断，老板急得像{热锅上的蚂蚁}，到处打电话借钱。
ctx.en: When the money ran out the boss was in a frenzy, phoning everyone he knew for a loan.

ctx.s: 航班突然取消，候机厅里的旅客个个都像{热锅上的蚂蚁}。
ctx.en: When the flight was suddenly cancelled, every passenger in the lounge was in a frantic state.

ctx.s: 报告明天就要交，电脑却坏了，他像{热锅上的蚂蚁}一样在屋里转来转去。
ctx.en: The report was due the next day and his computer died; he paced round the room like a cat on hot bricks.

bad.s: 夏天太热了，我们像{热锅上的蚂蚁}一样出了很多汗。
bad.en: (meant: it was so hot in summer that we sweated a lot)
bad.why: It describes frantic anxiety in a crisis, not feeling physically hot.

bad.s: 他工作很忙，每天像{热锅上的蚂蚁}一样努力。
bad.en: (meant: he is busy and works hard every day)
bad.why: It means helpless panic, not busy hard work; for diligence a different image such as lao huangniu fits.

cards.mean: to give up on oneself after failing and let things get worse
cards.lit: the jar is cracked already, so you might as well smash it

use.how: Verb phrase, often after 干脆、索性、别: 别破罐子破摔。 Said of someone who, after a failure or a ruined reputation, stops trying and makes things worse.

near.diff: 自暴自弃 is the bookish word for giving up on oneself; 破罐子破摔 is colloquial and stresses 'it's ruined already, so why care'.

cards.cue: After failing two exams a student stops going to class altogether: 'My grades are wrecked anyway, so why bother?' What is he doing?

ctx.s: 一次没考好不要紧，千万别{破罐子破摔}。
ctx.en: One bad exam doesn't matter; whatever you do, don't give up on yourself.

ctx.s: 他觉得反正名声已经坏了，干脆{破罐子破摔}。
ctx.en: He figured his reputation was ruined anyway, so he stopped caring altogether.

ctx.s: 减肥第一天就吃了块蛋糕，算了，今天就{破罐子破摔}吧！
ctx.en: First day of my diet and I've already had cake. Oh well, today's a write-off anyway!

ctx.s: 父母越骂他，他越{破罐子破摔}，成绩一落千丈。
ctx.en: The more his parents scolded him, the more he just stopped trying, and his grades plummeted.

ctx.s: 公司已经亏成这样了，老板却没有{破罐子破摔}，而是咬牙从头再来。
ctx.en: The company had already lost so much, yet instead of letting it all go to ruin the boss gritted his teeth and started again from scratch.

ctx.s: 很多人犯过一次错就{破罐子破摔}，其实只要改正，机会还很多。
ctx.en: Many people give up on themselves after one mistake, when in fact there are plenty of chances if they put it right.

bad.s: 计划失败了，大家决定{破罐子破摔}，换个方法重新来。
bad.en: (meant: the plan failed, so we decided to try again another way)
bad.why: It means giving up and letting things get worse, the opposite of starting over with a new approach.

bad.s: 他很勇敢，敢{破罐子破摔}，最后成功了。
bad.en: (meant: he bravely staked everything and succeeded)
bad.why: It is not bold risk-taking (that is po fu chen zhou); it is giving up on oneself, the opposite of fighting on to win.

cards.r: hǎo le shāng bā wàng le téng
cards.mean: to forget a painful lesson once the trouble has passed
cards.lit: once the wound has healed into a scar, you forget how much it hurt

use.how: Predicate, often with 别、又、总是: 你可别好了伤疤忘了疼。 Criticises someone who repeats a mistake once its bad consequences have faded.

near.diff: 重蹈覆辙 states that a past mistake is being repeated, often in writing; 好了伤疤忘了疼 blames forgetting the pain as soon as it eases.

cards.cue: Last year your friend lost a lot of money on a get-rich-quick scheme and swore 'never again'. Now he's excited about a new one. What is he doing?

ctx.s: 上次喝酒喝进了医院，你可别{好了伤疤忘了疼}。
ctx.en: Last time drinking landed you in hospital; don't forget that lesson just because you've recovered.

ctx.s: 他刚还完信用卡，又开始乱花钱，真是{好了伤疤忘了疼}。
